[{:db/id 17592186539387 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c8e42dd-1135-55d6-baea-5eaf5e395812" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{182 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{9}" :db/id 17592186539362} {:answer/id #uuid "5775d9e0-17da-5f4b-97d4-d8327fe13f79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{671 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{6}" :db/id 17592186539368} {:answer/id #uuid "bee804f0-fe47-54f2-82b3-1ab225bbaa16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{3}" :db/id 17592186539381} {:answer/id #uuid "c8511436-e484-5251-a621-0417962a64ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{182 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{3}" :db/id 17592186539383} {:answer/id #uuid "f7a1ff94-668d-56c9-ab15-77c13bfdd79a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- \frac{182 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{9}" :db/id 17592186539391}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539362} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a87ecd3-6574-5e98-aac6-eaeb2a2a41af" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539361}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dc1cd88b-9881-56a3-9ef5-53708f7c4b33" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}$ and $v=xy,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 4{x}^{2},\,5\le xy\le 6\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,5\le v\le 6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{{v}^{2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{4}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\,{|}_{5}^{6} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{9}\cdot (216-125) \\  & =\frac{182\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186539398 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b62b53-1b76-5884-8cf6-e623e6a2f279" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "89.3\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539394} {:answer/id #uuid "1d6d3790-da14-581b-85b9-f63924341cef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "89.8\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539400} {:answer/id #uuid "49ad23b9-5753-5821-bf10-fcf46d63b245" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "89.9\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539414} {:answer/id #uuid "4e0087ee-6487-5333-81b9-0c1398c381ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "89.6\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539416} {:answer/id #uuid "8e62ca35-4a8a-52bf-a4f8-7c4ea42efb76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90.0\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539433}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539400} :answer-field/id #uuid "b807e3c0-f519-5770-bffe-d3aeea20ea64" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539442}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1a0728d4-a0d3-515f-805e-eb1a7d3c019c" :question/problem "A disinfectant reservoir in a water treatment facility can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of disinfectant solution with $10\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved disinfectant. A more concentrated solution with concentration $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $25\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/retired true :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir minus the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of disinfectant enters the reservoir at a rate of $25\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *disinfectant* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =12.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $25\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $20\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=60+25t-20t=5(12+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min},$ *disinfectant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{4Q}{12+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12.5-\frac{4Q}{12+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{12+t}\,Q=12.5.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 4/(12+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡|12+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(12+t)^{4}} \\  & =(12+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(12+t)^{4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(12+t)^{4}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{12+t}\,Q) & =(12+t)^{4}\cdot 12.5 \\ (12+t)^{4}\frac{dQ}{dt}+4(12+t)^{3}Q & =12.5(12+t)^{4} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{4}) & =12.5(12+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{4})\,dt & =\int 12.5(12+t)^{4}\,dt \\ Q(12+t)^{4} & =12.5\cdot \frac{1}{5}(12+t)^{5}+C \\ Q(t) & =2.5(12+t)+\frac{C}{(12+t)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $10\,\text{lb}$ of disinfectant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 2.5(12+0)+\frac{C}{(12+0)^{4}} & =10 \\ 30+\frac{C}{(12)^{4}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{12}^{4}} & =-20 \\ C & =-20(12)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2.5(12+t)-\frac{20(12)^{4}}{(12+t)^{4}} \\  & =2.5(12+t)-20{\left(\frac{12}{12+t}\right)}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 60+25{t}_{o}-20{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 60+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =120 \\ {t}_{o} & =24\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(24) & =2.5(12+24)-20{\left(\frac{12}{12+24}\right)}^{4} \\  & =90-20{\left(\frac{12}{36}\right)}^{4} \\  & ≈89.8\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186539401 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3544b068-279b-57e6-9f38-0c9eaa23d33f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "235.5\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539406} {:answer/id #uuid "69907d51-3bf1-5b65-bbb2-ae831146ccb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "222.2\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539422} {:answer/id #uuid "872c8957-d06f-5407-86a5-616dbaa82761" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "117.7\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539430} {:answer/id #uuid "d8fcf795-dfb5-51ba-9ea4-76d781abc0a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "246.4\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539450} {:answer/id #uuid "e82e736f-6d11-5a2d-83f2-a27bd4f7db0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "294.4\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539454}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539406} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f10b853-d565-5f3f-8bc1-e376bfffca18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539417}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "21bb65fc-94da-5d56-9b2a-2fe8f762fdb9" :question/problem "A disinfectant reservoir in a water treatment facility can hold up to $368\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $300\,\text{gal}$ of disinfectant solution with $160\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved disinfectant. A more concentrated solution with concentration $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/retired true :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir minus the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ of disinfectant enters the reservoir at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *disinfectant* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =16\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $300\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $20\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=300+20t-12t=8(37.5+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *disinfectant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{1.5Q}{37.5+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =16-\frac{1.5Q}{37.5+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1.5}{37.5+t}\,Q=16.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 1.5/(37.5+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{1.5\operatorname{ln}⁡|37.5+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(37.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =(37.5+t)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(37.5+t)^{1.5}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(37.5+t)^{1.5}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1.5}{37.5+t}\,Q) & =(37.5+t)^{1.5}\cdot 16 \\ (37.5+t)^{1.5}\frac{dQ}{dt}+1.5(37.5+t)^{0.5}Q & =16(37.5+t)^{1.5} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(37.5+t)^{1.5}) & =16(37.5+t)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(37.5+t)^{1.5})\,dt & =\int 16(37.5+t)^{1.5}\,dt \\ Q(37.5+t)^{1.5} & =16\cdot \frac{1}{2.5}(37.5+t)^{2.5}+C \\ Q(t) & =6.4(37.5+t)+\frac{C}{(37.5+t)^{1.5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $160\,\text{lb}$ of disinfectant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=160,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =160 \\ 6.4(37.5+0)+\frac{C}{(37.5+0)^{1.5}} & =160 \\ 240+\frac{C}{(37.5)^{1.5}} & =160 \\ \frac{C}{{37.5}^{1.5}} & =-80 \\ C & =-80(37.5)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =6.4(37.5+t)-\frac{80(37.5)^{1.5}}{(37.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =6.4(37.5+t)-80{\left(\frac{37.5}{37.5+t}\right)}^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $368\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=368$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =368 \\ 300+20{t}_{o}-12{t}_{o} & =368 \\ 300+8{t}_{o} & =368 \\ 8{t}_{o} & =68 \\ {t}_{o} & =8.5\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(8.5) & =6.4(37.5+8.5)-80{\left(\frac{37.5}{37.5+8.5}\right)}^{1.5} \\  & =294.4-80{\left(\frac{37.5}{46}\right)}^{1.5} \\  & ≈235.5\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186539408 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09aa09e5-f47d-5621-9398-dc8978b0d87a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "316.3\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539393} {:answer/id #uuid "3c471766-6b4e-5806-89be-2166ca930256" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "328.0\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539409} {:answer/id #uuid "89c88c07-7e92-5645-a2bb-e6beb66e7182" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "301.0\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539431} {:answer/id #uuid "b9a76597-8ded-5bde-a591-93a2815617ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "287.6\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539443} {:answer/id #uuid "d57c8381-a0fe-5352-bcb4-fdc5674d137c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "265.7\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539448}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539431} :answer-field/id #uuid "b68e3566-38f2-5496-a173-8df05cbc7a77" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539441}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3a39de0b-a8fb-57f4-97a8-3f35b38b481a" :question/problem "A saline reservoir for a medical research lab can hold up to $492\,\text{gal}$ of solution. First, note that a solution containing $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =10\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}

The reservoir initially contains $213\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $9\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=213+15t-9t=6(35.5+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{6(35.5+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$

$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =10-\frac{1.5Q}{35.5+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1.5}{35.5+t}\,Q=10.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 1.5/(35.5+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{1.5\operatorname{ln}⁡|35.5+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(35.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =(35.5+t)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}

$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(35.5+t)^{1.5})\,dt & =\int 10(35.5+t)^{1.5}\,dt \\ Q(35.5+t)^{1.5} & =10\cdot \frac{1}{2.5}(35.5+t)^{2.5}+C \\ Q(t) & =4(35.5+t)+\frac{C}{(35.5+t)^{1.5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $\frac{142}{3}\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=\frac{142}{3},$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =\frac{142}{3} \\ 4(35.5+0)+\frac{C}{(35.5+0)^{1.5}} & =\frac{142}{3} \\ 142+\frac{C}{(35.5)^{1.5}} & =\frac{142}{3} \\ \frac{C}{(35.5)^{1.5}} & =-\frac{284}{3} \\ C & =-\frac{284}{3}(35.5)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4(35.5+t)-\frac{\frac{284}{3}(35.5)^{1.5}}{(35.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =4(35.5+t)-\frac{284}{3}{\left(\frac{35.5}{35.5+t}\right)}^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =492 \\ 213+15{t}_{o}-9{t}_{o} & =492 \\ 213+6{t}_{o} & =492 \\ 6{t}_{o} & =279 \\ {t}_{o} & =46.5\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $32\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $8\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $6\,\text{gal/min}.$

$$

$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{2(16+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(16+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{2(16+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{6Q}{2(16+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{16+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =4-\frac{3Q}{16+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{16+t}\,Q=4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(16+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|16+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(16+t)^{3}} \\  & =(16+t)^{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =1(16+t)-\frac{12(16)^{3}}{(16+t)^{3}} \\  & =1(16+t)-12{\left(\frac{16}{16+t}\right)}^{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Initially, it contains $110\,\text{gal}$ of saline solution with $55\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A more concentrated saline solution with concentration $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $25\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/retired true :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $1.0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $25\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $110\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $25\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $20\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=110+25t-20t=5(22+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(22+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(22+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(22+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{5(22+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{4Q}{22+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =25-\frac{4Q}{22+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{22+t}\,Q=25.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 4/(22+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡|22+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(22+t)^{4}} \\  & =(22+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(22+t)^{4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(22+t)^{4}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{22+t}\,Q) & =(22+t)^{4}\cdot 25 \\ (22+t)^{4}\frac{dQ}{dt}+4(22+t)^{3}Q & =25(22+t)^{4} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(22+t)^{4}) & =25(22+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(22+t)^{4})\,dt & =\int 25(22+t)^{4}\,dt \\ Q(22+t)^{4} & =25\cdot \frac{1}{5}(22+t)^{5}+C \\ Q(t) & =5(22+t)+\frac{C}{(22+t)^{4}}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =5(22+t)-\frac{55(22)^{4}}{(22+t)^{4}} \\  & =5(22+t)-55{\left(\frac{22}{22+t}\right)}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $290\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=290$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =290 \\ 110+25{t}_{o}-20{t}_{o} & =290 \\ 110+5{t}_{o} & =290 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ {t}_{o} & =36\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(36) & =5(22+36)-55{\left(\frac{22}{22+36}\right)}^{4} \\  & =290-55{\left(\frac{22}{58}\right)}^{4} \\  & ≈288.9\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186539451 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33657fab-2d53-58a0-98a5-5356a1b0e53a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "226.4\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539405} {:answer/id #uuid "481acaa8-6906-5974-ae76-54c5df18a291" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "226.9\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539412} {:answer/id #uuid "49a7b172-e749-59a4-86e1-727a1b566135" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "227.5\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539413} {:answer/id #uuid "a6d6b5ed-3b6b-5ab9-afd8-dc8db825fe1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "228.0\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539436} {:answer/id #uuid "ecee97e7-7992-52dc-9300-131e135e7abf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "227.8\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539456}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539413} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6be6c4b-dcbc-5ac0-a692-8e76768f9b9c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539453}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "df8520ff-a1e4-578f-8153-7bfeb8954209" :question/problem "A nutrient tank for a hydroponic greenhouse can hold up to $342gal$ of solution. $$"} {:db/id 17592186539462 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17d1e1a0-3c64-5ef9-9dbe-759c9e661398" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "386.0\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539395} {:answer/id #uuid "2bf04547-57c3-53c4-840a-33e618532e81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "284.9\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539403} {:answer/id #uuid "5acc0bd1-19cd-5dac-ac79-38ebff3903c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "588.0\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539420} {:answer/id #uuid "797eee29-2209-55c5-906c-e8f2d054d896" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "458.1\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539427} {:answer/id #uuid "a62cbaf9-65b9-5cb1-860f-98a4438ffabe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "273.7\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186539435}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539395} :answer-field/id #uuid "f243c2a4-f8d5-5f1f-93bf-3f804ba469a6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539457}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ff0fe97f-83da-58e7-9a2a-1f41369f6103" :question/problem "A saline reservoir for a medical research lab can hold up to $490\,\text{gal}$ of solution. Initially, it contains $315\,\text{gal}$ of saline solution with $126\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A more concentrated saline solution with concentration $1.2\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $5\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/retired true :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the reservoir minus the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $1.2\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.2\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.2\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =18\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $315\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $5\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=315+15t-5t=10(31.5+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{10(31.5+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $5\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{10(31.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(5\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{10(31.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{5Q}{10(31.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{0.5Q}{31.5+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =18-\frac{0.5Q}{31.5+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{0.5}{31.5+t}\,Q=18.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 0.5/(31.5+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{0.5\operatorname{ln}⁡|31.5+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(31.5+t)^{0.5}} \\  & =(31.5+t)^{0.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(31.5+t)^{0.5}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(31.5+t)^{0.5}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{0.5}{31.5+t}\,Q) & =(31.5+t)^{0.5}\cdot 18 \\ (31.5+t)^{0.5}\frac{dQ}{dt}+0.5(31.5+t)^{-0.5}Q & =18(31.5+t)^{0.5} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(31.5+t)^{0.5}) & =18(31.5+t)^{0.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(31.5+t)^{0.5})\,dt & =\int 18(31.5+t)^{0.5}\,dt \\ Q(31.5+t)^{0.5} & =18\cdot \frac{1}{1.5}(31.5+t)^{1.5}+C \\ Q(t) & =12(31.5+t)+\frac{C}{(31.5+t)^{0.5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $126\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=126,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =126 \\ 12(31.5+0)+\frac{C}{(31.5+0)^{0.5}} & =126 \\ 378+\frac{C}{(31.5)^{0.5}} & =126 \\ \frac{C}{(31.5)^{0.5}} & =-252 \\ C & =-252(31.5)^{0.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =12(31.5+t)-\frac{252(31.5)^{0.5}}{(31.5+t)^{0.5}} \\  & =12(31.5+t)-252{\left(\frac{31.5}{31.5+t}\right)}^{0.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $490\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=490$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =490 \\ 315+15{t}_{o}-5{t}_{o} & =490 \\ 315+10{t}_{o} & =490 \\ 10{t}_{o} & =175 \\ {t}_{o} & =17.5\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(17.5) & =12(31.5+17.5)-252{\left(\frac{31.5}{31.5+17.5}\right)}^{0.5} \\  & =588-252{\left(\frac{31.5}{49}\right)}^{0.5} \\  & ≈386.0\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "75eaed8c-a198-5c3a-b426-50603d367304" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(1-\frac{1}{2}y-\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}})\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539676} {:answer/id #uuid "7f54ff01-aed0-58e9-858f-625c9907586d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}y+1)\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539689} {:answer/id #uuid "89944f1d-1e72-5cb7-b5b1-8e207883c50a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}y-1)\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539709} {:db/id 17592186540025 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e540eb0-8cac-5747-b4e7-b7ccd316406a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{15}" :db/id 17592186539509} {:answer/id #uuid "19977cc3-abaa-5675-a5a2-9c0cb09a3a33" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186539533} {:answer/id #uuid "3f2d1a27-b068-55ec-bdb4-71d7924738b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{15}" :db/id 17592186539592} {:answer/id #uuid "b1c54165-081f-572b-8aab-18d7b5b1b30e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186539782} {:answer/id #uuid "d0b025ce-348b-58ed-829c-e108dbb26644" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186539837}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539533} :answer-field/id #uuid "eefd7b42-cc63-5201-b954-24eada1a35de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186540012}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1404f19f-22e0-51b4-954a-73312901eafa" :question/math-academy-id "q-107142" :question/problem "![](images/92/920aca572a3b6fc828d6c37246b348aa2b017d1bc4e022ea06c12d0fa09ad6ee.png)

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=(1-y)^{2}$ and $y=\sqrt{1-x},$ as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, we write the second function in terms $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{1-x} \\ {y}^{2} & =1-x \\ x & =1-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $f(y)=1-{y}^{2}$ and $g(y)=(1-y)^{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 1-{y}^{2} & =(1-y)^{2} \\ 1-{y}^{2} & =1-2y+{y}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{2}-2y & =0 \\ 2y(y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/02/02e6b4204b1edf682dd332e28830dc84aa0e41d3728c66442d777f6fe9daccfc.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=(1-y)^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=1-{y}^{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([1-{y}^{2}]-[(1-y)^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([1-{y}^{2}]-[1-2y+{y}^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2y-2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =4\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =4\pi ({\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =4\pi ((\frac{1}{3}-0)-(\frac{1}{4}-0)) \\  & =4\pi \left(\frac{1}{12}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186540031 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1853b3af-28f4-5ef9-aad8-03a6eaf50446" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186539528} {:answer/id #uuid "9ee05a02-1be6-5002-8a40-86020d83d578" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{81\pi }{10}" :db/id 17592186539743} {:answer/id #uuid "aedf06dc-11bf-5210-87fb-2324f78a6574" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\pi " :db/id 17592186539777} {:answer/id #uuid "e847bcfd-c659-5ed7-a215-e4e98478c99c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186539872} {:answer/id #uuid "efd08d18-ffa2-5e0a-8532-bcddc6c9bf2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{81\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186539881}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539528} :answer-field/id #uuid "410a3349-db09-5c6c-877b-7b43454d7322" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539947}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1e2fc7b4-11f3-5f1c-807e-b40bd8df74a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-107304" :question/problem "![](images/5e/5eac1b1d21378d64b90fc2463eb7664b30224594ba5d63aa70a7c412097012a0.png)

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=1+y$ and $x=1-2y+{y}^{2},$ as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(y)=1+y$ and $g(y)=1-2y+{y}^{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 1+y & =1-2y+{y}^{2} \\ 3y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y(3-y) & =0 \\ y & =0,3\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions corresponding to our region are $y=0$ and $y=3.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=3.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/84/84e62b99598649ac48d55171b0d6bf7e5d26e38a6ad94c46ef9c89145e60e29a.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=1-2y+{y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=1+y.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}y([1+y]-[1-2y+{y}^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}y(3y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(3{y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (3{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({3\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{3}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{3}) \\  & =2\pi (3(\frac{27}{3}-0)-(\frac{81}{4}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (27-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186540083 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "63c110bb-5316-5161-b14e-6b363f107559" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2-y-\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}})\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539645} {:answer/id #uuid "75eaed8c-a198-5c3a-b426-50603d367304" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(1-\frac{1}{2}y-\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}})\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539676} {:answer/id #uuid "7f54ff01-aed0-58e9-858f-625c9907586d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}y+1)\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539689} {:answer/id #uuid "89944f1d-1e72-5cb7-b5b1-8e207883c50a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}y-1)\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539709} {:answer/id #uuid "b4882823-b7fc-57ca-8289-748a54539d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}+y-2)\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186539790}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539709} :answer-field/id #uuid "0601c164-985b-5dd4-912d-b59e95bef8da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539921}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b0ffc976-87a0-51e6-8ff5-4a0a8b70546a" :question/math-academy-id "q-126325" :question/problem "![](images/b6/b61c628a012f6bde3144254b521e11f8803e089cd7f83f2c19a1255cf22c0e3a.png)

Find an integral expression for the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(y)=\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}$ and $g(y)=-\frac{1}{2}y+1.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ \sqrt{4-{y}^{2}} & =-\frac{1}{2}y+1 \\ 4-{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}-y+1 \\ -\frac{5}{4}{y}^{2}+y+3 & =0 \\ 5{y}^{2}-4y-12 & =0 \\ (5y+6)(y-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/12/122a21e72dc7473cc34ed3ece0325294eadcc86cbe8a5b91e4dfe4be77b369c0.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=-\frac{1}{2}y+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y([\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}]-[-\frac{1}{2}y+1])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}y-1)\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186540100 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d56b3b6-d2ee-5a6a-ac79-f166c602aad7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186539536} {:answer/id #uuid "5bbc6a18-26ef-5ee7-a216-046a93109cdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186539634} {:answer/id #uuid "684d8919-d630-53ec-be88-da83985b9cfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186539650} {:answer/id #uuid "adf72623-7732-5460-b0b6-5cc1011adb27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{6}" :db/id 17592186539775} {:answer/id #uuid "f71975b1-e674-5e94-a227-f47c16e02797" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/id 17592186539894}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186539894} :answer-field/id #uuid "746714c2-cc0f-5a43-9606-b934d8793273" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186539966}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "dba16e2f-f755-5c6f-b25b-801d348b9282" :question/math-academy-id "q-67435" :question/problem "Solve the equation $-\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{1}{x-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{x-1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $4.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{4x-4}{4}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot \left(\frac{x-2}{-4}\right) & =(-4)\cdot \frac{4x-4}{4} \\ x-2 & =-4x+4 \\ x+4x & =4+2 \\ 5x & =6 \\ \left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\cdot (5x) & =\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\cdot (6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\cdot (6) \\ x & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=f(y)={y}^{2},$ and

$$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)=f_y(1,e)i-f_x(1,e)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x^{2} - x y - 3 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(- x - \frac{3 x}{y})\,i-(- 2 x - y - 3 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(1,e)&=(- \left(1\right) - \frac{3 \left(1\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(- 2 \left(1\right) - \left(e\right) - 3 \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(- \frac{3}{e} - 1)\,i-(-5 - e)\,j \\ &=-\left(1 + \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(e + 5\right)\, j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $-\left(1 + \frac{3}{e}\right)\, i+\left(e + 5\right)\, j.$"} {:db/id 17592186540230 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1543914f-316c-5f25-bea9-5cdd64882bbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left(4 - \frac{4}{e}\right)\, i+\left(6 - 4 e\right)\, j" :db/id 17592186540205} {:answer/id #uuid "51347c57-56fd-5985-8234-25791aa98247" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left(6 - 4 e\right)\, i+\left(4 - \frac{4}{e}\right)\, j" :db/id 17592186540223} {:answer/id #uuid "c57ea5cd-e457-5e00-bac3-dca0b7e0b6db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\, i+\left(2 - 4 e\right)\, j" :db/id 17592186540253} {:answer/id #uuid "d9295c28-7e01-5c51-9026-53433bd610a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left(4 - \frac{4}{e}\right)\, i-\left(6 - 4 e\right)\, j" :db/id 17592186540258} {:answer/id #uuid "e19aaae6-85d8-59e4-8696-f5dbf93483d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\left(6 - 4 e\right)\, i+\left(4 - \frac{4}{e}\right)\, j" :db/id 17592186540262}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540205} :answer-field/id #uuid "5bb9392e-0719-5c02-9f00-dcae9268c3d3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186540225}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6983a7a6-901e-55d5-ae50-467a154dc618" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $- x^{2} + 4 x y - 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)}=-5 + 4 e.$ Find a tangent vector to that curve at the point $(1,e).$" :question/worked-solution "First, if we set $f(x,y)=- x^{2} + 4 x y - 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-5 + 4 e.$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,e)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,e)=f_y(1,e)i-f_x(1,e)j

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x^{2} + 4 x y - 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,i-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x^{2} + 4 x y - 4 x \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ &=(4 x - \frac{4 x}{y})\,i-(- 2 x + 4 y - 4 \ln{\left(y \right)})\,j \\ t(1,e)&=(4 \left(1\right) - \frac{4 \left(1\right)}{\left(e\right)})\,i-(- 2 \left(1\right) + 4 \left(e\right) - 4 \ln{\left(\left(e\right) \right)})\,j \\ &=(4 - \frac{4}{e})\,i-(-6 + 4 e)\,j \\ &=\left(4 - \frac{4}{e}\right)\, i+\left(6 - 4 e\right)\, j\end{aligned}

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-2,e)$ can be computed as follows:

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,e^{2})$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(2,e^{2})=f_y(2,e^{2})i-f_x(2,e^{2})j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(2,e^{2}):$

$$

A solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved sugar is pumped into the tank at a rate of $24\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $36\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of sugar $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$\frac{dQ}{dt}=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}.$$
The units of these rates are $\text{kg/min}.$

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which substance enters the tank.
$$\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{in}}&=(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot(24\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\\
&=(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot(24\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\\&=0.96\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which substance exits the tank.
The volume is
$$V(t)=1200+24t-36t=(1200-12t)\,\text{L}.$$
The concentration is $\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\text{kg/L}.$ Hence,
$$\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{out}}&=(36\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\\
&=(36\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\\
&=\frac{36Q}{1200-12t}\,\text{kg/min}=\frac{3Q}{100-t}\,\text{kg/min}.\end{aligned}$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}&=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}\\&=0.96-\frac{3Q}{100-t}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus,
$$\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100-t}Q=0.96.$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.
This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:
$$\begin{aligned}I(t)&=e^{\int 3/(100-t)\,dt}\\&=e^{-3\ln|100-t|}\\&=e^{\ln (100-t)^{-3}}\\&=(100-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}$$
Multiplying both sides by $I(t)=(100-t)^{-3}$ yields
$$\begin{aligned}(100-t)^{-3}\cdot(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{100-t}Q)&=(100-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.96\\

$$\begin{aligned}\int\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100-t)^{-3})\,dt&=\int 0.96(100-t)^{-3}\,dt\\Q(100-t)^{-3}&=0.96\cdot\frac{1}{2}(100-t)^{-2}+C\\Q(t)&=0.48(100-t)+C(100-t)^{3}.\end{aligned}$$
Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.
The initial condition is $Q(0)=22.$ Thus,
$$\begin{aligned}0.48(100-0)+C(100-0)^{3}&=22\\
48+C(100)^{3}&=22\\C(100)^{3}&=-26\\C&=- \frac{13}{500000}.\end{aligned}$$
Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$
$$Q(t)=- \frac{12 t}{25} - \frac{13 \left(100 - t\right)^{3}}{500000} + 48.$$
Writing this in the supplied normalized form gives
$$Q(t)=48(1-\frac{t}{100})-26(1-\frac{t}{100})^{3}.$$

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}x(-4+5x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}(-4x+5{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {(-2{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4})|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2\pi ((-2({4}^{2})+\frac{5}{3}({4}^{3})-\frac{1}{4}({4}^{4}))-(-2+\frac{5}{3}-\frac{1}{4})) \\  & =2\pi \left(\frac{45}{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{45\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186541063 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "88892d02-3412-5492-af0a-49ebe61d9b7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "60" :db/id 17592186540755}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540755} :answer-field/id #uuid "70887428-4f7c-590f-a390-58a8f2bf8ee3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186540987}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "143c70c1-44db-5544-97bc-c449974fa03d" :question/math-academy-id "q-133292" :question/problem "The eagle's total displacement in the $y$-direction over the first $6$ seconds is given by $$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt[5]{{x}^{7}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{7/5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{7/5+1}}{(\frac{7}{5}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{12/5}}{\left(\frac{12}{5}\right)}+C \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{12/5}}{12}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5{x}^{12/5}}{12}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{5{x}^{12/5}}{12}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{5}{12}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{12/5})+0 \\ &= \frac{5}{12}\cdot \frac{12}{5}{x}^{12/5-1} \\ &= {x}^{7/5}\hspace{1em}{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186541074 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "141b96db-d2b7-5c1e-ba1e-d4cec0dff378" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "136.1\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186540562} {:answer/id #uuid "56903a87-08bb-5210-b21a-15bdc9bdba3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "135.9\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186540671} {:answer/id #uuid "6eb90bb5-f5d6-5864-b41d-7da56b21a5e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "136.4\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186540720} {:answer/id #uuid "bba99957-7e8d-5791-b9fd-9c58160a4cde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "135.7\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186540843} {:answer/id #uuid "c0463d14-2b9e-5fba-b2c4-9802c27cf249" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "135.2\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186540849}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540562} :answer-field/id #uuid "464a658d-9140-58a9-ae22-53b8f7f33f64" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186540976}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "36a65a87-c8d0-5bbf-adbe-0789f4e08164" :question/math-academy-id "q-336500" :question/problem "A syrup mixing tank at a bottling plant can hold up to $220\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of syrup solution with $24\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved sugar. A more concentrated sugar solution with concentration $0.7\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.7\,\text{lb/gal}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.7\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.7\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =8.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $8\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=120+12t-8t=4(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =8.4-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=8.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 8.4 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =8.4(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =8.4(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 8.4(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =8.4\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $24\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=24,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =24 \\ 2.8(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =24 \\ 84+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =24 \\ \frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =-60 \\ C & =-60(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)-\frac{60(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =2.8(30+t)-60{\left(\frac{30}{30+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $220\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=220$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =220 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =100 \\ {t}_{o} & =25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =2.8(30+25)-60{\left(\frac{30}{30+25}\right)}^{2} \\  & =154-60{\left(\frac{30}{55}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈136.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186541077 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "45835387-0c1c-5d4b-8457-ff714a80c9d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2})\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186540647} {:answer/id #uuid "66549397-7ffc-5509-bf4a-c170eda19f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2})\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186540701} {:answer/id #uuid "a1f04dfc-2a73-5512-bd3a-e55c9fef4431" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2{x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186540797} {:answer/id #uuid "a4049b8a-8825-5669-9caa-a14e90d86938" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2{x}^{2}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186540802} {:answer/id #uuid "e80076d7-c03b-5639-b30a-dfb3cf2ac755" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(2x-{x}^{4})}^{2}\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186540921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540647} :answer-field/id #uuid "43ca6906-7838-5f5e-b687-6a0de5308bd3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186540975}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4022977e-c101-551c-847a-d892e1fa6f2e" :question/math-academy-id "q-139260" :question/problem "![](images/11/11b85e35604a0350a9fd7754dfda481000debb20397d9aa593a1b887409a97c7.png)

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨y\operatorname{cos}y+y{x}^{3},\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt[3]{x}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/fa/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}y+x)\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{-1}^{1}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[((1)^{3}y+1)-((-1)^{3}y+(-1))]\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =[{y}^{2}+2y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =((2)^{2}+2(2))-0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186541084 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "074012c5-6ca1-5495-8009-0d0c255d3ee8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{4}" :db/id 17592186540534} {:answer/id #uuid "1bc800b9-5ce9-51df-9646-ad28b4b5f5dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186540575} {:answer/id #uuid "81f7e7be-4c3c-5db4-9e89-a897730e6bd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{155}{32}" :db/id 17592186540748} {:answer/id #uuid "afc9329d-23eb-511f-aef5-7c8e3284646b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{41}{4}" :db/id 17592186540823} {:answer/id #uuid "d18a0d10-9bd4-5e8e-9023-0b2590d9b92f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186540882}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540534} :answer-field/id #uuid "3a192929-90b9-5ade-b716-7719dbfc5bbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186540967}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "59606949-3c87-521e-a2c2-60c040472354" :question/math-academy-id "q-109956" :question/problem "For two independent random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=16$ and $\text{Var}[Y]=6.$ Find $\text{Var}[\frac{3}{8}X+\frac{1}{2}Y].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

Initially, it contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of wastewater with $40\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved contaminant. A more concentrated wastewater stream with concentration $1.25\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $1.25\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminant enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =15\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $8\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=120+12t-8t=4(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =15-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=15.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 15 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =15(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =15(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 15(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =15\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =5(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $40\,\text{lb}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=40,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =40 \\ 5(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =40 \\ 150+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =40 \\ \frac{C}{{30}^{2}} & =-110 \\ C & =-110(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =5(30+t)-\frac{110(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =5(30+t)-110{\left(\frac{30}{30+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =60 \\ {t}_{o} & =15\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(15) & =5(30+15)-110{\left(\frac{30}{30+15}\right)}^{2} \\  & =225-110{\left(\frac{30}{45}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈176.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186541096 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "beda0c51-788b-57b5-9c1d-b837a9961c32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{t^2+25}" :db/id 17592186540846}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540846} :answer-field/id #uuid "a16e017f-d9d9-54ce-97a3-a549b27da1ca" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186541011}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6e20ee7e-741b-5069-a51c-7de25cc32da7" :question/math-academy-id "q-133285" :question/problem "Calculate the horizontal velocity of the eagle as a function of time.

{{field-1}}$\,\text{m/s}.$" :question/worked-solution "The horizontal velocity of the eagle is given by ${x}^{′}(t),$ where

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we will calculate the axis of symmetry in terms of $k.$ Then, since we know that the axis of symmetry is $x=-\frac{5}{12},$ we will set our result equal to $-\frac{5}{12}.$ 

From the equation $y=(3x+7)(2x-k),$ we find that the roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-\frac{7}{3}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{k}{2}.$ 

To find the axis of symmetry, we take the average of the roots, as follows:

$$

$$

A solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved nutrient is pumped into the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of nutrient $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,(1-\frac{t}{18})+\beta {(1-\frac{t}{18})}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which minerals enter the tank minus the rate at which minerals leave the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which minerals enter the tank.

First, note that a water solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of minerals enters the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *minerals* enter the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.8\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which minerals exit the tank.

To find the rate at which minerals leave the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $180\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $20\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $30\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
180+20t-30t=(180-10t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of minerals in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min},$ *minerals* leave at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{30Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{18-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.8-\frac{3Q}{18-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{18-t}Q=0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(18-t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|18-t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(18-t)^{-3}} \\  & =(18-t)^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(18-t)^{-3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(18-t)^{-3}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{18-t}Q) & =(18-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.8 \\ (18-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(18-t)^{-4}Q & =0.8(18-t)^{-3} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(18-t)^{-3}) & =0.8(18-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(18-t)^{-3})\,dt & =\int 0.8(18-t)^{-3}\,dt \\ Q(18-t)^{-3} & =0.8\cdot \frac{1}{2}(18-t)^{-2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.4(18-t)+C(18-t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $5\,\text{kg}$ of minerals. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=5,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =5 \\ C(18-0)^{3}+0.4(18-0) & =5 \\ C(18)^{3}+7.2 & =5 \\ C & =-\frac{2.2}{{18}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.4(18-t)-\frac{2.2}{{18}^{3}}(18-t)^{3} \\  & =0.4\cdot 18\,\left(\frac{18-t}{18}\right)-2.2{\left(\frac{18-t}{18}\right)}^{3} \\  & =7.2\,(1-\frac{t}{18})-2.2{(1-\frac{t}{18})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have $\alpha =7.2,\beta =-2.2,$ and

$$
\alpha -\beta =7.2-(-2.2)=9.4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186541126 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "de636aa5-cf99-5e6d-9779-b79decf69364" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.337" :db/id 17592186540907}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540907} :answer-field/id #uuid "66359473-563b-5acf-a793-afdba80eb7ff" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186540984}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "bf9b3381-1894-58e7-8430-4bb3204c16fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-279683" :question/problem "If $X∼B(5,\frac{2}{5}),$ then, **rounded to $3$ decimal places**, $P(X\le 1)≈${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial, we have the following probability mass function:

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $y=x$ and $y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{4},$ as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(x)=x$ and $g(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{4}.$

$$

The solutions are $x=0,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2$ because we are only concerned about $x\ge 0.$

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=f(x)=x.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
