$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the tangent line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /6} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )} \\  & =\frac{[3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})]}{[3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})]} \\  & =\frac{[3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)]}{[3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)]} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 1)}{(3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 0-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1)} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\  & =-\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ {y}_{1} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent:

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =-\sqrt{3}\cdot (x-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =-\sqrt{3}\,x+\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =-\sqrt{3}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

\displaystyle \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
$$ for $0\le x<\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\frac{\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{3}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & 2x+\frac{\pi }{3} & =\frac{2\pi }{3}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =2n\pi  & \, & \, & 2x & =\frac{\pi }{3}+2n\pi  \\ x & =n\pi  & \, & \, & x & =\frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi \end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<\pi .$

Finally, since ${x}_{1}=0$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6},$ we have

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0+\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186542134 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07bac355-b88f-5b7d-9809-b280d5116526" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186541437}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541437} :answer-field/id #uuid "465d8139-eff1-5a62-b741-0958ddc43158" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186542004} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3f76616c-2327-566a-9ae8-01e2ede0a56b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value ">" :db/id 17592186541554}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541554} :answer-field/id #uuid "615ffce8-4d1d-5d35-af0c-b2aca3ff273c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186542018}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3a94e199-2676-5231-8dfa-fab7d29de94f" :question/math-academy-id "q-278633" :question/problem "Solve the inequality $\operatorname{log}⁡(2x-7)-1\le \operatorname{log}⁡(x+3).$

{{field-1}}{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x-7)-1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3)} \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x-7)}\cdot {10}^{-1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3)} \\ (2x-7)\cdot \frac{1}{10} & \le x+3 \\ 2x-7 & \le 10x+30 \\ -8x & \le 37 \\ x & \ge -\frac{37}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-7 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{7}{2} \\ x+3 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-3\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge -\frac{37}{8},$ which can be expressed as $[-\frac{37}{8},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{7}{2}$ and $x>-3,$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{7}{2},\infty )$ and $(-3,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[-\frac{37}{8},\infty )\cap (\frac{7}{2},\infty )\cap (-3,\infty )=(\frac{7}{2},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{7}{2},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>\frac{7}{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186542140 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6d892d4b-1f41-59fa-8ad3-d3472fa4e6d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x<\frac{6}{7}" :db/id 17592186541643} {:answer/id #uuid "770500f6-2d7b-540a-b09e-bb29a81643a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}<x<\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186541667} {:answer/id #uuid "a32c9ddf-299e-58be-bd3f-212dafb64901" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x>\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186541761} {:answer/id #uuid "a863da24-b3b9-5ace-b9ec-e3e2fd599ad2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}<x<\frac{6}{7}" :db/id 17592186541769} {:answer/id #uuid "d7541595-2650-5a3c-a576-f7811636ecbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{7}<x<\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186541883}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541769} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7f0155d-d662-520e-9a57-f5d8914eb1be" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186542061}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "43fb940b-f6bb-5ab7-9419-983a08453584" :question/math-academy-id "q-102985" :question/problem "Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)<\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x).$" :question/worked-solution "We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x)} \\ 3x-1 & <5-4x \\ 7x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{1}{3} \\ 5-4x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<\frac{6}{7},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7}).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{1}{3}$ and $x<\frac{5}{4},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1}{3},\infty )$ and $(-\infty ,\frac{5}{4}),$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)+\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right))}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)-\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right))} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (-1)+\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot 0}{(2\cdot 0-\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot (-1))} \\  & =\frac{-2}{\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & ={\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & ={\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\left(-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\right) & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot (x-0) \\ y+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4} & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\,x \\ y & =\frac{3\pi }{4}x-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{3} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\sqrt{3},1).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-\sqrt{3}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}x+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=3]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|3}=\frac{22}{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=9$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{27}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ |

| $X=9$ | $\frac{5}{27}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=9$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $X=6$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |

$$"} {:db/id 17592186542175 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2020696f-a58a-5bea-9042-7644a64564bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2<x<\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186541489} {:answer/id #uuid "2f955151-5811-59d2-8a3a-8e38ffc5da58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}<x<7" :db/id 17592186541516} {:answer/id #uuid "6b7b2476-f5c3-533e-b71b-3b272d7d38bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x<2" :db/id 17592186541639} {:answer/id #uuid "c7c82291-5bcc-5669-952a-35cb81cb2451" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x<\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186541844} {:answer/id #uuid "dac08641-2e13-5838-9a68-0bb5101691ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186541889}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541889} :answer-field/id #uuid "e453b4f4-6b05-567d-8a7e-2835ff4071a2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186542081}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9adad641-ba08-51a7-99da-8781356ee913" :question/math-academy-id "q-102984" :question/problem "Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x)>\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-7).$" :question/worked-solution "We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at

\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}?
$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=Ax-b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)=y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}={y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=Ax-b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}={\sum }_{j=1}^{2}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}={x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & ={y}_{i}{x}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{-\theta }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the tangent line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )={e}^{-\theta }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-\theta }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{{e}^{-\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =-\frac{\cancel{{e}^{-\theta }}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{\cancel{{e}^{-\theta }}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={e}^{-\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={e}^{-\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={e}^{-\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={e}^{-\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $$
\displaystyle (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4}).
$$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent:

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4} & =0\cdot (x-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4}) \\ y-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4} & =0 \\ y & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{e}^{-\pi /4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =2\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3})}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right)}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{2}-2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right))\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =(1-2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right))\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-1 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right))\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =(1-2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right))\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,\sqrt{3}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}x+3\sqrt{3} \\ y & =3\sqrt{3}x+4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+4\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-4\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})}{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})-4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{2}{2-\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\theta {\cos }^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\pi \cdot {\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{\pi }{2} & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}\,x+\frac{\pi (4-\pi )}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{4}{3}).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0$ and $b=\frac{3}{2}\,i+\frac{4}{3}\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t(b) \\  & =t(\frac{3}{2}\,i+\frac{4}{3}\,j) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}t\,i+\frac{4}{3}t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=\frac{3}{2}t$ and $y=\frac{4}{3}t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}t)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i+\frac{4}{3}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\frac{3}{2}}^{2}+{\frac{4}{3}}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{145}{36}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{145}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{\frac{3}{2}t+\frac{4}{3}t} \\  & ={e}^{\frac{17}{6}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{\frac{17}{6}t}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{145}}{6}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{145}}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{\frac{17}{6}t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{2}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=5-2\cdot y=-2\cdot r\cdot \sin(\theta)+5.$

\Delta=\{(r,\theta,z):0\le r\le \sqrt{2},\ 0\le\theta<2\cdot \pi,\ 0\le z\le -2\cdot r\cdot \sin(\theta)+5\}.

For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{10},$ you're given that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=41.2,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=182.6.
$$

 
Given that the log-likelihood function of the sample is

$$
l(\theta )=-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2},
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$

*Hint: The probability density function for a normal random variable with mean $\theta $ and standard deviation $1$ is given by* 

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=10$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}=41.2,
$$ $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{x}_{i}^{2}=182.6,
$$ and $n=10.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{10}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(182.6-2\theta \cdot 41.2+10{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-91.3)+41.2\theta +(-5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=(-91.3)+41.2+(-5)=-55.1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186543505 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5f7bf1e4-9398-55b3-bd2b-8515162867e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4.14" :db/id 17592186542897} {:answer/id #uuid "94e0befa-4705-51e9-9630-de948e992209" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.18" :db/id 17592186543030} {:answer/id #uuid "a8ba97b2-62e5-5ad9-99a5-29d92dd18008" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.54" :db/id 17592186543086} {:answer/id #uuid "e5189590-8a2a-5040-af84-68d2107b8f6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4.39" :db/id 17592186543222} {:answer/id #uuid "f57a279b-4104-5ca5-8808-72ea4b362832" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4.99" :db/id 17592186543269}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186543222} :answer-field/id #uuid "32c3ae4e-5559-5bc7-8d50-9bcf40432395" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186543321}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5c4c55fe-2946-5795-a8c6-76c349270710" :question/math-academy-id "q-159960" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. Finally,

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0<x<\pi .$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{17\pi }{18}$ and $x=\frac{7\pi }{6}.$  We reject the solution $\frac{7\pi }{6}$ since it lies outside the domain of interest.

\displaystyle \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-\frac{7\pi }{6})=-\frac{1}{2}
$$ for $0\le x<2\pi .$ If the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ are written in ascending order, what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{4}?$" :question/worked-solution "We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186543544 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "47698303-8d61-5840-8827-86edae5c0ca9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3.1" :db/id 17592186542834} {:answer/id #uuid "48989a49-93e8-5124-b600-ec90d999d72c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.3" :db/id 17592186542838} {:answer/id #uuid "7eef2b9f-e7ca-51a3-b197-a936d17dd502" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3.7" :db/id 17592186542981} {:answer/id #uuid "cc28b179-5541-543f-9559-8ecc8381e121" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3.5" :db/id 17592186543171} {:answer/id #uuid "e5647be5-c113-5d6c-87be-376b749ccd3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.9" :db/id 17592186543223}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186542981} :answer-field/id #uuid "2253fa4d-3bff-5c5d-817e-be26b444097e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186543313}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "aaf34c24-70f2-59f0-ad3e-3eb728abaa5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-159961" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4},{X}_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,{1}^{2}),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown mean. The log-likelihood function of the sample $0.7,\,0.6,\,-0.5,\,1.7,\,-1.1$ is

$$
l(\theta )=-2.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+a+b\theta +c{\theta }^{2}
$$

What is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x,\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{\left(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma }\right)}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Next, we write down the log-density function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡f(x,\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{(x-\theta )^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{n}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0.7+0.6+(-0.5)+1.7+(-1.1) \\  & =1.4 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(0.7)^{2}+(0.6)^{2}+(-0.5)^{2}+(1.7)^{2}+(-1.1)^{2} \\  & =5.2\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=5.$ Therefore,  

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{1}{2}(5.2-2\theta \cdot (1.4)+5{\theta }^{2}) \\  & =-2.5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\pi )+(-2.6)+(1.4)\theta +(-2.5){\theta }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=-2.6+(1.4)+(-2.5)=-3.7.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186543548 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18eb997a-9844-5aac-b91f-00f5f300d39b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{24}" :db/id 17592186542703} {:answer/id #uuid "33d9c60f-2f9d-53f4-980f-9aa97023962f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7{\pi }^{2}}{24}" :db/id 17592186542779} {:answer/id #uuid "d7168513-56cb-58e5-b423-239ea3770fba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{48}" :db/id 17592186543192} {:answer/id #uuid "da5f6ffe-39d2-5021-9518-42610f548da9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186543198} {:answer/id #uuid "edf9637c-aede-513e-8154-e840c0b4d689" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7{\pi }^{2}}{48}" :db/id 17592186543246}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186543246} :answer-field/id #uuid "c6635c31-8a89-581f-88ba-c9350baa70ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186543439}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "af242b6e-a0fa-5102-becb-649e55619922" :question/math-academy-id "q-8422" :question/problem "Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $$

$$ for $0\le x<\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=- t^{2} + t,\quad y=t^{3} - t^{2},\quad z=- 2 t^{2} + 2 t
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\langle - 2 z, 0, - 3 y\rangle \\ & =\langle - 2 \left(- 2 t^{2} + 2 t\right), 0, - 3 \left(t^{3} - t^{2}\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle 4 t^{2} - 4 t, 0, - 3 t^{3} + 3 t^{2}\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r\prime(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\langle \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- t^{2} + t\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(t^{3} - t^{2}\right), \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(- 2 t^{2} + 2 t\right)\rangle \\ & =\langle 1 - 2 t, 3 t^{2} - 2 t, 2 - 4 t\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t) & =\langle 4 t^{2} - 4 t, 0, - 3 t^{3} + 3 t^{2}\rangle\cdot \langle 1 - 2 t, 3 t^{2} - 2 t, 2 - 4 t\rangle \\ & =\left(4 t^{2} - 4 t\right)\cdot \left(1 - 2 t\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot \left(3 t^{2} - 2 t\right)+\left(- 3 t^{3} + 3 t^{2}\right)\cdot \left(2 - 4 t\right) \\ & =\left(- 8 t^{3} + 12 t^{2} - 4 t\right)+\left(0\right)+\left(12 t^{4} - 18 t^{3} + 6 t^{2}\right) \\ & =12 t^{4} - 26 t^{3} + 18 t^{2} - 4 t \\ & =12 t^{4} - 26 t^{3} + 18 t^{2} - 4 t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S\operatorname{curl}F\cdot\mathrm dS & =\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr \\ & =\int_{0}^{1} F(r(t))\cdot r\prime(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(12 t^{4} - 26 t^{3} + 18 t^{2} - 4 t\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[\left(- \frac{13 t^{4}}{2}\right) + \left(- 2 t^{2}\right) + \left(\frac{12 t^{5}}{5}\right) + \left(6 t^{3}\right)\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =\left(\left(- \frac{13}{2}\right) + \left(-2\right) + \left(\frac{12}{5}\right) + \left(6\right)\right)-\left(\left(0\right) + \left(0\right) + \left(0\right) + \left(0\right)\right) \\ & =- \frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186543965 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b3ae743-91b5-55a1-8181-4d006345cf95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12 \pi" :db/id 17592186543974} {:answer/id #uuid "79ecbd6c-e61f-5ce9-86c4-e7caec648e2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186543984} {:answer/id #uuid "935747a9-235d-528c-9945-b1717c8e562a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 12 \pi" :db/id 17592186543989} {:answer/id #uuid "f0a3acee-6209-5db5-8d34-42ddc39d0af2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 6 \pi" :db/id 17592186544007} {:answer/id #uuid "f27e1353-adf9-5977-b05b-7f5737daaa15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186544008}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186543989} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7bac8ec-76be-58f5-9f6a-bfd5a83edd1b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544000}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "07a605d5-0ef0-5420-9db8-ccb3e82bd11b" :question/problem "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\langle 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}, 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}, 1\rangle$ for $t\in [0,2 \pi).$

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Now, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =6\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =6\cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =3\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /3} & =\frac{{y}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)}{{x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{(-3)} \\  & =-\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544793 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3bdda5ba-c7b8-5b1e-8e9a-e2ebee5f3bc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{11\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544216} {:answer/id #uuid "45b57772-1a24-517a-95cc-031e14b7b047" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{9\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(2\theta -\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544240} {:answer/id #uuid "4c27fd42-8cff-578f-b7b7-132d0e72f699" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9{\int }_{-\pi /8}^{13\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544251} {:answer/id #uuid "640c8082-9d89-5f36-b453-20aa27bdcf44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{13\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544303} {:answer/id #uuid "ee2ff5b2-7d3f-5bc8-8b07-edf54d53bb3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /8}^{13\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544603}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544303} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3f71d5c-aae5-521c-b9e4-78cdc0efc697" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544773}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1ca5b3d9-2cf9-5f0b-b261-8040bf2d2224" :question/math-academy-id "q-125695" :question/problem "![](images/17/172737d1a5b28b9a60958dc7e6b1748db1912021b7df4ad26045648063037fd8.png)

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?" :question/worked-solution "The given polar curve is the polar rose with $2\cdot 2=4$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{3\pi }{8}$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{8},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{2}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{2}=-\frac{3\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{8} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{9\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{7} & ={\theta }_{5}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{9\pi }{8} \\ {\theta }_{8} & ={\theta }_{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{9\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{13\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $4$ petals of our rose:

$$
\underbrace{[-\frac{3\pi }{8},\frac{\pi }{8}]}_{1\text{st}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{\pi }{8},\frac{5\pi }{8}]}_{2\text{nd}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{5\pi }{8},\frac{9\pi }{8}]}_{3\text{rd}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{9\pi }{8},\frac{13\pi }{8}]}_{4\text{th}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{8}$ to $\theta =\frac{13\pi }{8}:$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{13\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}\theta 
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544796 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d461234f-027a-557e-9d34-651597fcb58b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{-2(s+2)}{s(s-5)}" :db/id 17592186544537}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544537} :answer-field/id #uuid "337fbbd0-2104-528d-b75a-5b62951f2ab9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186544675}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "229cdf1d-b683-5de3-b351-27b1d6a26233" :question/math-academy-id "q-332026" :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=\frac{2(2s-3)}{s(s-5)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)-3{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-4=2{X}_{1}(s)-3{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+2=-2{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$

Rewriting the system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(s-2){X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s)=4 \\ 2{X}_{1}(s)+(s-3){X}_{2}(s)=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, from the second equation, we have 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{-2-(s-3){X}_{2}(s)}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(s-2)[\frac{-2-(s-3){X}_{2}(s)}{2}]+3{X}_{2}(s) & =4 \\ (s-2)[-2-(s-3){X}_{2}(s)]+6{X}_{2}(s) & =8 \\ -2(s-2)-[(s-2)(s-3)-6]{X}_{2}(s) & =8 \\ -({s}^{2}-5s){X}_{2}(s) & =8+2(s-2) \\ -s(s-5){X}_{2}(s) & =2s+4 \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{-2(s+2)}{s(s-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${X}_{1}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2-(s-3){X}_{2}(s)}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2-(s-3)\cdot \frac{-2(s+2)}{s(s-5)}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-2s(s+5)+2(s-3)(s+2)}{2s(s-5)} \\  & =\frac{2(2s-3)}{s(s-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{2(2s-3)}{s(s-5)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{-2(s+2)}{s(s-5)}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544800 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c54c735-3838-59f7-9d18-f9c4833f0ed2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544222} {:answer/id #uuid "4fab53b6-6248-5945-8620-04b4fd64fbe0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{3\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544260} {:answer/id #uuid "c50a1248-20d5-5e72-88fe-eb63c706b7e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{-\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544506} {:answer/id #uuid "cb989c47-35ee-5257-b346-93de6ab5fb9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544519} {:answer/id #uuid "d65fab8c-cab0-5add-bbca-2b554091e44d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{-\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544545}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544506} :answer-field/id #uuid "94f7246e-f57b-594c-be96-bb72d5c5cb6b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544721}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2be045cc-480f-57a5-b39f-c617f83c588d" :question/math-academy-id "q-125349" :question/problem "![](images/94/9405ee6a4b24ef36c2a59a9f4a984728716e9c281456d1459d591393d3c73720.png)

  represented by the shaded region shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )} & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal lies in the fourth quadrant. Since the petal lies in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $4\theta +\pi $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
4\theta +\pi =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,4\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{8},-\frac{\pi }{8}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{3\pi }{8},-\frac{\pi }{8}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies in the fourth quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{-\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544802 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "32e39f4a-397e-573f-8267-d6dff3c45d27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544201} {:answer/id #uuid "6028d4af-94c2-52de-a2e3-29fdb44dd06c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544295} {:answer/id #uuid "69c80d92-4c28-5a07-8592-a922020c016a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /12}^{5\pi /12}(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544315} {:answer/id #uuid "8f7607b6-fff2-5114-adf4-8abe60405481" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544400} {:answer/id #uuid "e41bf703-af8a-5e9d-9f4f-8722fbf336bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /12}^{5\pi /12}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544578}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544578} :answer-field/id #uuid "18e19576-c2ce-57ce-a908-4860ee2c8b3f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544663}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3922fac2-663d-5efa-bc44-c819bbafb745" :question/math-academy-id "q-125357" :question/problem "![](images/d9/d9985c6afd3e5440dbe1e51e4046e7744c9a2e01472354054796247d40ed7ed6.png)

\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $2\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
2\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{6},\frac{5\pi }{6}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{12},\frac{5\pi }{12}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{5\pi }{12},\frac{5\pi }{12}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /12}^{5\pi /12}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544804 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27ef4703-6639-5623-8c0b-2ffb2cd82831" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}{\cos }^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544178} {:answer/id #uuid "42047be1-5cd9-5f0f-9112-70b8e78c7e75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}{\cos }^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544233} {:answer/id #uuid "6c6a7060-6e4d-5e7b-9e87-0feb10e6a475" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544325} {:answer/id #uuid "a98b5b54-648a-5f5c-abff-c03076a297d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544451} {:answer/id #uuid "e724f53d-777b-5184-bede-b852c936bd20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}{\cos }^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544583}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544583} :answer-field/id #uuid "5db885ae-a359-50aa-b94a-866c4319d576" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544692}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3aec8613-8bc5-55d8-bb63-25dfe3e5bcce" :question/math-academy-id "q-127800" :question/problem "![](images/44/446278a820ba21da7f5a1f15639e8cc4f96e38f38f3b5905b926bb9d2a106948.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$

Since $r(\theta )=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{\cos }^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$

$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $6\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$

$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $$
\displaystyle \theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{\pi }{12}].
$$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}{\cos }^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544806 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11660d74-dd0a-5819-9d4e-b50594a56164" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-32" :db/id 17592186544122} {:answer/id #uuid "184012f0-2b52-515a-b494-8bc567e92f28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16" :db/id 17592186544137} {:answer/id #uuid "5327fde3-a474-599f-919c-4b4af0d58991" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186544270} {:answer/id #uuid "662a97ed-0348-5971-99ff-f6ffd17244cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186544308} {:answer/id #uuid "d209e16c-aeb8-54b1-b37c-3084d1b1f440" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186544532}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544532} :answer-field/id #uuid "d3b13d40-42f8-5fcf-b562-1fbe4a131420" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544752}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3c4eccd2-7dd0-53ca-8b67-e044fcc594a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-123856" :question/problem "Let $R=[-3,1]\times [2,4]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}-{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}-{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
{y}_{j-1}-{x}_{i}\le \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})\le {y}_{j}-{x}_{i-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{j-1}+{x}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2}-(-3)^{2})(4-2)=-8 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})(1-(-3))=24\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 24-(-8)\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 32\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=32.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544811 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a7dd673-0f1c-53a4-bf23-823dac58c3bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{9}" :db/id 17592186544212} {:answer/id #uuid "71a909e6-6f08-5712-bc83-1b6bad8b11a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{18}" :db/id 17592186544339} {:answer/id #uuid "76d4658d-76b6-5b33-aa64-aa0bb388f498" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{24}" :db/id 17592186544351} {:answer/id #uuid "ab42cc66-3ec7-5fba-ba3f-33b3a69e4979" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{18}" :db/id 17592186544454} {:answer/id #uuid "eb3e916a-1d77-5240-920d-86d1b61a5940" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/id 17592186544594}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544351} :answer-field/id #uuid "4824d498-2640-5207-a210-a8d05507618a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544682}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "427792fe-a52b-5a35-ba4b-43ed95fe05d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-143573" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following conditional probability density function:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{2x+3} & \,0\le x\le 1,\,x+1\le y\le x+2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find $P(Y<2\,|\,X=\frac{3}{4}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}x,
$$

where ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$ 

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<2\,|\,X=\frac{3}{4}) & ={\int }_{1+x}^{2}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=\frac{3}{4})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1+3/4}^{2}\frac{2y}{(2\cdot \frac{3}{4}+3)}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{\int }_{7/4}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}[{y}^{2}]_{7/4}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(4-\frac{49}{16}) \\  & =\frac{5}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544813 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6eb18d81-1f63-599d-9330-be80543a661b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}{\cos }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544329} {:answer/id #uuid "b2eef91a-4bda-57e9-8dc9-d19c65f2191b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}{\cos }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544465} {:answer/id #uuid "e8c8d26d-0f5e-5aa7-80ac-7d5f0bd84561" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{5\pi /4}{\cos }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544590} {:answer/id #uuid "ebc61141-892a-5b47-bb30-ac12b2c0629b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{5\pi /8}{\cos }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544597} {:answer/id #uuid "f2b98e86-56c1-5a75-b49c-7e744474633d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}{\cos }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544614} :answer-field/id #uuid "3c945d12-5ddf-5d29-b1ff-6f3e26849c7d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544678}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "43e3bf66-f5d8-57b0-9e72-5dc370f879ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-83484" :question/problem "![](images/34/34e3bbdee3f70fe0111574f0d0fab772acf98de668e2eeb72464e6611a1fabcd.png)

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?" :question/worked-solution "The given polar curve is the polar rose with $3$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A=2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{\cos }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

![](images/34/34e3bbdee3f70fe0111574f0d0fab772acf98de668e2eeb72464e6611a1fabcd.png)

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{3}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{3}=-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{6} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{3}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $3$ petals of our rose:

$$
\underbrace{[-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}]}_{1\text{st}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{2}]}_{2\text{nd}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{5\pi }{6}]}_{3\text{rd}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6}$ to $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6}:$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}=2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}{\cos }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta 
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544817 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00e7683d-837d-5f5c-88b4-9f43a2d9f138" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /7}^{\pi /7}{\cos }^{2}⁡(7\theta +\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544088} {:answer/id #uuid "1747e57c-4ef9-5157-a45d-bc4f36bf748e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-3\pi /7}^{6\pi /7}{\cos }^{2}⁡(7\theta -\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544135} {:answer/id #uuid "4bb3e12e-9656-5b69-bd45-2db95263545f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /7}^{\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡(7\theta -\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544249} {:answer/id #uuid "831d59c7-dc3e-55d3-969a-79579b8a2e00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /7}^{6\pi /7}{\cos }^{2}⁡(7\theta +\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544373} {:answer/id #uuid "dacb2b57-d53d-5242-94a7-23fcf1973ca7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /14}^{3\pi /7}{\cos }^{2}⁡(7\theta +\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544559}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544373} :answer-field/id #uuid "7cf4a6ed-16c7-5aba-80c0-63cd22eaebcb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544711}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "50affdee-0a40-5255-b196-53de7a7824c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-125863" :question/problem "![](images/66/66616f493d84804ec9c7c2a1e3b8598404f1f57ffda2e0a68718342f508010af.png)

$$

$$

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?" :question/worked-solution "The given polar curve is the polar rose with $7$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /7}^{0}{\cos }^{2}⁡(7\theta +\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{7}$ to ${\theta }_{2}=0,$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{7}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{7}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{7}=-\frac{\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=0 \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{7}=0+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{7}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{7}=0+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{\pi }{7} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{2\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{7}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{7} & ={\theta }_{5}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{2\pi }{7} \\ {\theta }_{8} & ={\theta }_{6}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{2\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{3\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the fifth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{7}$ to both ends of the interval of the fourth petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{9} & ={\theta }_{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{2\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{3\pi }{7} \\ {\theta }_{10} & ={\theta }_{8}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{3\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{4\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the interval for the sixth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{7}$ to both ends of the interval of the fifth petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{11} & ={\theta }_{9}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{3\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{4\pi }{7} \\ {\theta }_{12} & ={\theta }_{10}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{4\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{5\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the seventh petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{7}$ to both ends of the interval of the sixth petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{13} & ={\theta }_{11}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{4\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{5\pi }{7} \\ {\theta }_{14} & ={\theta }_{12}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{5\pi }{7}+\frac{\pi }{7}=\frac{6\pi }{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $7$ petals of our rose:

$$
\underbrace{[-\frac{\pi }{7},0]}_{1\text{st}},\,\underbrace{[0,\frac{\pi }{7}]}_{2\text{nd}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{\pi }{7},\frac{2\pi }{7}]}_{3\text{rd}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{2\pi }{7},\frac{3\pi }{7}]}_{4\text{th}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{3\pi }{7},\frac{4\pi }{7}]}_{5\text{th}}\,\underbrace{[\frac{4\pi }{7},\frac{5\pi }{7}]}_{6\text{th}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{5\pi }{7},\frac{6\pi }{7}]}_{7\text{th}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{7}$ to $\theta =\frac{6\pi }{7}:$

 represented by the shaded region shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $6\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
6\theta =-\pi ,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}].
$$

Notice that this interval matches the angular region traced by the shaded petal in the diagram.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544821 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6fd65f66-345e-5e02-a44f-83cf02b3d0b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{3}x+9" :db/id 17592186544335}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544335} :answer-field/id #uuid "248fba5d-72db-5572-a2be-4b009978848e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186544666}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5bcca525-fc41-52cc-be8b-f245ac9162a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-133231" :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent line to our polar curve at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Previously, we found that the slope of the tangent line at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ is

$$
m=-\sqrt{3}.
$$

The equation of the tangent is

$$
y-{y}_{0}=m(x-{x}_{0}),
$$

where $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ are the coordinates of the point on the curve that correspond to $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Let's work these out. 

In part 1, we found that

$\,$ $x(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,$ and $\,y(\theta )=6{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta .$

As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{0} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =3\cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}, \\ {y}_{0} & =6{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =6{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =6{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $$
\displaystyle ({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{9}{2}).
$$ 

Finally, the equation of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{0} & =m(x-{x}_{0}) \\ y-\frac{9}{2} & =-\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{9}{2} & =-\sqrt{3}x+\frac{9}{2} \\ y & =-\sqrt{3}x+9.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/b8/b8546c0b6c51577acf25587fc1ebfc88e15e5f3b9456a64c499d640851bb44d0.png)"} {:db/id 17592186544823 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f7f5d76-1e7f-57ed-8313-e71643d50b2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}+x}{2y+1}" :db/id 17592186544158} {:answer/id #uuid "63ff8546-8d92-58c2-a62b-b0c34bccc272" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y+x}{2(y+1)}" :db/id 17592186544302} {:answer/id #uuid "75565937-5318-5439-b48d-e16cca219a95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}+x}{2({y}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186544347} {:answer/id #uuid "af8c864f-3d09-5723-889c-3b0bde2faabe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y+x}{{y}^{2}+2}" :db/id 17592186544459} {:answer/id #uuid "f451b045-2660-545d-8769-46b5280b5182" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{y}^{2}+x}{y+2}" :db/id 17592186544618}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544347} :answer-field/id #uuid "2568d719-6258-502f-b42f-c59bbe997028" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544667}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5ffa5cf0-3e04-5a20-bfc9-964d09fea30a" :question/math-academy-id "q-145091" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8}({y}^{2}+x), & \,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the expression of the conditional probability density function ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ for $0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{8}({y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{3{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3x}{8})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{16}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{6{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{12}{16}-0 \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1), & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{8}({y}^{2}+x))}{(\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1))} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}+x}{2({y}^{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}+x}{2({y}^{2}+1)}, & \,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544828 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12d3ae86-fe5b-5459-9248-c229a4cb9d95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\sin }^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544126} {:answer/id #uuid "1844ef73-602c-5b30-88ea-ffffbf088136" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /7}{\sin }^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544139} {:answer/id #uuid "682eb163-f2ab-5256-9c37-ff22d6e12633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /7}{\sin }^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544313} {:answer/id #uuid "82bafe14-c2b9-5557-b37c-58363f34c732" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\sin }^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544371} {:answer/id #uuid "85fa656d-5dd4-543f-afaa-83f9f26d96bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186544377}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544313} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ca50bb8-65fb-5887-be84-d31d773a1ff8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544725}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "68c240a3-d1c2-54cd-a001-e4698ed241e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-125494" :question/problem "![](images/a0/a010feba178f2db834e1939a91c81fd95131d65b10c7616bd92140fa46eaa305.png)

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?" :question/worked-solution "The given polar curve is the polar rose with $3$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{\sin }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

![](images/85/85730909004322c2c8b6d065ff1cdb4b0662830007bd5aa14c8c8c4bda798206.png)

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=0$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{3}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{3}=0+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{3}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3}=\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $3$ petals of our rose:

$$
\underbrace{[0,\frac{\pi }{3}]}_{1\text{st}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{2\pi }{3}]}_{2\text{nd}},\,\underbrace{[\frac{2\pi }{3},\pi ]}_{3\text{rd}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =0$ to $\theta =\pi :$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$"} {:db/id 17592186544845 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b33f10d-c2bd-51b2-9314-14748e5b22b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi " :db/id 17592186544143} {:answer/id #uuid "1fd2fcc1-904f-5624-a891-21600d6a3559" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186544159} {:answer/id #uuid "319af86b-63e6-5b3a-8f84-af301c7e96fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186544198} {:answer/id #uuid "5de93751-8e37-5c0e-ade7-b00a0286b1d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186544291} {:answer/id #uuid "b62a2b7d-1d9a-5e11-8aa5-b6a9b07a1289" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186544474}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186544143} :answer-field/id #uuid "38f2fe27-3752-50bd-8e74-45d47d4357a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186544677}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9182ab7c-62c2-510f-9183-c91606315f00" :question/math-academy-id "q-125329" :question/problem "![](images/94/94a5da0925a82b91d345fa7811e41c219c19ca48d76b30927e920efed3b2edb3.png)
