{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{9}{4}{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2(1)}=\frac{9}{4}{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=\frac{9}{4}{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2(2)}=\frac{9}{4}{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\frac{9}{4}{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{4}}{\frac{9}{4}{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}}={\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

 

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{9}{4}{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{\frac{9}{4}\left(\frac{1}{9}\right)}{(1-\frac{1}{9})} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}{\left(\frac{8}{9}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{9}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548003 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66021cb4-d4dc-5536-b740-cb112f549955" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{25} & \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{80}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547542} {:answer/id #uuid "8ab77c8f-f65f-5385-b65d-d3ff9200abe8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{75} & \frac{1}{120} \\ \frac{1}{120} & \frac{1}{80}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547618} {:answer/id #uuid "8bea8944-aeb8-56ab-bc44-a9115f9d6b4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{75} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{10}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547621} {:answer/id #uuid "c0675adb-146f-509c-9662-380def9fc9b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{50} & \frac{1}{120} \\ \frac{1}{120} & \frac{1}{20}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547730} {:answer/id #uuid "fa4fcec9-3717-5441-ad16-3b9193cd5316" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{75} & \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{4} & \frac{3}{20}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547829}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547618} :answer-field/id #uuid "bcc58af9-a17d-54ac-a6d0-c02b4698e66a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547935}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4f28747a-e241-5f89-b726-699a85c63f84" :question/math-academy-id "q-159419" :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}48y(x-y),\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \frac{x}{2}, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{4}{5},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1}{4},$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=\frac{2}{3},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48{y}^{3}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}(x{y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{160}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{3}{320}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{20}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}-{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48x{y}^{2}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{24}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{5}{192}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{24}-\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{120}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{75} & \frac{1}{120} \\ \frac{1}{120} & \frac{1}{80}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548004 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ec2f68f-3a5c-5320-80df-4677e1be6e00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-\pi }-1}{10}" :db/id 17592186547347} {:answer/id #uuid "6081e439-1860-5222-91b9-aee228c648b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-\pi }+2}{5}" :db/id 17592186547525} {:answer/id #uuid "842dae31-aac6-5e10-b497-9abe5c499c5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2{e}^{-\pi /2}-1}{10}" :db/id 17592186547599} {:answer/id #uuid "8bff236b-251c-5407-acdf-108c7f7dd322" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}+1}{5}" :db/id 17592186547623} {:answer/id #uuid "c07201a8-c8e4-5b0a-831a-ee4bce670816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2{e}^{-\pi /2}+1}{5}" :db/id 17592186547731}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547623} :answer-field/id #uuid "2392f4ba-bd38-5a07-8e70-90353132c90f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547859}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "509669b5-ef46-5eb1-8d54-7bbaca5f8fc9" :question/math-academy-id "q-115002" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $$
\displaystyle I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}\right)-\int \left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}\right)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}\right)-\int \left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}\right)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}J \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{1}{2}I) \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}I \\ \frac{5}{4}I & =\frac{2{e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4} \\ I & =\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})))-(\frac{1}{5}{e}^{-0}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0))-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0)))) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi /2}+1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548006 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e77a6f5-b85a-52a5-a006-9b7d292f2cc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{401}{16}" :db/id 17592186547345} {:answer/id #uuid "13ad4530-88a4-53d4-8e25-b235bdfe115f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{209}{8}" :db/id 17592186547355} {:answer/id #uuid "16ac0b96-91a3-5dfc-b5ef-29cbc766835a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{417}{16}" :db/id 17592186547364} {:answer/id #uuid "80d7caca-10f2-5451-a96d-795017485bf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{449}{16}" :db/id 17592186547591} {:answer/id #uuid "92e2c5b9-18da-53a6-8dd8-6cb2c77bfba7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{401}{8}" :db/id 17592186547642}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547364} :answer-field/id #uuid "69965209-526e-5658-899a-44e6dd8b07be" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547892}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "510f41a7-5712-55db-b50d-5c80967bb9fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-12889" :question/problem "Given that

$$
{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4}=A{x}^{8}+B{x}^{6}+C{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, find the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ and $b=4.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)}^{4}(4)^{0}+4{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)}^{3}{(4)}^{1}+6{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}{(4)}^{2} \\  & \,+4{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)}^{1}{(4)}^{3}+1{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)}^{0}{(4)}^{4} \\  & =1\left(\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}\right)(1)+4\left(\frac{{x}^{6}}{8}\right)(4)+6\left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\right)(16) \\  & \,+4\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)(64)+1(1)(256) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+\frac{16{x}^{6}}{8}+\frac{96{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{256{x}^{2}}{2}+256 \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+2{x}^{6}+24{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $A=\frac{1}{16},B=2$ and $C=24.$ So, finally

$$
A+B+C=\frac{1}{16}+2+24=\frac{417}{16}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548007 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04876404-2581-5642-a614-ac8532d94ee0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{51}{80}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547326} {:answer/id #uuid "28e7f859-7126-5457-a4e0-c1a1e1d2204b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} \\ -\frac{2}{5} & \frac{11}{40}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547390} {:answer/id #uuid "32e2ee64-527c-5c83-b039-b6ea6f47e219" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{23}{40}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547422} {:answer/id #uuid "f06f1240-944d-5a7e-801d-c1580106d19c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} \\ -\frac{2}{5} & \frac{23}{40}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547811} {:answer/id #uuid "f530e59e-19da-56aa-a5f6-c0afac7fd1bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{11}{40}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547814}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547326} :answer-field/id #uuid "3653cd9d-fe12-51a1-8be3-fd825c0586b5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547870}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "53e9c56c-8467-523e-bd98-6ac7236cb57e" :question/math-academy-id "q-159402" :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\, & -1\le x\le 1,\,\,-1\le y\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.

If $\text{E}[X]=0$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{5}{4},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{4}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-{(0)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{-1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{33}{5} \\  & =\frac{11}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186548016 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c09fbcf-e1dc-5950-9508-6766eb430f44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{45} & \frac{5}{63} \\ \frac{5}{63} & \frac{67}{548}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547447} {:answer/id #uuid "8486b2b4-5627-54ae-9bfc-12a68a4ca561" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{63} & \frac{1}{21} \\ \frac{1}{21} & \frac{56}{843}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547600} {:answer/id #uuid "cd3456dc-3ee8-5bd4-b669-70e0e8adddde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{4}{21} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547753} {:answer/id #uuid "ce082f30-4d9c-529e-8724-6a216a95f170" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{63} & \frac{5}{63} \\ \frac{5}{63} & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547758} {:answer/id #uuid "ff923f25-09d1-59df-bac6-3e88c64bc811" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{45} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{56}{843}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547843}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547758} :answer-field/id #uuid "3850f8d6-6285-5466-abaf-4c01feeefec9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547871}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7039fb00-3d4a-54d6-a4b0-1bcf58d49ef2" :question/math-academy-id "q-159422" :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{16}({x}^{2}-y),\, & 0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{3},$ $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{20}{21},$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=\frac{40}{27},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$
We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{4}-y{x}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[y{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{6})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{32}{[\frac{1}{7}{x}^{7}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{7}-{\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{Var}[Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{40}{27}-{\left(\frac{20}{21}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{760}{1\,323}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\frac{5}{16}xy({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{2})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}x]}_{y=0}^{y={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{5}{16}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}{x}^{7})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{7}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{96}{[\frac{1}{8}{x}^{8}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{3}-\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{20}{21}\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{63}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{63} & \frac{5}{63} \\ \frac{5}{63} & \frac{760}{1\,323}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548019 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d5afcd8-4cf8-5778-a410-d996de8caa7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186547343} {:answer/id #uuid "3b943b2d-ea0b-5325-b2aa-3e8653e1e477" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{25}" :db/id 17592186547444} {:answer/id #uuid "6ef15147-7c05-56d2-a62e-10a55dfa362d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186547562} {:answer/id #uuid "a306fe67-74bc-5773-80ce-c1513aa6afc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186547673} {:answer/id #uuid "e32c4540-3e5c-5944-a86d-c76ecf3c6add" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186547789}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547673} :answer-field/id #uuid "be9f989d-d56a-54a6-a664-496350494e54" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547938}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7ac43aed-fdf1-5439-85aa-b688b91d01e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-124590" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{25}{27}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{n}=
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{3},$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & =\frac{25}{27}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{3}=\frac{25}{27}\left(\frac{27}{125}\right)=\frac{1}{5} \\ {a}_{4} & =\frac{25}{27}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{4}=\frac{25}{27}\left(\frac{81}{625}\right)=\frac{3}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{\left(\frac{3}{25}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}=\frac{3}{5}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{25}{27}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}{(1-\frac{3}{5})} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)}{\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)} \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)\cdot \frac{5}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548020 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "60c7ef0e-ae5f-5788-8442-58796873f024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2,9)" :db/id 17592186547526} {:answer/id #uuid "84e944cf-269e-5563-8b06-449f37d3b2c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-6,27)" :db/id 17592186547601} {:answer/id #uuid "b2ab2f07-2154-5eaf-9f99-57f63be7b49d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-18,9)" :db/id 17592186547705} {:answer/id #uuid "d0e15f87-be8f-5c3b-8a1b-1ee813c884df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-6,3)" :db/id 17592186547764} {:answer/id #uuid "e91d2864-f866-5e4b-b852-31fa590ce52f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2,3)" :db/id 17592186547801}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547705} :answer-field/id #uuid "0dc935dc-f462-5bbc-b210-6779d4c833a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547845}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7ec57449-f520-50b3-b823-1f98b4f880f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-79428" :question/problem "The point $P$ with coordinates $(-6,9)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x).$ Which of the following points must lie on $y=f(\frac{1}{3}x)?$" :question/worked-solution "The function $y=f(\frac{1}{3}x)$ represents a stretch of the function $y=f(x)$ by a factor of $3$ parallel to the $x$-axis. This has the effect of multiplying the $x$-coordinates of all points on $y=f(x)$ by $3.$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{1}=5.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{10{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}}{10{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{1}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }10{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{5}{(1-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{5}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{1} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548033 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "34950a5f-0e45-502b-a869-e016971bd6d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{18} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{8}{75}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547425} {:answer/id #uuid "4c028ae0-4e46-5185-bea4-b79e305dc544" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{9} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{8}{75}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547489} {:answer/id #uuid "4dfa5556-a2dc-5232-9d7f-e3796a0407dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{9} & -1 \\ -1 & \frac{8}{75}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547494} {:answer/id #uuid "8675456c-15df-5d06-a100-2d7b178a0c1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{18} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{4}{25}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547606} {:answer/id #uuid "ddc276fa-92de-5c9e-be25-aa6ec3df6cac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{18} & -1 \\ -1 & \frac{4}{25}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186547779}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547425} :answer-field/id #uuid "294a6c0d-e8c4-539b-87eb-6c2be022c57a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547862}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9895539f-08a9-52d3-aba6-0550c7a4d108" :question/math-academy-id "q-159407" :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

If $\text{E}[X]=\frac{2}{3}$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{8}{5},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}.

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-{\left(\frac{8}{5}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[0,1]\times [0,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=2x$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{4}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{18} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{8}{75}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548037 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c6372b2-3f3a-5d2d-9b9b-d69b71a08c40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13}{42}" :db/id 17592186547404}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547404} :answer-field/id #uuid "96f0fd95-c9b0-5cbe-abcc-ca8956c4e2ea" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186547914}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a3b460f4-8f03-59ea-8d4e-3d88c9d8d99f" :question/math-academy-id "q-126768" :question/problem "Using the first two non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $f(x),$ approximate $$

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We have that

$$
f(x)≈{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}.
$$

We can approximate $$
\displaystyle \int f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$ by integrating the above series term-by-term, as follows:

$$
{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{{3}^{n}}{n+2}\,{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n}=\frac{1}{2}+(x+\frac{1}{4})+\frac{{3}^{2}}{4}\,{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{2}+\frac{{3}^{3}}{5}\,{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{3}+⋯\,.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To apply the ratio test we define $$
\displaystyle {a}_{n}=\frac{{3}^{n}}{n+2}\,{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n}.
$$Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{3}^{n+1}{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n+1}}{n+3}\cdot \frac{n+2}{{3}^{n}{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{n}}| \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{3(n+2)}{n+3}(x+\frac{1}{4})| \\  & =|x+\frac{1}{4}|\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{3(n+2)}{n+3} \\  & =|x+\frac{1}{4}|\cdot 3 \\  & =3|x+\frac{1}{4}|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied if $|x+\frac{1}{4}|<\frac{1}{3}.$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\frac{1}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186548041 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "45708bae-dc50-5c9d-9e5d-04417b00fc2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A parabola centered at $(-\frac{2}{5},0)$" :db/id 17592186547470} {:answer/id #uuid "6b4a85ba-f52f-5884-8c16-83695d5c66ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An ellipse centered at $(\frac{2}{5},0)$" :db/id 17592186547555} {:answer/id #uuid "97e12641-e027-541c-99c1-6366461603f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An ellipse centered at $(-\frac{1}{5},1)$" :db/id 17592186547647} {:answer/id #uuid "d8394f66-6c5c-5f76-a6ef-29a7574673c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola centered at $(\frac{2}{5},0)$" :db/id 17592186547774} {:answer/id #uuid "efefd15d-7892-53ae-9529-407152a306e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola centered at $(0,-\frac{2}{5})$" :db/id 17592186547809}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547774} :answer-field/id #uuid "7b399ec8-7eac-5c54-a396-185538576377" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547903}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "aad779ca-b824-50cb-b4dc-f0dd2ba06356" :question/math-academy-id "q-35267" :question/problem "Which of the following best describes the projection of the intersection between the elliptic cone ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}={z}^{2}$ and the plane $2x-y=0$ onto the $xz$-plane?" :question/worked-solution "Since we want to find the projection onto the $xz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $y.$ First, we solve the equation of the plane for $y,$ as follows:

$$
2x-y=0\,⟹\,y=2x
$$

Substituting the expression for $y$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(2x-1)^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+4{x}^{2}-4x+1 & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2}-5{x}^{2}+4x & =1 \\ {z}^{2}-5({x}^{2}-\frac{4}{5}x+\frac{4}{25})+\frac{4}{5} & =1 \\ {z}^{2}-5{({x}^{2}-\frac{2}{5})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ 5{z}^{2}-25{(x-\frac{2}{5})}^{2} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is the equation of a hyperbola centered at $(\frac{2}{5},0)$ in the $xz$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186548044 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3208f809-5202-519c-a4c1-b2c071b30e1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$0.78$ grams" :db/id 17592186547420} {:answer/id #uuid "3633d1c4-a4bd-5d6c-9a1e-fe155268f04d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$0.82$ grams" :db/id 17592186547428} {:answer/id #uuid "70486f57-d8c6-5d88-9e76-73287f23fb7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$0.75$ grams" :db/id 17592186547567} {:answer/id #uuid "b360a2fc-6825-56f7-a4ae-202963cd606a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$0.8$ grams" :db/id 17592186547706} {:answer/id #uuid "bf33ba30-f07a-5c5e-8673-051f5a7fed51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$0.85$ grams" :db/id 17592186547724}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547420} :answer-field/id #uuid "c889ce98-c36c-5100-9ccc-2833887780d6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547943}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b642f61b-90d3-52e8-a698-ed0e6fdd52ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-132849" :question/problem "In a factory, the average amount of sugar in a cookie is $15$ grams. However, $10\%$ of cookies contain no more than $14$ grams of sugar. Assuming that the amount of sugar in each cookie is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the amount of sugar in a cookie, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $p$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.10\,$ | $\,0.15\,$ | $\,0.20\,$ | $\,0.25\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the amount (in grams) of sugar in a cookie. Then we have $X∼N(15,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 14)=0.10.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 14) & =0.10 \\ P(Z\le \frac{14-15}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ Φ\left(-\frac{1}{\sigma }\right) & =0.10 \\ -\frac{1}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.10).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.10)=-1.2816.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sigma } & =-1.2816 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =1.2816 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{1.2816} \\  & ≈0.78.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548046 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c5745e4-3ad7-502f-bce7-234772762acf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/id 17592186547448} {:answer/id #uuid "5dbc9f32-3c2a-5c31-81b2-2d34ba3625e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186547521} {:answer/id #uuid "6771ee98-f25a-5cdc-91d7-e1d71d8eda3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{12}" :db/id 17592186547546} {:answer/id #uuid "83542680-0c0f-5bce-90df-2f3546c7a3e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186547596} {:answer/id #uuid "b01056a8-96d8-5259-85d4-db47041ed857" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{6}" :db/id 17592186547700}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547546} :answer-field/id #uuid "caa5996b-3602-50fb-816f-2fafeaae3fc0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547944}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b82a91db-40b3-51bf-b539-d94cf7913732" :question/math-academy-id "q-146284" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|4}=\frac{3}{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)]-{\mu }_{X|4}^{2} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}+{2}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}+{3}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}]-{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{2}-\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{7}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548055 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02e5024b-1c1c-54cb-83fb-120b748a9ccc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{{e}^{-\pi }+2{e}^{\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186547322} {:answer/id #uuid "423c048e-ea22-5f3a-ad4f-122dccb7ad0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1-{e}^{-2\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186547462} {:answer/id #uuid "4a9bb87c-c499-5aa9-adb7-e327fbd1e96b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-\pi }-{e}^{\pi }}{2}" :db/id 17592186547484} {:answer/id #uuid "9e2c4c31-6263-5a76-9ab5-f8cd0d8c8d92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{\pi }+{e}^{-\pi }}{4}" :db/id 17592186547660} {:answer/id #uuid "d48a3ee5-6a7b-5611-a42f-6f64ee2d3a9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2\pi }-1}{4}" :db/id 17592186547768}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547484} :answer-field/id #uuid "feba3f58-6495-56d8-aeb6-29990aa6bdd2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547967}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ce3e4235-61fa-5c48-8fde-1e9523a76255" :question/math-academy-id "q-115005" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $$
\displaystyle I=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I) \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I \\ 2I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ))-(\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}-\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }-{e}^{\pi }}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548062 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4763c363-04cb-5256-9ea2-4b8bec8c523b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/59/59b1c2add545d32140218fd886da190b5e6df8ba129f9a46d73bcc08ac67d82c.png" :db/id 17592186547475} {:answer/id #uuid "9d6ef56e-b549-54f0-819a-fb9fce9fde13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/db/db7c91f4a7041d85f55a800e791bd03f89b30285f5110126c5304ee21c197276.png" :db/id 17592186547659} {:answer/id #uuid "bb8ec659-c89b-58b5-8135-e398706146c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/4b/4b669fb58389bbe57e4e1c9c9cfb81631611163e5db3b92bb3d4b4081d32f726.png" :db/id 17592186547716} {:answer/id #uuid "d819a2a6-e5b3-547c-af82-631ab6a9d33b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/f2/f246bdc3d3d291e80089dd9c2f745923f7da92641e6c28602378543465b77b18.png" :db/id 17592186547773} {:answer/id #uuid "f9144efe-3cf6-5e18-826c-6e90ee15bf3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/6b/6b245838980c413d1f29912f5c8dfb51176057603c1c10743c602bc196c27c4b.png" :db/id 17592186547824}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547824} :answer-field/id #uuid "833540e8-f57c-5001-94b6-f95ad72e285f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547907}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d363b88c-fb75-5b26-bd10-c56875f40c1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-79427" :question/problem "![](images/75/75f479ff700f106f5cae6bafa94df87381d5fc0fca1758aad55f6bc5be1d7c38.png)

:question/math-academy-id "q-340658" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=2{x}^{3}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ &= \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548080 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d1be747-8a94-5aed-aafa-3f8e379525df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\text{m}" :db/id 17592186547374} {:answer/id #uuid "2bcb7040-6f3f-5555-bdad-85da6ddd1886" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}\,\text{m}" :db/id 17592186547401} {:answer/id #uuid "59823227-e905-5977-a5d2-bb84aa45354b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}\,\text{m}" :db/id 17592186547512} {:answer/id #uuid "a6c9df96-aec1-55e9-a6fa-579b1f853ec1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\text{m}" :db/id 17592186547684} {:answer/id #uuid "e0fc4746-3be8-5122-9467-181003e3756b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\text{m}" :db/id 17592186547784}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547784} :answer-field/id #uuid "1f66651c-8f9c-52e6-9972-14e6f7d0c2a3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547856}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fbeb0099-1c78-5b43-8e43-b8ec47f11368" :question/math-academy-id "q-50028" :question/problem "A fly’s position relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by the function $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\pi }{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t)\,\text{m},
$$ where $t$ is the time in minutes. Find its average position of the fly between $0$ and $2$ minutes." :question/worked-solution "To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{x}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{2-0}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\pi }{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t))\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}t))|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((\frac{{2}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot 2))-(\frac{{0}^{2}}{4}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot 0))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((1+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0+1)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average position is $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\text{m}.$"} {:db/id 17592186548195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0819b00b-ddf8-51fd-b337-f67bbb68e05a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{24 \sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186548189} {:answer/id #uuid "2d2d0946-fae9-532f-80d5-010b263a3d4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4 \sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186548190} {:answer/id #uuid "66c7d9c2-81ae-5068-8c96-91f51d97a8ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{24}{5}" :db/id 17592186548191} {:answer/id #uuid "895ba611-f922-55ef-9624-62e08b1e4ef5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- \frac{16 \sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186548193} {:answer/id #uuid "c4eef04d-da15-5f2a-aac3-6cfce868c8fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186548194}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548189} :answer-field/id #uuid "70e128fd-ce69-5958-8d26-3af81c7ff0b1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186548192}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e4d2c788-fb3a-5910-a90d-014c2de97596" :question/problem "Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=4 x^{2} y + 2 x e^{y}$ at the point $A(2,0)$ in the direction towards the point $B(4,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨4,1⟩-⟨2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(1)^{2}}}⟨2,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(4 x^{2} y + 2 x e^{y}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(4 x^{2} y + 2 x e^{y})⟩ \\  & =⟨8 x y + 2 e^{y},2 x \left(2 x + e^{y}\right)⟩ \\ ∇f(2,0) & =⟨8 (2) (0) + 2 e^{(0)},4 (2)^{2} + 2 (2) e^{(0)}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,20⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(2,0) & =∇f(2,0)\cdot u \\  & =⟨2,20⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{2 \sqrt{5}}{5},\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}⟩ \\  & =\frac{24 \sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "02f3a371-90b3-5820-b7e7-347e54e54605" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x+\frac{5}{2})^{2}+(y+\frac{3}{2})^{2}=\frac{17}{2}" :db/id 17592186548198} {:db/id 17592186548201 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b2745c4-1441-5995-aaf6-0adbc665aef0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x+\frac{9}{2})^{2}+(y+\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{25}{2}" :db/id 17592186548213} {:answer/id #uuid "37d4082a-8911-5b7c-b50a-10c433cbf0c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x+\frac{9}{2})^{2}+(y-\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{25}{2}" :db/id 17592186548215} {:answer/id #uuid "da3ff54f-5a25-50da-b204-8695bcb437f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x-\frac{9}{2})^{2}+(y+\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186548257} {:answer/id #uuid "ea42b5fa-8d2f-550e-9160-d2ffdc3c564b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x-\frac{9}{2})^{2}+(y+\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{25}{2}" :db/id 17592186548262} {:answer/id #uuid "ec1aadba-47b2-5657-83f5-47a149777663" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x+\frac{9}{2})^{2}+(y-\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186548264}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548215} :answer-field/id #uuid "16be170c-c7ff-5a97-93c7-1025786aea44" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186548209}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "0d76f3ef-fa61-505b-b0e2-335ce30237ba" :question/problem "![](images/07/0760173ffa9ede7dc926ff42ddc2a2474433408c2320bc6e37f7dc95ffde2dd1.png)

:question/problem "Evaluate ${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{\sinh }^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the following identity:

$$
\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{1}{{\sinh }^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{csch} }^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡9$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{csch} }^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡9}{\operatorname{csch} }^{2}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡9}{\operatorname{csch} }^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{coth}⁡u){|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡9} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡9)+\operatorname{coth}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡9}+1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡9}-1}+\frac{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+1}{{e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{{9}^{2}+1}{{9}^{2}-1}+\frac{{4}^{2}+1}{{4}^{2}-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{41}{40}+\frac{17}{15}) \\  & =\frac{13}{240}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186548978 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "075ae8f3-57cb-5b60-ba7d-7b522771c11d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186548370} {:answer/id #uuid "1b055083-25b0-50bd-915e-94df9cc030f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186548400} {:answer/id #uuid "321c8f80-1da5-598f-8ac9-48d513b22952" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186548454} {:answer/id #uuid "a9848c7d-6940-59ef-bdc8-e27fe80c778e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186548689} {:answer/id #uuid "b874085c-4187-5a6d-8924-748d9c4f64b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186548724}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548370} :answer-field/id #uuid "810830be-38ed-57ee-8e7a-4d8bf93a0313" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186548927}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0404d67e-b2ba-59db-a275-bcabad92e41d" :question/math-academy-id "q-145010" :question/problem "Consider the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\cos }^{2}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0$

II. $\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results.*

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )\to {0}^{-}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{-} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )\to {0}^{+}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{+}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi ) \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{-}$ using L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))^{′}}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{′}}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi ) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the first hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{4}{-2\cdot {0}^{-}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, and the second hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{4}{-2\cdot {0}^{+}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

$$

$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & ={\tan }^{2}⁡(0)\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)({\cos }^{2}⁡(0)+2) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot ({1}^{2}+2) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {0}^{+},$ we obtain

$$

- Statement III is false. Since the right limit of our derivative is not infinite, the curve does *not* have a vertical tangent at $\theta =0.$ In fact, it is a horizontal tangent.

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta $ where ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ 2\theta  & =\pi n \\ \theta  & =\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only two belong to the required domain, namely

$$
{\theta }_{1}=0,\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether any candidates have ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

We substitute our candidate solutions into ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(0) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =3 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ is a valid solution.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is also a valid solution.

Therefore, in ascending order, our curve has horizontal tangents at ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only one belongs to the required domain, namely

$$

$$

where ${\sigma }_{i}^{2}=\text{Var}[{X}_{i}],$ ${\sigma }_{12}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}],$ and $\rho $ is the correlation, then the joint probability density function of $X$ is

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{|Σ|}}\exp (-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu ))
$$

and $|Σ|$ denotes the determinant of $Σ.$

Using the given values of ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}$, and $\rho ,$ our covariance matrix is

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5 & \frac{4}{5}\cdot \sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\cdot \sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{5} & 5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
|Σ|=5\cdot 5-4\cdot 4=9.
$$

Substituting this value into our expression for the joint PDF, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{9}}\exp (-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )) \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }\exp (-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y=a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have ${\mu }_{1}=5$ and ${\mu }_{2}=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+3\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & ={\mu }_{1}+3\cdot {\mu }_{2} \\  & =5+3\cdot 1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}=1,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=5,$ and ${\sigma }_{12}={\sigma }_{21}=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var} [Y] & =\operatorname{Var} [{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}] \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 1+{3}^{2}\cdot 5+2\cdot 1\cdot 3\cdot (-2) \\  & =1+45-12 \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(8,34).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(1\le Y\le 5).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le Y\le 5) & =P(\frac{1-8}{\sqrt{34}}\le Z\le \frac{5-8}{\sqrt{34}}) \\  & =P(-1.20\le Z\le -0.51)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.20\le Z\le -0.51) & =P(Z\le -0.51)-P(Z<-1.20) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.51)-P(Z\le -1.20) \\  & =Φ(-0.51)-Φ(-1.20)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.20) & =0.1151 \\ Φ(-0.51) & =0.3050\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=2{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=2{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).
$$" :question/worked-solution "We have a horizontal tangent when

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.
$$

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=2{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=2{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta $ where ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =-1 \\ \theta  & =-\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only one belongs to the required domain, namely

$$
{\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{4}.
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether our candidate has ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solution into ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right) & =2{e}^{(3\pi /4)}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)) \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{(3\pi /4)} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, our curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}.$

*Hint: It is not necessary to use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the limit in part II.*" :question/worked-solution "When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$

$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & ={\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)({\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-3{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta ({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\cos }^{3}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{\cancel{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta }({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{\cancel{3}}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-3{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the limit in part II does *not* equal to $0,$ there curve does *not* have a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$ In fact, it is a vertical tangent.

$$

Therefore, our curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),
$$

and ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0$

II. $\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results.*

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\to {0}^{-}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{-} \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )\to {0}^{+}\,\text{as}\,\theta \to {\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{+}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =-1-(-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{-}$ using L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ))}^{′}}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ) \\  & =-(-1)+2\cdot (-1) \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the first hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, and the second hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.$
