$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y=2{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}.$ Calculate $P(Y\le 10).$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5596\,$ | $\,0.5636\,$ | $\,0.5675\,$ |
| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5987\,$ | $\,0.6026\,$ | $\,0.6064\,$ |
| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6368\,$ | $\,0.6406\,$ | $\,0.6443\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]^{T}$ is a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y=a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have ${\mu }_{1}=-2$ and ${\mu }_{2}=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[2{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}] \\  & =2\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+4\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & =2{\mu }_{1}+4{\mu }_{2} \\  & =2(-2)+4(3) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}=2,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=4,$ and ${\sigma }_{12}={\sigma }_{21}=-1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var} [Y] & =\operatorname{Var} [2{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}] \\  & ={2}^{2}(2)+{4}^{2}(4)+2(2)(4)(-1) \\  & =8+64-16 \\  & =56.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(8,56).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(Y\le 10).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le 10) & =P(Z\le \frac{10-8}{\sqrt{56}}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.27) \\  & =Φ(0.27)\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.27)=0.6064.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(Y\le 10)=0.6064.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549058 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28d2be98-9a4d-5c88-abaa-0360571b0ab6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186548436} {:answer/id #uuid "41c64781-3167-56a3-b3e8-fd75bb289c1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186548480} {:answer/id #uuid "61db2b55-0411-5c2c-8bcf-dbb5a9ead9bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186548540} {:answer/id #uuid "7b7f8da8-6744-55ff-b218-c7923a9889bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186548584} {:answer/id #uuid "e3396cf7-276b-5255-a8b9-c8f3c0ee558c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186548795}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548795} :answer-field/id #uuid "ae057d8d-edb0-54d6-852b-f3d8185d31f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186548940}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e38cbfdc-40f4-5e23-81ff-d9532344f653" :question/math-academy-id "q-118856" :question/problem "Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}$ and the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u=-{x}^{4}$,  then $\text{d}u=-4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{4}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\lim_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{x}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\lim_{a\to -\infty }{(-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-{x}^{4}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\lim_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{-{a}^{4}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x{|}^{3}{e}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549063 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8c8e07c3-2def-544a-a55d-b8aa75578002" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186548628} {:answer/id #uuid "8eda6459-1c9a-583b-ad18-38a2797dce2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186548633} {:answer/id #uuid "d52a3250-40d4-5be6-bebf-0f7260791e00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186548770} {:answer/id #uuid "de0fb6b2-1d44-5d73-8290-45b87e7ed17d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186548786} {:answer/id #uuid "e9bac1f0-5ba2-5a77-97be-1d6bcee5c1f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186548814}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548786} :answer-field/id #uuid "ed169fc4-26e4-5919-a511-cdee5f9fe8ac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186548969}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ea9cfed4-0f16-55b7-9b0d-f746c7584998" :question/math-academy-id "q-20588" :question/problem "Compute the value of $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$ for which the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ has vertical tangents, given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=-{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta .
$$" :question/worked-solution "We have a vertical tangent when

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.
$$

To find the vertical tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=-{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta $ where ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1) & =0 \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations: 

$$
-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =0,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1=0
$$

Let's solve each equation separately.

- First, we solve the equation

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =0,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
{\theta }_{1}=0.
$$

- Then, we solve the equation

$$
2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1=0,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

There are no solutions to this equation for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether our candidate has ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solution into ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${y}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =-{\sin }^{2}⁡(0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+{\cos }^{2}⁡(0) \\  & =2 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ is a valid solution.

So, our curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =0.$

$$

$$

where $\mu $ is the mean vector and $Σ$ is the corresponding covariance matrix, find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]^{T}$ is a bivariate normal vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{pmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{pmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} \\ \rho {\sigma }_{1}{\sigma }_{2} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\sigma }_{i}^{2}=\text{Var}[{X}_{i}],$ ${\sigma }_{12}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}],$ and $\rho $ is the correlation, then the joint probability density function of $X$ is

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{|Σ|}}\exp (-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu ))
$$

and $|Σ|$ denotes the determinant of $Σ.$

Using the given values of ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}$, and $\rho ,$ our covariance matrix is

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}20 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\cdot \sqrt{20}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\cdot \sqrt{20}\cdot \sqrt{2} & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}20 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
|Σ|=20\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot (-2)=36.
$$

Substituting this value into our expression for the joint PDF, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{36}}\exp (-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )) \\  & =\frac{1}{12\pi }\exp (-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu )^{T}\,{Σ}^{-1}\,(x-\mu )).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $k=12\pi .$"} {:db/id 17592186549069 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27c3cfe2-4355-5ff2-ab48-e1edb2a062fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\le \frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/id 17592186548434} {:answer/id #uuid "30f97a9c-235e-5b9d-ad94-5f5faf7b30d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\le \frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/id 17592186548452} {:answer/id #uuid "65ce5038-a8fa-57b9-ae79-4389ab61c39d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/id 17592186548547} {:answer/id #uuid "975cd023-3182-5ea3-b55f-a53cbc308e13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\ge \frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/id 17592186548650} {:answer/id #uuid "f340d91e-1c83-5dd3-a48f-6d49a10addf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\le \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/id 17592186548837}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186548434} :answer-field/id #uuid "6516c76a-3a0c-5cff-b332-8d24558288a2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186548918}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f9ce2daa-e38d-5bb8-b99f-f6261d8e2ed1" :question/math-academy-id "q-365328" :question/problem "Solve the inequality $3\cdot {2}^{1-3x}\ge {\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{x-4}.$" :question/worked-solution "Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot {2}^{1-3x} & \ge {\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{x-4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot {2}^{1-3x}) & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡[{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{x-4}] \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+(1-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \ge (x-4)\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+(1-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \ge (x-4)(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+(1-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \ge (x-4)(0-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+(1-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \ge (4-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2-3x\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \ge 4\operatorname{ln}⁡3-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡3-3x\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \ge 4\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \ge 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}

:question/problem "$$

The Fourier series of the $4\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function 

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}5, & x\in [0,2\pi ) \\ -2, & x\in [-2\pi ,0)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

is shown above. Find the exact value of ${b}_{3}.$

${b}_{3}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the sine coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2\pi .$ Also, $f(x)=5$ for $x\in [0,2\pi )$ and $f(x)=-2$ for $x\in [-2\pi ,0).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$

$$

$$

The disjoint union ${S}_{0}⊔{S}_{1}⊔{S}_{2}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$

$$

$$

$$

- Since $46\%$ of children with scoliosis are female, we have

$$

$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen child who practices one sport has scoliosis, which is represented as $P(C∣{S}_{1}).$

$$

$$

$$
y=5\sqrt[3]{x}+3
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=5\sqrt[3]{y}+3.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\sqrt[3]{y}+3 \\ 5\sqrt[3]{y} & =x-3 \\ \sqrt[3]{y} & =\frac{1}{5}(x-3) \\ (\sqrt[3]{y})^{3} & ={(\frac{1}{5}(x-3))}^{3} \\ y & =\frac{1}{125}(x-3)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{125}(x-3)^{3}.

$$" :question/worked-solution "For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=7x-4$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(7x-4)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=7x-4\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=7 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(\frac{1}{n}[(7x-4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{7}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(((7\pi -4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{7}{n}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{2}{n\pi }(0+\frac{7}{n}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{14(\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-1)}{{n}^{2}\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{14((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is

$$
f(x)∼(-4+\frac{7\pi }{2})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{14((-1)^{n}-1)}{\pi {n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549959 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "824395f4-e1d3-5e0f-879c-0d03e310d7a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186549559}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549559} :answer-field/id #uuid "6c30a88d-8e13-5d71-9185-007060f3d4e5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186549846}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "46598e7e-81d3-578b-80cc-94d59f9707e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-341861" :question/problem "$$

${a}_{2}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=x+1$ for $x\in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(uv\,{|}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{\pi }{[(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)]}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{\pi }[3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-(-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )]-\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{\pi }\right){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)]}_{-2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot 0+\frac{1}{{\pi }^{2}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2\pi )]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{\pi }^{2}}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549979 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "67d2eb68-0652-5e48-b001-a45c2700c7e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186549515} {:answer/id #uuid "94798f5c-574c-53cd-bb0e-eb9396410fae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186549605} {:answer/id #uuid "c199e1eb-7983-554d-81aa-b675e5252dbd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186549680} {:answer/id #uuid "e8394076-ef1d-5d29-b139-67414f969f56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186549743} {:answer/id #uuid "ee167035-8819-5d49-80a8-31c9bebffaab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186549753}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549515} :answer-field/id #uuid "63772144-9630-582a-8d79-f08320bc64ad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186549842}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8e8e30b7-68c9-50ac-bfbf-42853c6a4c1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-161305" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v),$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}y,\hspace{0.222em}xz⟩,\hspace{1em}\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}uv⟩,\hspace{1em}(u,v)\in D⊂{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}a{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+bu{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y,\,xz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-2{v}^{2})+{v}^{2}\cdot (-u)+{u}^{2}v\cdot 2v \\  & =-2u{v}^{2}-u{v}^{2}+2{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}-3u{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\cdot {u}^{2}{v}^{2}+(-3)\cdot u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2-3=-1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549980 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15b65751-5861-527d-bc09-9b006f1be127" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-341780" :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $7$th sine coefficient of the series is

$$
{b}_{7}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)=x$ and $L=2\pi ,$ the $7$th sine coefficient becomes

$$
{b}_{7}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, $7$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{7} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(7s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(7s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=2\pi $ and $f(x)=x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{7} & =\frac{1}{2\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{2\pi }x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7}{2}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549988 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "70556f37-c5ed-583c-a04b-123cc8508968" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{(x-6)^2}{16}" :db/id 17592186549528}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549528} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7ff35a3-b189-5c5b-b194-1dd1bc180b94" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186549898}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "aa587d06-3d76-54dc-bc14-c7a25e414d3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-277045" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=6-4\sqrt{x}.$

${f}^{-1}(x)=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=6-4\sqrt{x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=6-4\sqrt{y}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6-4\sqrt{y} \\ 4\sqrt{y} & =6-x \\ \sqrt{y} & =\frac{1}{4}(6-x) \\ (\sqrt{y})^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{4}(6-x))}^{2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{16}(6-x)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{16}(6-x)^{2}.
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x\ge 0,\,f(x)\le 6.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of ${f}^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x\le 6,\,{f}^{-1}(x)\ge 0.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186549993 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f47cc34-1a40-54f8-8f21-1937b1207c8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186549377}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549377} :answer-field/id #uuid "b3e4d068-52a7-54b2-9f52-ab0c0b143b6e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186549888}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "bc08f5e3-6f0e-55df-87af-7552a06bb9df" :question/math-academy-id "q-341802" :question/problem "$$

$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,9{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+16{x}_{2}^{2}-50{x}_{1}+25{x}_{2}=0.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=9{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+16{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $25{y}_{1}^{2}$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,\underbrace{9{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+16{x}_{2}^{2}}_{Q(x)}-50{x}_{1}+25{x}_{2}=0
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{4}{5}{y}_{2}-\frac{3}{5}{y}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{4}{5}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}_{1}^{2}-24{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+16{x}_{2}^{2}-50{x}_{1}+25{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 25{y}_{1}^{2}-50(\frac{4}{5}{y}_{2}-\frac{3}{5}{y}_{1})+25(\frac{4}{5}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{y}_{2}) & =0 \\ 25{y}_{1}^{2}+50{y}_{1}-25{y}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{1}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}25{y}_{1}^{2}+50{y}_{1}-25{y}_{2} & =0 \\ {y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} & =0 \\ {y}_{1}^{2}+2{y}_{1}+1-1-{y}_{2} & =0 \\ ({y}_{1}+1)^{2}-1-{y}_{2} & =0 \\ ({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & ={y}_{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}+1, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2}+1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{1}+1)^{2} & ={y}_{2}+1 \\ {z}_{1}^{2} & ={z}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

${a}_{1}=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3$ and $f(x)=2x+7$ for $x\in [-3,3).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(2x+7)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=2x+7\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{3}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}(uv\,{|}_{-3}^{3}-{\int }_{-3}^{3}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3}{\pi }{[(2x+7)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}-{\int }_{-3}^{3}\frac{3}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\cdot 2\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3}{\pi }[13\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )]-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{-3}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{3}{\pi }\cdot 0-\frac{6}{\pi }\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{\pi }\right){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}x)]}_{-3}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{18}{{\pi }^{2}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )]) \\  & =\frac{6}{{\pi }^{2}}(-1-(-1)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186550013 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8ca68a00-32fb-52b6-9611-af784188ac51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{4}(x+10)^2" :db/id 17592186549584}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549584} :answer-field/id #uuid "87121302-8c37-5665-97c7-f22db0a986f9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186549864}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f2fd8190-fb82-5675-b05f-057d697af7cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-270776" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}-10.$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}-10
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{y}-10.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{y}-10 \\ \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{y} & =x+10 \\ \sqrt{y} & =\frac{3}{2}(x+10) \\ (\sqrt{y})^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{2}(x+10))}^{2} \\ y & =\frac{9}{4}(x+10)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{9}{4}(x+10)^{2}.
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x\ge 0,\,f(x)\ge -10.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of ${f}^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x\ge -10,\,{f}^{-1}(x)\ge 0.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186550017 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f5a02a6-edc8-579d-9f3e-8685852c250f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{64}(x+7)^{3}" :db/id 17592186549340} {:answer/id #uuid "2a68acc7-11c9-53ec-9edf-5225b6802e14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=64{x}^{3}+7" :db/id 17592186549411} {:answer/id #uuid "41a67b62-1927-57c7-b8fd-09c8ea128d9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=4(x+7)^{3}" :db/id 17592186549450} {:answer/id #uuid "b3dda357-db83-5268-bb16-701863b5d617" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{7}(x+4)^{3}" :db/id 17592186549651} {:answer/id #uuid "f16acb2b-4b5f-577f-b3ff-41c909981ff7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{7}{x}^{3}+4" :db/id 17592186549762}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549340} :answer-field/id #uuid "1e400004-8c3b-55eb-9c62-48d0e98c825c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186549813}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f867e6a6-dbb2-59f4-99c3-23f6d9793b91" :question/math-academy-id "q-148737" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=4\sqrt[3]{x}-7.$" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

"fb364528-cf72-5941-b3b8-fc021ca9ace0" :question/math-academy-id "q-341777" :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $6$th cosine coefficient of the series is

$$
{a}_{6}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)={e}^{-{x}^{2}}$ and $L=5,$ the $6$th cosine coefficient becomes

$$
{a}_{6}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

$$
u=\frac{2}{x y},\qquad v=4 x^{3} y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the curves

$$
y=\frac{1}{x},\qquad y=\frac{2}{5 x},\qquad y=\frac{1}{4 x^{3}},\qquad y=\frac{7}{4 x^{3}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{2}{x y},\,v=4 x^{3} y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{2}{x y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{2}{5 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=5 & ⟹\, & u=5\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=4 x^{3} y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{7}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=7 & ⟹\, & v=7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 7\}
$$

![](images/d3/d3dd7067bbcb0a6e3c901d12a2795500e192594a14e7f1373dd325e4fd270363.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{2}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{2}{x y^{2}} \\ 12 x^{2} y & 4 x^{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{16 x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{y}{16 x}=\frac{x^{2} y^{2}}{16 x^{3} y}=\frac{1}{u^{2} v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{u^{2} v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{u^{2} v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{u^{2}}\,\mathrm d u\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{v}\,\mathrm d v \\  & =(- \frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2})\cdot (\ln 7-\ln 1) \\  & =\frac{3 \ln{\left(7 \right)}}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186550274 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "091b43cb-3824-5278-b02a-80954580abf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\ln{\left(3 \right)}" :db/id 17592186550253} {:answer/id #uuid "0a734b23-70c8-5a87-b181-df0896bb13b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{6}" :db/id 17592186550254} {:answer/id #uuid "178d842d-884a-503a-aed8-8f5a489cdee1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{6}" :db/id 17592186550257} {:answer/id #uuid "4e095de2-8e72-5c9f-a025-ba50adefeaf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}{6}" :db/id 17592186550273} {:answer/id #uuid "788699c0-c7c8-57d6-9abc-ef6f6c7c2cb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5 \ln{\left(6 \right)}}{6}" :db/id 17592186550286}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186550257} :answer-field/id #uuid "783e65fb-53de-5f75-a984-ad63c97517df" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186550285}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4f546348-0394-5bd9-acc6-4dd4084bdee8" :question/problem "Using the change of variables

$$

$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$

$$

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{3 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{x y}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3 \\  & y=\frac{1}{8 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{1}{x y}=8 & ⟹\, & u=8\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=x^{2} y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{x^{2}} & ⟹\, & x^{2} y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{4}{x^{2}} & ⟹\, & x^{2} y=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 8,\,1\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](images/f5/f506bb81b18dce423e50eedc19841b7a5896230413f7f1a876aa93d27e68edf9.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{1}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{1}{x y^{2}} \\ 2 x y & x^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=y=\frac{x^{2} y^{2}}{x^{2} y}=\frac{1}{u^{2} v}.

$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "0eabe319-fbfe-5f66-832c-db699322266a" :question/math-academy-id "q-114899" :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{2}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[4{(2+\frac{k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{1}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{1}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=4{x}_{k}^{3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[4{(2+\frac{k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].
$$

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "336eb7d8-27df-584e-adc9-df5d1de8bc4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-344058" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}-3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}} & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)) \\  & \,-3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)) \\  & \,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-3 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=2,$ which means the constant term is given by

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=1.
$$

Next, from the third equation, 

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
\left(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9}\right)\frac{n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{9} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{9}\cdot \left(-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\right) \\  & =\frac{18}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}∼1 & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{162}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \\  & +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{18}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+81)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186551260 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15c18ebe-c675-5bcf-b34d-fee9f38573de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+15x+25+\frac{100}{3x-5}" :db/id 17592186550415} {:answer/id #uuid "5afbc067-5499-538e-a8b6-7c624c3edc2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-50+\frac{100}{3x-5}" :db/id 17592186550591} {:answer/id #uuid "62a672e0-4667-5d14-94ed-8c58ba311d8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}-9x+2-\frac{100}{3x-5}" :db/id 17592186550605} {:answer/id #uuid "af6c1d59-c605-55b7-98a8-43b605decc44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+5x+25-\frac{100}{3x-5}" :db/id 17592186550845} {:answer/id #uuid "d952f828-349f-5d26-a20c-bf66dfa362fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+9x+21+\frac{100}{3x-5}" :db/id 17592186550955}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186550415} :answer-field/id #uuid "a916e5ab-d2bf-5c35-99df-efcacc3f8e56" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186551167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "343c6002-3a70-5903-a244-0acddb5859ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-73818" :question/problem "$\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}=$" :question/worked-solution "We can calculate $\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}$ using synthetic division.

For synthetic division to work, we need the coefficient of $x$ in the denominator to be equal to $1.$ So first, we factor the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5} & =\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3(x-\frac{5}{3})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})}\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $$
\displaystyle \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})},
$$ we arrive at the following:

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrrrr} & {x}^{4} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{5}{3} & 9 & 12 & 0 & 0 & -25 \\  & ↓ & 15 & 45 & 75 & 125 \\ \hline  & 9 & 27 & 45 & 75 & 100\end{array}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})} & =\frac{1}{3}(9{x}^{3}+27{x}^{2}+45x+75+\frac{100}{(x-\frac{5}{3})}) \\  & =3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+15x+25+\frac{100}{3x-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, our final result is

$$
\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}=3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+15x+25+\frac{100}{3x-5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186551269 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d65c081f-46e7-50d2-b0af-c99aac626906" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/id 17592186550948}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186550948} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1767cf0-549a-5130-876d-9403ed25774d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186551197}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "44100483-c880-5325-8cb2-5b4178bd1ae8" :question/math-academy-id "q-267389" :question/problem "![](images/fe/fe2f1266db9f675a2c82803728d37f53d0995c25cf61f74304a731c3d21c64c8.png)

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{3}\,\, & \le \,\,3 \\ (-3)\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{3}\right)\,\, & \ge \,\,(-3)\cdot 3 \\ (-3)\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{3}\right)\,\, & \ge \,\,-9\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{3}\right) & \ge -9 \\ (\cancel{-}3)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{y}{3}) & \ge -9 \\ 3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $3$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -9 \\ \frac{3y}{3} & \ge -9 \\ \frac{\cancel{3}y}{\cancel{3}} & \ge -9 \\ y & \ge -9\end{aligned}
$$

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a503430-335a-52ca-a8f2-1a25c8b18de5" :question/math-academy-id "q-343819" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+3y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot \cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)+{{field-2}}\cdot \sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)+{b}_{n}\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)+{b}_{n}\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{2}\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{2}\cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}\cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)) \\  & \,+3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)+{b}_{n}\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{3{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{a}_{n})\cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n})\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3{a}_{0}}{2}=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{a}_{n}=0 \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n}=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the second equation, 

$$
{a}_{n}=-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6}.
$$

Substituting this into the third equation gives

$$
-\left(-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6}\right)\frac{n\pi }{2}+3{b}_{n}=\frac{2(-1)^{n}}{n\pi }\,⇒\,{b}_{n}=\frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}
$$

Therefore, for ${a}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{6} \\  & =-\frac{n\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)} \\  & =-\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,-\frac{4(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36}\cdot \cos \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right)+\frac{24(-1)^{n}}{n\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+36)}\cdot \sin \,\left(\frac{n\pi x}{2}\right).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186551348 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01413d91-53a9-5c2f-95f0-dd975a28a04f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value 17592186551174}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ed658204-766e-56cd-a12e-1cf2b14b40f7" :question/math-academy-id "q-343391" :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of the function $F(x)=3{x}^{2}$ defined on $[-\pi ,\pi ).$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below, showing the derivation of a series converging to the $2\pi $-periodic extension of

from the corresponding Fourier series of $f(x).$

The Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

Since $f$ is

on $R,$ we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term to get

$$
{x}^{3}∼{\pi }^{2}x+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{{field-3}}\cdot {{field-4}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that $F(x)$ is an even function. So, the Fourier series of its $2L$-periodic extension has the form

$$
\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right).
$$

In our case, $L=\pi $ and we are already given the coefficients for $n\ge 1.$ Thus, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\pi }^{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Now, notice that the function $F$ is continuous on $(-\pi ,\pi ).$ 
Therefore, the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f$ is $\text{piecewise continuous}$ on $R,$ so we may integrate its Fourier series term-by-term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t & ∼{\int }_{0}^{x}({\pi }^{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nt))\text{d}t \\ [{t}^{3}]_{0}^{x} & ∼[{\pi }^{2}t]_{0}^{x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot [\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nt)]_{0}^{x} \\ {x}^{3} & ∼{\pi }^{2}x+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{12(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186551357 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28f1f4b7-57c0-56e1-a117-8415a85c841e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(3+\frac{2i}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]" :db/id 17592186550468} {:answer/id #uuid "34501985-19ea-50dc-8d60-3b788c0405c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(3+\frac{2i}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}]" :db/id 17592186550497} {:answer/id #uuid "51e949c9-0d0e-5fdb-bb95-ab16798be0f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{2i}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{n}]" :db/id 17592186550562} {:answer/id #uuid "6591ea6e-2346-5c79-acf4-89b87782b7b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{i}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{n}]" :db/id 17592186550616} {:answer/id #uuid "dfa0ac59-d407-5702-ab18-aa0299efd7dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{4i}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{4}{n}]" :db/id 17592186550978}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186550497} :answer-field/id #uuid "2bc5e161-63d6-5b2f-8b4b-8f2692b551e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186551091}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fea7dc0c-332b-5e65-b34c-aa74602e656a" :question/math-academy-id "q-113885" :question/problem "What is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x
$$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{4}(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=(x+1)^{2},$ the lower bound is $a=2,$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-2}{n}=\frac{2}{n},
$$

and therefore
