$$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "If we let $u=4x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /12$ | $\pi /8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /8}3{\csc }^{2}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}3{\csc }^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\csc }^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(u))\,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(-\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(0+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553507 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "57c13dfc-1ac7-5356-938c-6c2321bc1f4c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186553057} {:answer/id #uuid "6fc4d700-b68c-5883-8732-9a880579eb80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186553096} {:answer/id #uuid "998b0089-057f-547f-a803-33516e8d42f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186553179} {:answer/id #uuid "b3c1059f-3768-5550-b92c-3b1eac23c433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186553230} {:answer/id #uuid "eaf263e5-3844-5480-8ed4-14e1d316bb2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186553334}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553230} :answer-field/id #uuid "43dbda7b-1743-5761-a7b9-ff0017ff6e6e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "27367b15-5da8-51eb-9ba6-49205792b06d" :question/math-academy-id "q-162976" :question/problem "The lamina $$
\displaystyle D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x\}
$$ has the mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=3y\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Find the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "The moment of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\lambda (x,y)$ about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{M}_{x}={∬}_{D}y\,\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, $D$ is represented as a type I plane region and $\lambda (x,y)=3y\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ 

Therefore, the moment is

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\cdot 3y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}3{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot {[{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\sin }^{3}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{\sin }^{4}⁡x}{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553508 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "043a47af-d945-52f5-a2ff-8dbd6cbb4d74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "99" :db/id 17592186552873} {:answer/id #uuid "084f29ee-31a1-58ac-a67f-c03a521c322a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100" :db/id 17592186552877} {:answer/id #uuid "0c339ee0-0900-5543-a85c-daf2f6f91a9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80" :db/id 17592186552881} {:answer/id #uuid "1ba0bf79-9f84-57c9-91e2-72a01fc879ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "81" :db/id 17592186552916} {:answer/id #uuid "e589549d-f5f7-5a08-a2a2-44640623c1a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90" :db/id 17592186553324}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186552873} :answer-field/id #uuid "9e1b0569-2ef4-5afb-bff6-cf96b04525ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553453}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "27c3df67-079e-5e01-9714-60648afd83ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-162628" :question/problem "![](images/84/84cfc63faa3514c7b6151d5ab8f3f8e4e7deaafa8739fa637af2f0ce7453b7fb.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(1,1)$ and $B(5,4).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy)=2x-2x=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,1)$ to $B(5,4)$ and  ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](images/18/18b1a5bdc11ca3c2b4b728cf8df3a3e1c4b6c2fbbe86549e9ad773367495c533.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+j+t\cdot [(5\,i+4j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=(4t+1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}+8t+1, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2xy=-2(4t+1)(3t+1)=-24{t}^{2}-14t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((16{t}^{2}+8t+1)\cdot (3)-(-24{t}^{2}-14t-2)\cdot (4))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,144{t}^{2}+80t+11\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[48{t}^{3}+40{t}^{2}+11t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(48+40+11) \\  & =99.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=99.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553509 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "42a492d9-cf7a-517a-a388-35a26f6d769e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}+\frac{7-3t}{9}" :db/id 17592186553006} {:answer/id #uuid "58f86b27-aaef-5734-b574-cf851cfc63b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}+\frac{3t-5}{9}" :db/id 17592186553059} {:answer/id #uuid "5f13f1d2-9669-574a-b992-547d64c416c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}+\frac{5-3t}{9}" :db/id 17592186553070} {:answer/id #uuid "aa54b773-38b6-5c26-897c-a183baeabac4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}-\frac{7-3t}{9}" :db/id 17592186553211} {:answer/id #uuid "bacb037c-ce80-5974-9d4b-3e4d832343d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}-\frac{3t-5}{9}" :db/id 17592186553239}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553239} :answer-field/id #uuid "6cbf215b-97cc-524e-b504-f280dea50225" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553426}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "305f1606-0562-59f2-b1e4-3359528e4a32" :question/math-academy-id "q-342786" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-3y={u}_{2}(t)\cdot (t-2)\,,\,y(0)=5,
$$

where ${u}_{2}(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

You're given that the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{5}{s-3}+\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}
$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as 

$$
y(t)=5{e}^{3t}+u(t-2)\cdot g(t).
$$

Find the function $g(t).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$

We focus on the term with the exponential ${e}^{-2s}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s-3)$ and a repeated linear factor ${s}^{2},$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{1}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{C}{s-3}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
1=As(s-3)+B(s-3)+C{s}^{2}.
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=0,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(-3)+C(0)\,⟹\,B=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

- Setting $s=3,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(0)+C(9)\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+C\,⟹\,A=-C=-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=-\frac{1}{9s}-\frac{1}{3{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{9(s-3)}.
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{1}{9s}-\frac{1}{3{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{9(s-3)}\} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{t}{3}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-2s}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=2.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-2)f(t-2) & =u(t-2)(-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{t-2}{3}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}) \\  & =u(t-2)(-\frac{3t-5}{9}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=5{e}^{3t}+u(t-2)\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}-\frac{3t-5}{9}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553511 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a1689b3-c36c-5147-a643-ad05385c39c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186552946} {:answer/id #uuid "2d67fef5-d17a-5044-86dd-9b0dd6104d49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186552954} {:answer/id #uuid "513e98ed-26b8-5fdd-95e1-91a5c0e76825" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{x}^{2}" :db/id 17592186553043} {:answer/id #uuid "a031cdff-6a41-52e9-aeab-5a6e16f24cf8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{x}^{2}+xy" :db/id 17592186553192} {:answer/id #uuid "d69014c4-c493-5bef-9f1c-7c17c3e7aba8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4({x}^{2}-1)" :db/id 17592186553300}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553043} :answer-field/id #uuid "7efa0a56-60d9-584e-8007-e5d380ed9d48" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553436}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "30b095cd-424c-553d-bb7d-82a5c5e826eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-127225" :question/problem "According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨{x}^{3}+{y}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{2}y⟩$
across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(1,0),(0,2),$ and $(-1,2)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $\mathbf{n}$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/84/848dfedddea9803dcf39b4624f2966b63f080920ed19b875dc691e8fe9d3b038.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186553515 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f27cc60-4ad8-593e-9ef5-5d362258831b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{{n}^{4}}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,(j-2)^{3}" :db/id 17592186552888} {:answer/id #uuid "1b99b866-cfcd-5ab3-97e9-6c269fcfe9fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{81}{{n}^{2}}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,{j}^{3}" :db/id 17592186552915} {:answer/id #uuid "265541b8-e6de-5a62-ba09-d145d5094973" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{{n}^{2}}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,{j}^{3}" :db/id 17592186552935} {:answer/id #uuid "93fd0fdd-bb74-5b4c-9cce-c52e5835da23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{81}{{n}^{4}}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,{j}^{3}" :db/id 17592186553167} {:answer/id #uuid "dfa60640-75f4-50e0-8054-4fd539a3b520" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{{n}^{3}}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,{j}^{3}" :db/id 17592186553312}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553167} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c5920c5-4b86-5a6d-b9f0-0d98e11b6c2d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553418}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "37c41f7c-c697-50e0-8b4c-374dcc3f004e" :question/math-academy-id "q-73165" :question/problem "The area under the curve $y=(x+2)^{3}$ between $x=-2$ and $x=1$ and the $x$-axis is approximated by a left Riemann sum using $n$ subintervals of equal length. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?" :question/worked-solution "The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})Δx,
$$

where $n$ is the number of subintervals,   ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx$, and  $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

The endpoints indicate that $a=-2$ and $b=1,$ so the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{1-(-2)}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the left Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})Δx & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(a+jΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(-2+j\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(-2+\frac{3j}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}{(-2+\frac{3j}{n}+2)}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{3}{n}{\left(\frac{3j}{n}\right)}^{3} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{3}{n}\cdot \frac{27{j}^{3}}{{n}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{81}{{n}^{4}}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,{j}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553521 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9af70380-e503-50b8-8456-a4d26ba605ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{2x+1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{-x(x+1)}}" :db/id 17592186553182} {:answer/id #uuid "a95d1f7e-3ad0-5e4e-bba3-859fd658d6d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{2x+1}(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{-x(x+1)}})" :db/id 17592186553208} {:answer/id #uuid "aa65b81f-556d-5759-8d4a-d96a8f580eb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{2x+1}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{-x(x+1)}}" :db/id 17592186553213} {:answer/id #uuid "ad6f8b25-d391-5520-b35a-d57fb931c15e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{2x+1}(1+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{-x(x+1)}})" :db/id 17592186553216} {:answer/id #uuid "c5520221-3ee7-520d-9922-76e4e5d7251d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{2x+1}(1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{-x(x+1)}})" :db/id 17592186553259}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553216} :answer-field/id #uuid "f6f2ed98-5841-5a83-8d7d-7fd91c809d2d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553485}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5339fa9a-9297-5700-9672-1deb7e152857" :question/math-academy-id "q-95527" :question/problem "If $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(2x+1),$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic secant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(2x+1)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡(2x+1)) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}-\left(-\frac{1}{(2x+1)\sqrt{1-(2x+1)^{2}}}\right)\cdot (2x+1)^{′} \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}+\frac{1}{(2x+1)\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}-4x-1}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}+\frac{2}{(2x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-4x}} \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{-4x(x+1)}}) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}(1+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{-x(x+1)}}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553530 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2aeb199f-b948-5795-9348-3e5e109c2652" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y" :db/id 17592186552948} {:answer/id #uuid "42dfda97-5990-5386-9a3e-eab1d6c81981" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡y" :db/id 17592186553007} {:answer/id #uuid "436a0b26-8a41-555d-8ec3-92df6c6037dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡y" :db/id 17592186553008} {:answer/id #uuid "4cb7ea56-a736-5085-98e7-33c9b2e06200" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y" :db/id 17592186553036} {:answer/id #uuid "7302919e-aae8-52d6-be57-1c5a122ace53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡y" :db/id 17592186553104}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553104} :answer-field/id #uuid "2184ddd6-bb84-56f9-ac10-b6a376a8e0a3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553388}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "64924153-c273-5495-a9b7-e1268d0994d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-143696" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables with the joint probability density function 

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y, & 1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables with the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.
$$

Let's draw the region $D$ in the $uv$-plane where the function $f(u,v)$ is nonzero. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/00/00e0dcbd7ea22f09db76b03fc4d7bda328f1b1f17ceeb998cf039241dafd8da3.png)

For the purposes of computation, we're only interested in the region inside $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. This is given by

$$
D\cap Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le x,\,0\le v\le y\}.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v & ={\int }_{0}^{y}{\int }_{1}^{x}\frac{1}{4}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡v{\int }_{1}^{x}u\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡v{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{u=1}^{u=x}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡v({x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1){\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)[\operatorname{sin}⁡v]_{v=0}^{v=y} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553533 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f15eefe-3a94-52eb-b0db-fbe7b7e8c5e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3j+3}{n}\right)" :db/id 17592186552926} {:answer/id #uuid "494d84f7-e321-5bbf-9260-a5d994e6bad2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{j=1}^{n-1}\,\frac{3}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{j}{n}+3)" :db/id 17592186553021} {:answer/id #uuid "637e03eb-1b6f-575b-8c6c-dcc21ef08a1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{j=0}^{n}\,\frac{3}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3j}{n}\right)" :db/id 17592186553081} {:answer/id #uuid "903605f0-bbb6-51e7-b29a-abff3e1d83c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,\frac{3}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3j}{n}\right)" :db/id 17592186553155} {:answer/id #uuid "9b0d2c49-0687-55c5-88d3-59452dabce7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\,\frac{3}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{j}{n}\right)" :db/id 17592186553183}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553155} :answer-field/id #uuid "0287ad59-5a09-5d14-b668-9a96a7a6d0a9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553376}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6c6f0b11-13a1-5912-b416-72a57173178b" :question/math-academy-id "q-116625" :question/problem "The area under the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+3)$ between $x=-3$ and $x=0$ and the $x$-axis is approximated by a left Riemann sum using $n$ subintervals of equal length. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?" :question/worked-solution "The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

where $n$ is the number of subintervals, ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx$, and  $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

The endpoints indicate that $a=-3$ and $b=0,$ so the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{0-(-3)}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the left Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(a+jΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(-3+j\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(-3+\frac{3j}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,\frac{3}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(-3+\frac{3j}{n}+3) \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,\frac{3}{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3j}{n}\right).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553540 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "954ddca6-7c11-5b1b-8b70-3aec8c910b12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-x^{8}}}" :db/id 17592186553170}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553170} :answer-field/id #uuid "f46cfecc-0cc8-5cc8-9940-d2b0180183b0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186553484}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7d72fdc8-4a06-597a-b4ee-b1daf23025f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-341503" :question/problem "If $y=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arsech}⁡({x}^{4}),$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic secant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arsech}⁡({x}^{4})] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot [-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}\sqrt{1-{({x}^{4})}^{2}}}]\cdot {({x}^{4})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{x}^{4}\sqrt{1-{x}^{8}}}\cdot 4{x}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{8}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553543 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4a57e159-8b9f-5e50-a811-ef9584e66726" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)" :db/id 17592186553027} {:answer/id #uuid "53bc9662-bdf2-5c5a-b51c-9e4907f321d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)" :db/id 17592186553047} {:answer/id #uuid "9f3a6c29-f691-50d0-a36e-fb4594dc00b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)" :db/id 17592186553189} {:answer/id #uuid "f6208ede-9d9d-5811-9f98-c396b7811777" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)" :db/id 17592186553354} {:answer/id #uuid "fe7c7845-1582-524e-ac10-277c2817e843" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)" :db/id 17592186553373}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553027} :answer-field/id #uuid "22643dcd-e934-597d-ad21-1b1e44a5206d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "847985b8-e342-54d5-a829-10e82cf593d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-342788" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}+y={u}_{\pi /2}(t)\cdot \sin \,(2t-\pi )\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /2}(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})$ is the unit step function.

You're given that the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{2{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}
$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as 

$$
y(t)=\frac{1}{5}\,u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot g(t).
$$

Find the function $g(t).$ 

Hint: You may make use of the following results:

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To solve the initial value problem, we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s).$

To find the inverse transform, we first ignore the exponential term ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ (which corresponds to a time shift) and focus on the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{2}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+1)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{2}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}=\frac{A}{s+1}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
2=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+1).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-1,$ we have

$$
2=A((-1)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,5A=2\,⟹\,A=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,B=-A=-\frac{2}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have

$$
2=4A+C\,⟹\,C=2-\frac{8}{5}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{2}{5}(\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{-s+1}{{s}^{2}+4})=\frac{2}{5}(\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{2}{5}({L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+1}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}\}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}({e}^{-t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ term in $Y(s).$ By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})f\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{2}{5}[{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}-\cos \,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{2}\sin \,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-\pi /2))=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-\pi /2))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{2}{5}[{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\,u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})(2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the form given in the problem statement $$
\displaystyle y(t)=\frac{1}{5}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot g(t),
$$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e4e0b48-8667-556e-81ec-ea459847a89c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{4(t-3)}-{e}^{-5(t-3)}" :db/id 17592186552922} {:answer/id #uuid "32046168-bf15-539e-a0bf-0354d06e8d28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4(t-3)}+{e}^{-5(t-3)})" :db/id 17592186552966} {:answer/id #uuid "9703e3d9-bfb7-5f17-8106-1258f1821bbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4(t-3)}-{e}^{-5(t-3)})" :db/id 17592186553177} {:answer/id #uuid "c72baafc-5ab2-555e-85d3-8cbb91b8e24a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4(t-3)}-{e}^{-5(t-3)})" :db/id 17592186553267} {:answer/id #uuid "d81c41ca-a50b-5956-9a30-f2989bbe8749" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{-5t})" :db/id 17592186553301}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553177} :answer-field/id #uuid "d7838ff7-32b3-503c-9d51-a06dd6fe14d2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553474}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8979fd62-065d-5783-b1c9-4baf45f041fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-342811" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}-4y={u}_{3}(t)\cdot {e}^{-5(t-3)}\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{3}(t)=u(t-3)$ is the unit step function.

$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as 

$$

Find the function $g(t).$" :question/worked-solution "To solve the initial value problem, we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s).$

To find the inverse transform, we first ignore the exponential term ${e}^{-3s}$ (which corresponds to a time shift) and focus on the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{(s-4)(s+5)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains distinct linear factors, the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{1}{(s-4)(s+5)}=\frac{A}{s-4}+\frac{B}{s+5}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
1=A(s+5)+B(s-4).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A$ and $B.$

- Setting $s=4,$ we have

$$
1=A(9)+B(0)\,⟹\,A=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

- Setting $s=-5,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(-9)\,⟹\,B=-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{9}(\frac{1}{s-4}-\frac{1}{s+5}).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{1}{9}({L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+5}\}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{-5t}).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-3s}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=3.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-3)f(t-3) & =u(t-3)\cdot \frac{1}{9}({e}^{4(t-3)}-{e}^{-5(t-3)}).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=u(t-3)\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4(t-3)}-{e}^{-5(t-3)}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553574 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bd42f49-0ece-5ce9-8b34-6a707862e044" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-24" :db/id 17592186552949} {:answer/id #uuid "3ab526ed-224c-541f-a66d-92563c921b58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{64}{3}" :db/id 17592186552987} {:answer/id #uuid "6ccab4e0-07a0-5a0f-b2ca-1faf663c12d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{28}{3}" :db/id 17592186553090} {:answer/id #uuid "7d16d138-325b-50ca-b473-15666930d48a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{76}{3}" :db/id 17592186553122} {:answer/id #uuid "95d56263-122e-5c18-988e-3b958f4009d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-18" :db/id 17592186553174}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186552987} :answer-field/id #uuid "441e4f24-d3a1-5f34-b559-dd35657f1f13" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553406}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d222c5e4-f6d8-59cd-b06f-5764984195b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-162651" :question/problem "![](images/c7/c7c48912df96585f7af01f3d0c1af904d1ca554555f7c63147fb5e0aa6676884.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(1,3)$ and $B(5,3).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,i+(x-1)^{2}\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector  ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{{y}^{3}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,3)$ to $B(5,3)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](images/3d/3d64ffb0e4cc313a2857d1c20922c1202619d0bdeb3d97f2808b4995c99f7f9f.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+3\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+3\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=-\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=-\sqrt{27}, \\ Q(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}=((4t+1)-1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\sqrt{27})\cdot (0)-(16{t}^{2})\cdot (4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-64{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{64{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-\frac{64}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553576 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21cf8068-05ed-55e2-ac2c-5cbee642e5eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{3}3{x}^{2}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186552928} {:answer/id #uuid "4bd0d3f5-7b2e-5d2b-abac-49bdcc1aa2cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186553033} {:answer/id #uuid "585d8ed2-ddec-5562-bde8-6c36dfbec00c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{3}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186553058} {:answer/id #uuid "de294dc0-1a3f-5566-a574-17c08dcba154" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}{y}^{2}(-{y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186553310} {:answer/id #uuid "fe53b468-ca8f-540a-b5a9-6cfac0008d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186553372}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553372} :answer-field/id #uuid "8bc52748-240b-5997-9e36-b5b9d7c36232" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553440}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d5c8c9fb-a926-5fe7-b24d-28d3915fc2cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-127230" :question/problem "Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(-1,-2),(3,-2),$ and $(3,0),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$\mathbf{F}(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$
through $C$ as a repeated integral." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e1/e1e4386f3cc75afb63823d74daa27b517e8e47d51fa08c5c9e5bf3ca6f3ca88c.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{6},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 3,\,-2\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{6}-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553578 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5c87e25c-189d-5204-85e6-f4884b92e797" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{se^{-\pi s/3}}{(s^2+4)(s+4)}" :db/id 17592186553067}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553067} :answer-field/id #uuid "45ab7f5f-7155-55c1-b6f0-ecb774ed5d33" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186553408}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "da40e310-ec0b-5b91-ae08-d59c190a3606" :question/math-academy-id "q-342771" :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}+4y={u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /3}(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})$ is the unit step function.

$$

$Y(s)=$
{{field-1}},$\,s>0$" :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}+4y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}+4L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0:$

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $f(t)=\cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3}).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. 

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} & ={e}^{-(\pi /3)s}\cdot L\{\cos \,(2\,(t+\frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s/3}\cdot L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s/3}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}\}+4L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\ sY(s)+4Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+4)}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553583 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "34a0c68b-e9f8-549e-842e-b401217d6da3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{i=0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{i\pi }{4}\right)" :db/id 17592186552968} {:answer/id #uuid "761a9645-004c-5d1a-a018-4e98c7126007" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{i\pi }{4}\right)" :db/id 17592186553106} {:answer/id #uuid "ca16e453-591e-50ca-b9b0-9c6c804546b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{i\pi }{2}\right)" :db/id 17592186553272} {:answer/id #uuid "dec5872d-a8a0-52d9-b1df-f39709699d7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{i=0}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{i\pi }{4}\right)" :db/id 17592186553311} {:answer/id #uuid "f70e4a83-804d-5d8d-a2bf-8321912f101c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}[-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{i\pi }{4}\right)]" :db/id 17592186553357}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553106} :answer-field/id #uuid "80c578ea-f1c8-5e3b-b6d6-b57c333da3a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553437}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e4c3e43e-fe55-559b-8cc6-a202da2850e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-49330" :question/problem "The area under the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)$ between $x=0$ and $x=2$ and the $x$-axis is approximated by a right Riemann sum using $4$ subintervals of equal length. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?" :question/worked-solution "The right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ with $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

We're told that there are $n=4$ subintervals. The endpoints indicate that $a=0$ and $b=2.$ So, the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{2-0}{4}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(a+iΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}f(0+i\cdot \frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}f\left(\frac{i}{2}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{i\pi }{4}\right).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553757 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "591a446f-82dd-564c-b15f-8e8267e36fdc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186553758} {:answer/id #uuid "5a7ef8e8-03eb-5e71-9954-b61f0cd0045d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186553759} {:answer/id #uuid "996ebf57-fd88-5775-876c-167c46de26ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186553763} {:answer/id #uuid "aab019ae-93c7-50b3-9811-d455898d1942" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186553765} {:answer/id #uuid "cc2ac1da-5902-5d50-a8d4-5ac0daceec12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186553766}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553763} :answer-field/id #uuid "779da836-a9bf-5772-a9db-115da484b79e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553761}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "391564c7-a751-5991-b788-dcbb08b27c2c" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=\left\langle 2 x^{2} + 4 y, \; 2 x^{2} + 4 x y \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/91/9168d2ed7eeaa5f1dd331a0a986ac7ecfd6b964217a2cb614deb0cdd54437d65.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 4 y$ and $Q(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 4 x y.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=4 x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=4 x.
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq 1,\quad 0\leq y\leq x^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds&=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx \\&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\&=\iint_D\left(8 x\right)\,dA \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{x^{2}}\left(8 x\right)\,dy\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left[8 x y\right]_{y=0}^{y=x^{2}}\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(8 x^{3}\right)\,dx \\&=\left[2 x^{4}\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\&=\left(2\right)-\left(0\right) \\&=2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553764 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "193c7f3f-1b13-52cf-b99e-2cb82e2ec402" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{12}{5}" :db/id 17592186553755} {:answer/id #uuid "30eb9b0a-3b5c-550c-97df-45c92636de58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186553756} {:answer/id #uuid "75dd0d96-1827-5799-ba11-bbee875c6ba2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186553760} {:answer/id #uuid "84167764-9866-593d-9f3f-728b74e99429" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186553762} {:answer/id #uuid "d900e075-bbea-5147-aeda-64c204455c22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186553767}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553762} :answer-field/id #uuid "05ec21ed-67a9-5f57-8257-9837d31fa900" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553754}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9f300428-dd28-5d22-81b0-c450650df73d" :question/problem "Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e6/e6f6a5cf9b37fe16f17fe74face946d85b426badf8db710ca4a7ea308a1ff2ec.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=28 x y$ and $Q(x,y)=12 x^{2} y + 2 \sin{\left(x \right)}.$ Therefore,

$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds&=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx \\&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\&=\iint_D\left(12 x^{2} + 28 y\right)\,dA \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{x^{3}}\left(12 x^{2} + 28 y\right)\,dy\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left[12 x^{2} y + 14 y^{2}\right]_{y=0}^{y=x^{3}}\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(x^{5} \left(14 x + 12\right)\right)\,dx \\&=\left[2 x^{7} + 2 x^{6}\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\&=\left(4\right)-\left(0\right) \\&=4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553771 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09332eae-5b2a-514b-8867-2093558d05b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\left(\frac{7}{6}\right)" :db/id 17592186553770} {:answer/id #uuid "420c6f0f-9dce-576e-9b0d-e95c7499ccb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\left(\frac{11}{6}\right)" :db/id 17592186553778} {:answer/id #uuid "776051fe-e8fa-5d70-877e-b7f12d71dc6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\left(\frac{14}{3}\right)" :db/id 17592186553782} {:answer/id #uuid "b8fa03e7-07e0-5b72-9c4a-d1951c6e832e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)" :db/id 17592186553790} {:answer/id #uuid "ed8388c4-b4b0-5c49-a3e6-c0618fd0f8f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)" :db/id 17592186553798}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553782} :answer-field/id #uuid "93450f91-e2e7-5d78-85f6-4f4af1e8b902" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553786}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0da10636-70da-5542-b982-fb7b4f87a3a4" :question/problem "![](images/09/09a38bb4306728f97b7fecbf9ab1bda7aa957607352c1ab27af09489c271c3ed.png)

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}9\left({y}^{2}-2x\right)\,\text{d}y,
$$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(2,3),$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,1)$ and $(2,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(0+t(2-0)),\,(1+t(3-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,1+2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9\left({y}^{2}-2x\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9\left((1+2t)^{2}-2(2t)\right)\\  & =9\left(1+4t+4{t}^{2}-4t\right)\\  & =9\left(4{t}^{2}+1\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =9\left({\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =9\left(2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4{t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t\right)\\  & =9\left(2{[\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+t]}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =9\left(2(\frac{4}{3}+1)-2(0)\right)\\  & =9\left(\frac{14}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553772 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0752d09c-5f6a-5f53-b2ee-4d14923c79a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\left(\frac{10}{3}\right)" :db/id 17592186553769} {:answer/id #uuid "618f68da-24b3-5f0a-805d-fbaacb6ec826" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\left(\frac{13}{6}\right)" :db/id 17592186553780} {:answer/id #uuid "83f08410-f8d4-5fcb-88cc-cce40721c333" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\left(\frac{15}{4}\right)" :db/id 17592186553783} {:answer/id #uuid "9ab18849-82d2-5380-bfc1-cc92cf4de014" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)" :db/id 17592186553787} {:answer/id #uuid "bf5790a3-b0de-5077-a139-ed86ea6ba02f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)" :db/id 17592186553791}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553780} :answer-field/id #uuid "5a51f296-5463-5808-9339-98064322cbb1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553779}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "108f6b56-f476-502d-ac1b-82f7c7bee892" :question/problem "![](images/ab/ab95b870025708090e40cbd7645072e8f4453cf50047b2a00036a30171c81994.png)

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}3\left(\sqrt{x-1}+y\right)\,\text{d}x,
$$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,2)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3\left(\sqrt{x-1}+y\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\left(\sqrt{(1+t)-1}+2-t\right)\\  & =3\left(\sqrt{t}-t+2\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3\left({\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{t}-t+2)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =3\left({\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{1/2}-t+2)\,\text{d}t\right)\\  & =3\left({[\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =3\left((\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+2)-(0)\right)\\  & =3\left(\frac{13}{6}\right)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186553774 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2cbd8d3d-bf94-5248-baf7-04662b6aadb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\left({e}^{2}+1\right)" :db/id 17592186553775} {:answer/id #uuid "c2a00b88-cc53-5b01-b917-ddbe6814de6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\left(\frac{3}{2}(e+1)\right)" :db/id 17592186553793} {:answer/id #uuid "e4284b1e-3a30-52a4-94c0-1caf9580e943" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\left(\frac{e}{2}-1\right)" :db/id 17592186553797} {:answer/id #uuid "f8e12e4a-0957-5b8e-85c2-01f0b3e26b26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\left(\frac{9}{2}(e-1)\right)" :db/id 17592186553801} {:answer/id #uuid "fdc5da25-166a-5b6b-820b-9a27ca4a5b8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7\left(\frac{1}{2}(e-1)\right)" :db/id 17592186553803}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553801} :answer-field/id #uuid "efbebf4f-659b-5cc4-bb41-66562e488f37" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186553800}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2b42b22b-83d6-590d-b354-39580363db2b" :question/problem "![](images/0e/0e5257867dae67451500793687a2da24ee31a73a17c691d8d8a6dcded46e8993.png)

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}7\left(x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\right)\,\text{d}x,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the three-quarters of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(3,0),$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}t,\,\operatorname{sin}t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}t)=-3\operatorname{sin}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=7\left(x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =7\left((3\operatorname{cos}t){e}^{1-\operatorname{sin}^{2}t}\right)\\  & =7\left(3\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =7\left({\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}t)\cdot \text{d}t\right)\\  & =7\left(-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\,\text{d}t\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}^{2}t,$ $\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7\left(-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t{e}^{\operatorname{cos}^{2}t}\,\text{d}t\right)& =7\left(-9{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u)\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{1}\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}[{e}^{1}-{e}^{0}]\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}\cdot (e-1)\right)\\  & =7\left(\frac{9}{2}(e-1)\right)\end{aligned}

Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=3.5,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.9,$ find a $98\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>6.965)=0.01,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the $y$-intecept is* 

$$

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=61.7+6.8x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$

$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=61.7+6.8x,$ our point estimate is

$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error.

$$

$$

$$

If the kite is rising vertically at a constant speed of $1\,\text{m/s},$ at what rate is the angle of elevation $\theta $ increasing when $\theta ={45}^{∘}?$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/23/236144ff93bd22f5c4460c31e20216c45d6f8ac85dc945321dadecc093f379e0.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the kite's height, and $z$ is the distance between the boy and the kite. The quantity $z=20$ meters does not change with time because the string's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{20} \\ y & =20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(20\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Converting the given information from degrees to radians, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $$
\displaystyle \theta ={45}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\pi }{{180}^{∘}}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(20\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{1}{20} & =\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{20}$ radians per second."} {:db/id 17592186554572 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "62649176-19b3-5dc9-882a-69ef22eb63b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.5" :db/id 17592186554061} {:answer/id #uuid "6fb2e354-67fd-5920-b3f1-8def0deb29e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.1" :db/id 17592186554095} {:answer/id #uuid "7ec24db7-f765-5318-ae89-7d5a90748c37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.8" :db/id 17592186554124} {:answer/id #uuid "94f6c867-15bb-5d02-aa0b-4ba6976af87a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6\pm 1.3" :db/id 17592186554198} {:answer/id #uuid "b3c741e7-dfd7-5769-bd67-c9d073965e46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6\pm 0.2" :db/id 17592186554266}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554198} :answer-field/id #uuid "67039e40-5de3-570b-bbed-0d3b0e5de178" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554471}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4f56dfe4-956b-5759-bcb7-ccce82fe1dbd" :question/math-academy-id "q-159556" :question/problem "| **Age ($x$)** | **$34$** | **$36$** | **$40$** | **$42$** |
