$$"} {:db/id 17592186554574 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7703407d-8788-52d9-8d23-7c0dd469068b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186554108} {:answer/id #uuid "a7281cf1-df65-5001-bdd3-ab6876280750" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186554239} {:answer/id #uuid "bd204788-03a2-5b3d-ac8e-82ebffa05caf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186554278} {:answer/id #uuid "c4208108-7b91-5e37-9f02-765baf72fbe9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186554296} {:answer/id #uuid "e264fdd1-c875-5ee0-914c-54600fb544c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186554360}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554239} :answer-field/id #uuid "5932e5d0-9d0c-54be-9a78-8ee0938071e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554464}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5964ffcf-bc61-5cdb-8ce3-fe3d629e8c05" :question/math-academy-id "q-340513" :question/problem "Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$

II. $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$

III. $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,2\pi ).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $2\pi $-periodicity:

$$
f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $2\pi $-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $2\pi $-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi )=f\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=F\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=F\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186554576 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80386a1f-1c68-542d-97ab-e6ec02fe80f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\sqrt[3]{(x+2)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186554125} {:answer/id #uuid "9eb339eb-1cc4-5d35-9e83-6c06760cd1fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt[3]{(3x+6)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186554219} {:answer/id #uuid "c88b7035-072c-5214-bd55-1804a6aa0ae7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt[3]{(3x+6)^{4}}" :db/id 17592186554310} {:answer/id #uuid "e2ae8cb1-1ad1-519a-a9ae-fc0f9b33b01f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt[3]{3x+6}" :db/id 17592186554361} {:answer/id #uuid "ec4a59e0-949a-5cc8-91d2-09ecb393925e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt[3]{(x+2)^{4}}" :db/id 17592186554386}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554310} :answer-field/id #uuid "8c497ffd-4cca-50b5-a7fc-dc93d720ea25" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554487}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5c789989-28b9-52e0-ac72-a0f8b7d66a60" :question/math-academy-id "q-138860" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{({x}^{2}+2)(11{x}^{2}+24x-2)}{g(x)}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}}{\sqrt[3]{3x+6}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6/3}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{2}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{2}}{(3x+6)^{1/3}}\right) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((3x+6)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+6)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2}\cdot 2x-\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3x+6}\cdot 3 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}(\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+2}-\frac{1}{3x+6}) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}\left(\frac{4x(3x+6)-({x}^{2}+2)}{({x}^{2}+2)(3x+6)}\right) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{({x}^{2}+2)^{6}}{3x+6}}\left(\frac{11{x}^{2}+24x-2}{({x}^{2}+2)(3x+6)}\right) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2)(11{x}^{2}+24x-2)}{\sqrt[3]{(3x-6)^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=\sqrt[3]{(3x-6)^{4}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554581 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15060daf-a4bc-5eb8-b79b-034a85e0bbf7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-26.6\pm 18.1" :db/id 17592186553910} {:answer/id #uuid "71ae2911-c3b0-54dd-b735-0b92451fc7ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-26.6\pm 9.8" :db/id 17592186554099} {:answer/id #uuid "c5f1300c-5d71-5a55-8165-193b27ab2363" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-26.6\pm 17.5" :db/id 17592186554302} {:answer/id #uuid "e4f2c162-946e-59cc-8842-379aa299e7ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-26.6\pm 16.2" :db/id 17592186554367} {:answer/id #uuid "e5ebf936-7757-56b0-a68f-58f3fcbd404b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-26.6\pm 10.3" :db/id 17592186554370}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553910} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f3ed31d-762f-57be-a238-32e2c1426527" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554467}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "69c89ef7-3131-5d48-9709-9716ca24bd0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-159557" :question/problem "| **Height ($x$)** | **$67$** | **$70$** | **$73$** | **$76$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Shoe size ($y$)** | $8.5$ | $9$ | $11$ | $13$ |

The table above shows the heights, in inches, and corresponding shoe sizes of four randomly selected men. The corresponding linear regression line fitted using this sample is $\widehat{\,y}=-26.6+0.5x.$ 
Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=71.5,$ and $\text{MSE}=0.338,$ find a $90\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.  

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>2.920)=0.05,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $2$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for the $y$-intecept is* 

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=-26.6+0.5x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=-26.6+0.5x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}=-26.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $90\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.920)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.05}=2.920.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(67-71.5)^{2}+(70-71.5)^{2}+(73-71.5)^{2}+(76-71.5)^{2} \\  & =20.25+2.25+2.25+20.25 \\  & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.920\cdot \sqrt{0.338\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{71.5}^{2}}{45})}≈18.1
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=-26.6\pm 18.1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554584 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1038e636-38ca-52da-90c5-a091da531eb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2ex+2ey+\frac{z}{e}-4e+\frac{1}{e}=0" :db/id 17592186553902} {:answer/id #uuid "27782ffe-f397-5d41-939c-10588c08a068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2ex-2ey-\frac{z}{e}-\frac{1}{e}=0" :db/id 17592186553943} {:answer/id #uuid "8605bb25-4120-54e0-870c-c12a2d8a2246" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2ex+2ey+\frac{z}{e}-2e+\frac{1}{e}=0" :db/id 17592186554145} {:answer/id #uuid "b1a1e914-b611-51ed-ac80-498a071f0b9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2ex+2ey+ez+3e=0" :db/id 17592186554262} {:answer/id #uuid "c1fe292e-1813-51b6-937f-ba4fbfabb74f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2ex+2ey-\frac{z}{e}-4e-\frac{1}{e}=0" :db/id 17592186554290}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554290} :answer-field/id #uuid "102d43bf-f5e9-5d2c-bd0c-f23bbb64ece6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554437}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6cd59b40-dc86-5174-9cba-78e6f66091cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-86454" :question/problem "Given the function $f(x,y,z)=2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,1,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }k \\  & =2y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+2{e}^{x}\text{ }j-{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,-1) & =2(1)e\text{ }i+2e\text{ }j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =2e\,i+2e\,j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =⟨2e,2e,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(1,1,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨2e,2e,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,\,y-1,\,z+1⟩ & =0 \\ 2ex+2ey-\frac{z}{e}-4e-\frac{1}{e} & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554591 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "489fcd75-9368-5e9b-acbf-94835400f3d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.4\pm 0.9" :db/id 17592186554008} {:answer/id #uuid "92b0899f-5335-5dd0-a82e-12c93b11cd39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.4\pm 1.1" :db/id 17592186554194} {:answer/id #uuid "93ebfe14-4c6e-5be6-8ef7-fc1066aec02c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.4\pm 0.7" :db/id 17592186554197} {:answer/id #uuid "b312c9b8-2b8a-552e-98f0-214625871779" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.4\pm 0.2" :db/id 17592186554265} {:answer/id #uuid "e8c71797-2619-523f-998b-4dc9f5e6a269" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2\pm 0.1" :db/id 17592186554375}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554197} :answer-field/id #uuid "b86a25e5-3ce1-5477-9eb2-c277e7527b4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554504}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "812d00c8-ff0e-5dde-8e15-88d6aa199ddf" :question/math-academy-id "q-159561" :question/problem "Let $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=2.4+0.2x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $({x}_{1},{y}_{1}),\,…,\,({x}_{12},{y}_{12})$ of $n=12$ paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, $\overset{―}{x}=1.2,$ the mean square error of the model is $0.7,$ and $$
\displaystyle {S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}=18.9,
$$ find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept of the regression line.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>2.228)=0.025,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $10$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is given by 

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

*" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=2.4+0.2x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept ${\beta }_{0}$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=2.4+0.2x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}=2.4.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We are given that $P(T>2.228)=0.025.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{10,0.025}=2.228.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.228\cdot \sqrt{0.7\cdot (\frac{1}{12}+\frac{{1.2}^{2}}{18.9})}≈0.7
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.4\pm 0.7
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554593 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33182b33-0b36-5640-a4c9-778cbc8910ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.55\,\text{km}/\text{h}" :db/id 17592186553959} {:answer/id #uuid "913b0f46-1aad-5da8-b8dd-1bf4b4bb9711" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.78\,\text{km}/\text{h}" :db/id 17592186554184} {:answer/id #uuid "b840f7bb-0678-5531-ad85-8cea6f5889e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.84\,\text{km}/\text{h}" :db/id 17592186554270} {:answer/id #uuid "cf8772f4-5572-5416-89ab-0f1ffa36973b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.62\,\text{km}/\text{h}" :db/id 17592186554322} {:answer/id #uuid "e24d129b-6aba-55f9-bf48-3093ebfec375" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.93\,\text{km}/\text{h}" :db/id 17592186554359}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554322} :answer-field/id #uuid "c44dc184-d6a9-51f1-aaf9-4f2394dbe32b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554510}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "847493a1-e66a-5ae4-9cf4-e1e68a84c19e" :question/math-academy-id "q-121713" :question/problem "![](images/ec/ecb02db9984510219c6209392c9f35df52eca11dacc802a133aa51c4e5065ede.png)

A drone $D$ takes off from a point $P$ and climbs with an angle of elevation of ${60}^{∘}$ and a vertical speed of $4\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$ Assuming the angle of elevation doesn't change, calculate the actual speed of the drone in the direction it is traveling.
Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "![](images/69/69314419f6e0b93236fc048c6b9b6b262b09ff2cc061996353fbe23870a12726.png)

Let $y$ denote the vertical distance from the drone's projection to the starting point, and $z$ be the distance between the drone and the starting point, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={60}^{∘},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({60}^{∘}) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ z & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=4\text{km}/\text{h}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot 4≈4.62
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the speed of the drone is approximately $4.62\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$"} {:db/id 17592186554594 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19ea48dc-2bbd-5e4f-9e61-02d95414ac74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\pm 2.3" :db/id 17592186553918} {:answer/id #uuid "3f4f31a4-eeac-52ca-b025-6e0b059772dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\pm 2.5" :db/id 17592186553983} {:answer/id #uuid "60c1e936-44cd-56c8-8e97-44a0822f3d4c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\pm 3.3" :db/id 17592186554057} {:answer/id #uuid "ce12ef9b-5ac2-5639-b917-770b6e5414d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\pm 2.7" :db/id 17592186554319} {:answer/id #uuid "dd53447b-e183-5dfb-8fe3-9f2284148e07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\pm 2.1" :db/id 17592186554351}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553983} :answer-field/id #uuid "caf088fc-e014-5a09-8ceb-3ba512fc68e7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554513}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "851fa16f-b92a-5672-9bbf-979f258829aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-159560" :question/problem "Let $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=5+0.4x$ be the regression line fitted using a sample $({x}_{1},{y}_{1}),\,…,\,({x}_{10},{y}_{10})$ of $n=10$ paired observations. \displaystyle {S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}=330,

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T>3.355)=0.005,$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $8$ degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is given by

*" :question/worked-solution "We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=5+0.4x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept ${\beta }_{0}$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=5+0.4x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}=5.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $99\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(T>3.355)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{8,0.005}=3.355.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=3.355\cdot \sqrt{3.7\cdot (\frac{1}{10}+\frac{{4.3}^{2}}{330})}≈2.5
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=5\pm 2.5
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554599 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2629af92-040b-52b8-9b80-03dbd9c188f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-165\pm 44.7" :db/id 17592186553938} {:answer/id #uuid "5d9eea9f-4d37-543c-9eaa-babf46254a0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-165\pm 43.4" :db/id 17592186554052} {:answer/id #uuid "8d6a69c6-a56f-5da5-a2f4-cda015f6c0cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-165\pm 43.2" :db/id 17592186554167} {:answer/id #uuid "91bc6383-5d46-59ca-b246-89d30592f06c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-165\pm 41.7" :db/id 17592186554187} {:answer/id #uuid "c3d3d801-fda0-5c5b-82eb-e97ceb523307" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-165\pm 42.8" :db/id 17592186554294}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554052} :answer-field/id #uuid "fcab1227-d753-5449-9bf0-127c2147993a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554536}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8c255cc5-a4ec-5d1f-be58-dbb45c0a4d57" :question/math-academy-id "q-159590" :question/problem "| **Height ($x$)** | **$64$** | **$68$** | **$72$** | **$76$** |

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 0,-1\le y\le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)[x]_{-1}^{0}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\cdot 1\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =[4y-{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(4(-1)-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}

- $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=2.8-3.3x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the $y$-intercept ${\beta }_{0}$ of our model can be written as

$$
\underbrace{{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}}_{\,\,\text{point}\,\text{estimate}}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=2.8-3.3x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}=2.8.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $99\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(T>3.355)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{8,0.005}=3.355.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=3.355\cdot \sqrt{3.6\cdot (\frac{1}{10}+\frac{{2.7}^{2}}{82.5})}≈2.8
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=2.8\pm 2.8
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554640 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "448ae3db-641d-5f64-a5c9-14f4cedec775" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186553995} {:answer/id #uuid "482bfb85-d1a0-5e37-9c53-93569bba7aac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}+1" :db/id 17592186554007} {:answer/id #uuid "b2d6645f-466a-52fe-b330-b115e7efc0a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186554264} {:answer/id #uuid "c5440dc0-7eb1-5868-85fb-0761762da9be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{3}" :db/id 17592186554300} {:answer/id #uuid "df1540ff-dda7-54f2-9afe-827410ca5f75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186554354}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554300} :answer-field/id #uuid "46815972-0754-5def-987e-4a8b3dd30f2a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554456}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f35d7c5d-0e2d-5ee0-b1c5-16c26213b1d0" :question/math-academy-id "q-162326" :question/problem "Evaluate
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.
$$

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{cos}⁡z\}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $x,$ the $x$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/ed/ed7308cf6c77f5d89b94ec90237fa9161fc85429182813f38b55d916bdbdaeef.png)

The region $D$ is type I region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we write $D$ as a type II region.

Notice that the left boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
y=0
$$

and the right boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $y=y(z),$ is

$$
z=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡z.
$$

Then, the type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡z\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/4f/4fb3323b2c295df8351910890f20266840b131a4dfd8a7bba0d61a3eb03bea23.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}[\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}\text{d}x]\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,[x]_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡z\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\text{d}y]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,[y]_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z\operatorname{cos}⁡z\sqrt{1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{3}{(1+{\cos }^{2}⁡z)}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[(1+0)^{3/2}-(1+1)^{3/2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(1-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554853 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b337fa7-bd8b-5c90-a0a9-70650e2fdcbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186554860} {:answer/id #uuid "7d135ef6-116e-5934-84c1-11a47c59668f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186554878} {:answer/id #uuid "836d5d14-56d9-58cb-9958-435971a6cb35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186554881} {:answer/id #uuid "8cf45132-d649-533a-9603-ef7dfcb122bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186554884} {:answer/id #uuid "ce656dd1-358f-523e-9af0-50c385c018ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-32" :db/id 17592186554904}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554884} :answer-field/id #uuid "46488809-31b0-5e06-a0e3-3b15d04132fc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554866}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0de1e67b-08b0-590a-987d-98f0797e3256" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=\left(x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- z\right)\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\left(4 - 4 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(4 t^{2}\right)\,j+\left(\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4 - 4 t^{2},\quad y=4 t^{2},\quad z=\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- z\right)\,k \\ & =\left(4\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 - 4 t^{2}\right)\,i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 t^{2}\right)\,j+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 8 t\right)\,i+\left(8 t\right)\,j+\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(\left(4\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\right)\cdot\left(\left(- 8 t\right)\,i+\left(8 t\right)\,j+\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\right) \\ & =\left(4\right)\cdot\left(- 8 t\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot\left(8 t\right)+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\cdot\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right) \\ & =\left(- 32 t\right)+\left(0\right)+\left(- \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)} \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right) \\ & =- 32 t - \frac{\pi \sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr & =\int_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{-1}^{1}\left(- 32 t - \frac{\pi \sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[- 16 t^{2} + \frac{\cos{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{4}\right]_{-1}^{1} \\ & =[\left(-16\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)]-[\left(-16\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)] \\ & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554863 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "38d9f40b-294c-5d0d-b920-423d8a07b7b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186554864} {:answer/id #uuid "59829333-e505-5da3-98f2-21a5554e8c75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-25" :db/id 17592186554870} {:answer/id #uuid "9b006bad-ce48-5e7e-a06c-1c336b782ab7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-15" :db/id 17592186554888} {:answer/id #uuid "c0dc3100-368a-5fe9-8467-27205633130c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186554902} {:answer/id #uuid "ed445195-4fe7-541a-8a1e-6f2a605ae973" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- \frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186554910}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554910} :answer-field/id #uuid "0d5efd9d-3e69-5f74-9f3d-3ac7e3057828" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554852}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "348e1450-060b-511e-ab1c-9ac3626ec2eb" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=\left(- 6 x + 5 y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\left(5 t^{2} - 5 t\right)\,i+\left(6 t^{3} - 6 t\right)\,j+\left(\sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5 t^{2} - 5 t,\quad y=6 t^{3} - 6 t,\quad z=\sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(- 6 x + 5 y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k \\ & =\left(30 t^{3} - 30 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(5 t^{2} - 5 t\right)\,i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(6 t^{3} - 6 t\right)\,j+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}\right)\,k \\ & =\left(10 t - 5\right)\,i+\left(18 t^{2} - 6\right)\,j+\left(2 \pi \cos{\left(2 \pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(\left(30 t^{3} - 30 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\right)\cdot\left(\left(10 t - 5\right)\,i+\left(18 t^{2} - 6\right)\,j+\left(2 \pi \cos{\left(2 \pi t \right)}\right)\,k\right) \\ & =\left(30 t^{3} - 30 t^{2}\right)\cdot\left(10 t - 5\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot\left(18 t^{2} - 6\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot\left(2 \pi \cos{\left(2 \pi t \right)}\right) \\ & =\left(300 t^{4} - 450 t^{3} + 150 t^{2}\right)+\left(0\right)+\left(0\right) \\ & =\left(10 t - 5\right) \left(30 t^{3} - 30 t^{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr & =\int_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{0}^{1}\left(\left(10 t - 5\right) \left(30 t^{3} - 30 t^{2}\right)\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[60 t^{5} - \frac{225 t^{4}}{2} + 50 t^{3}\right]_{0}^{1} \\ & =[\left(50\right)+\left(- \frac{225}{2}\right)+\left(60\right)]-[\left(0\right)+\left(0\right)+\left(0\right)] \\ & =- \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554872 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18df830f-ab86-5425-9738-33adc7144a61" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186554857} {:answer/id #uuid "7d2f5870-6bef-5a74-bac7-cea2f02dad0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186554879} {:answer/id #uuid "bbe93c39-19b8-5993-86a0-832c5694d298" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186554900} {:answer/id #uuid "bf92e1c7-9d7c-59ca-9b8b-0d362f20d0bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186554901} {:answer/id #uuid "eb3c9e86-4f1e-5d6f-beb8-32c3b7b03702" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186554909}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554909} :answer-field/id #uuid "86fe68d1-7c6d-53bc-9521-f981d69d8bbd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554882}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "62239d5b-2148-5cb6-b90b-702d31af6174" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=\left(x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- z\right)\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\left(2 - 2 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(2 t^{2}\right)\,j+\left(\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$

It is given by the formula

$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t^{2} - t,\quad y=3 t^{3} - 3 t,\quad z=\sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}.

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(- 3 x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k \\ & =\left(3 t^{3} - 3 t^{2}\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(0\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "15966dc5-b8d2-54f2-9092-584d157e0965" :question/math-academy-id "q-90603" :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ stated below. Given that $\text{E}[X]≈3.314\,81,$ compute $\text{Var}[X].$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}, & 0<x<3, \\ \frac{1}{9}(2x-5), & 3\le x<5, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{5}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{5}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{9}(2x-5)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{1}{9}(2{x}^{3}-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{27}|}_{0}^{3}+{\frac{1}{9}(\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{3}^{5} \\  & ≈13.074\,07\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & ≈13.074\,07-(3.314\,81)^{2} \\  & ≈2.09\end{aligned}
$$

 
rounded to $2$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186555766 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2395b540-2627-5ab1-83d5-405723b43cb3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=27-8{x}^{3}" :db/id 17592186555071} {:answer/id #uuid "4bd61b85-6adb-58d6-bd60-2cc7be863377" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=8(x-3)^{3}" :db/id 17592186555166} {:answer/id #uuid "755b6adb-f545-5977-ab1a-a3249a50e72f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}" :db/id 17592186555266} {:answer/id #uuid "d8c6a5b9-c9bf-5d05-847f-e7d34bd69641" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=27(x+2)^{3}" :db/id 17592186555522} {:answer/id #uuid "fd5c89a0-5bf5-5ae6-aa81-3cadda0a58cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=-\frac{27}{8}{x}^{3}" :db/id 17592186555632}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555632} :answer-field/id #uuid "93c160c4-3699-526a-aa75-85488137bfed" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555714}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "16fdfda4-c2d1-55b9-ac4e-fb5a2493ec8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-148735" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{y}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{y} \\ \sqrt[3]{y} & =-\frac{3}{2}x \\ (\sqrt[3]{y})^{3} & ={(-\frac{3}{2}x)}^{3} \\ y & =-\frac{27}{8}{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=-\frac{27}{8}{x}^{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186555802 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "37c00ba7-4e07-54ad-bdbc-1156749cc2e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8641" :db/id 17592186555120} {:answer/id #uuid "5189a220-76ea-5091-b49a-16f052b2f1d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8138" :db/id 17592186555182} {:answer/id #uuid "52750003-2d76-57fb-a067-cb80127c33cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8413" :db/id 17592186555187} {:answer/id #uuid "82993aab-8bd6-5d61-9861-50ee8d1879b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8587" :db/id 17592186555301} {:answer/id #uuid "e4152bbf-4ef2-5a5d-a6e2-4af52f0157e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8359" :db/id 17592186555559}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555187} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e5cc2f0-6725-5001-8935-9b10d946cfa9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555699}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4fcf6802-fc48-589d-8b96-17389df12736" :question/math-academy-id "q-159804" :question/problem "Let $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]^{T}$ be a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 6 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y=2{X}_{1}-{X}_{2}-{X}_{3}.$ Find $P(Y\le -2).$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7580\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8159\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8413\,$ | $\,0.8438\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{k}]^{T}$ is a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y={c}^{T}X={\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{c}_{i}{X}_{i}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable, where $c$ is any $k\times 1$ column vector, and  

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, since we wish to know the distribution of $Y=2{X}_{1}-{X}_{2}-{X}_{3},$ we have 

$$
c=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, for the mean of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu  \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-2-1-4 \\  & =-7,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the variance of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 6 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ -4 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =14+4+7 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
Y∼N(-7,25).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(Y\le -2).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le -2) & =P(Z\le \frac{-2-(-7)}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & =P(Z\le 1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\le 1) & =Φ(1).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
Φ(1)=0.8413.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\le 1)=0.8413.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(Y\le -2)=0.8413.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186555804 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39552913-1c07-56b5-b6b4-c97f61c68646" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}-3{x}^{4}z+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}{y}^{3}" :db/id 17592186555123} {:answer/id #uuid "4e9eedfb-df31-5fef-89f8-4a0a5bc39de6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}-\frac{4{x}^{4}z}{y}+6{x}^{2}{z}^{2}{y}^{4}" :db/id 17592186555177} {:answer/id #uuid "738b92d9-e5fc-511d-904f-c37c0cfe4696" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}+\frac{3{x}^{2}z}{y}+3x{z}^{2}{y}^{3}" :db/id 17592186555259} {:answer/id #uuid "a1e6de29-d31f-58b5-b882-4e6e62b0a4a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}-\frac{3{x}^{4}z}{y}+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}{y}^{4}" :db/id 17592186555389} {:answer/id #uuid "e5810984-6602-54b8-9000-97b31b9afc00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}-4{x}^{4}z+4{x}^{2}{z}^{2}{y}^{3}" :db/id 17592186555563}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555123} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d1ececc-599e-58e1-a6af-f6ea1d9aa196" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555659}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5386af7a-f43c-5f81-bd4e-2f8f31eb31ea" :question/math-academy-id "q-110680" :question/problem "Find, in ascending powers of $z$ and descending powers of $x,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}-z{y}^{2})}^{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=3,$ $a=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y},$ and $b=-z{y}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{3}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{3}.
$$

The $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,3,3,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}-z{y}^{2})}^{3} & =1{a}^{3}{b}^{0}+3{a}^{2}b+3a{b}^{2}+1{a}^{0}{b}^{3} \\  & =1{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\right)}^{3}{(-z{y}^{2})}^{0}+3{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\right)}^{2}{(-z{y}^{2})}^{1} \\  & \,+3{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\right)}^{1}{(-z{y}^{2})}^{2}+1{\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\right)}^{0}{(-z{y}^{2})}^{3} \\  & =1\left(\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}\right)(1)+3\left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\right)(-z{y}^{2}) \\  & \,+3\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\right)({z}^{2}{y}^{4})+1(1)(-{z}^{3}{y}^{6}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}-\frac{3{x}^{4}z{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}+\frac{3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}{y}^{4}}{y}-{z}^{3}{y}^{6} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}-3{x}^{4}z+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}{y}^{3}-{z}^{3}{y}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find, in ascending powers of $z$ and descending powers of $x,$ the first three terms are

$$
\frac{{x}^{6}}{{y}^{3}}-3{x}^{4}z+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}{y}^{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186555805 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11f333d9-733e-5389-8cda-5e1dfd790b4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8289" :db/id 17592186555035} {:answer/id #uuid "2270f878-d33b-5b4b-94a5-97c69457888a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9713" :db/id 17592186555068} {:answer/id #uuid "4c5cc44d-5d18-5731-a82e-007a6010f363" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8611" :db/id 17592186555170} {:answer/id #uuid "6b48f9bd-b48b-5648-9060-b92aee8c6760" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8002" :db/id 17592186555245} {:answer/id #uuid "eb6bab9b-a8ad-52b9-8e04-2ce38c845042" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9424" :db/id 17592186555579}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555245} :answer-field/id #uuid "5147a116-059b-5bc9-9e03-f4ccc1268a8e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555676}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "54165c1c-b41c-51d6-bf2e-f7ee2418543e" :question/math-academy-id "q-159922" :question/problem "Let $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]^{T}$ be a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{k}]^{T}$ is a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu $ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y={c}^{T}X={\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{c}_{i}{X}_{i}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable, where $c$ is any $k\times 1$ column vector, and  

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, since we wish to know the distribution of $Y=2{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+2{X}_{3},$ we have 

$$
c=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, for the mean of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu  \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-2+0+2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the variance of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =14+6+20 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(0,40).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(-6<Y\le 12).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-6<Y\le 12) & =P(\frac{-6-0}{\sqrt{40}}<Z\le \frac{12-0}{\sqrt{40}}) \\  & =P(-0.95<Z\le 1.90)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.95<Z\le 1.90) & =P(Z\le 1.90)-P(Z\le -0.95) \\  & =Φ(1.90)-Φ(-0.95).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.95) & =0.8289 \\ Φ(1.90) & =0.9713\end{aligned}
$$

By the symmetry of the normal distribution, we have

$$
Φ(-0.95)=1-Φ(0.95)=1-0.8289=0.1711.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.95<Z\le 1.90)=0.9713-0.1711=0.8002.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(-6<Y\le 12)=0.8002.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186555817 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fbec0d8-f92e-5399-9366-340075456307" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186555030} {:answer/id #uuid "1dc62f23-318c-50d0-87d4-4f837695b5fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186555054} {:answer/id #uuid "1f9bd6b5-dd49-56b3-aad5-18d9bbb43d04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186555058} {:answer/id #uuid "c158ba71-83f0-55e5-ab39-f9b125bbc5a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186555466} {:answer/id #uuid "df26bafd-3008-5692-9ec4-c15e5e10d340" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186555544}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555058} :answer-field/id #uuid "2306df6b-e9b2-5ebc-be81-284b6041ab6d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555655}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "68ad658e-fc68-5dd0-8313-20d02f0dbcab" :question/math-academy-id "q-143757" :question/problem "Suppose that $X$ is a continuous random variable. For which of the following transformations can the change-of-variables method be applied to find the probability density function of $Y?$

I. $Y={X}^{5}+1,$ where $X\in (-1,1)$

II. $Y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2X,$ where $X\in (0,\frac{\pi }{2})$

III. $Y=1-{X}^{4},$ where $X\in (-\infty ,\infty )$" :question/worked-solution "The change-of-variables method can be applied when a transformation $Y=u(X)$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing (i.e., strictly monotonic) over the entire support of $X.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each transformation in turn.

- Transformation I is strictly monotonic. The function $u(x)={x}^{5}+1$ is strictly increasing for $x\in (-1,1).$

- Transformation II is *not* strictly monotonic. The function $u(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is strictly increasing for $x\in (0,\frac{\pi }{4})$ and strictly decreasing for $x\in (\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2}).$

- Transformation III is *not* strictly monotonic. The function $u(x)=1-{x}^{4}$ is strictly increasing for $x\in (-\infty ,0)$ and strictly decreasing for $x\in (0,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186555831 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00ca160e-cb63-581e-915a-c85ad7372034" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{a}{2},b-3)" :db/id 17592186555005} {:answer/id #uuid "3e2798c6-7b71-50ce-a869-45a58fada49f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2a,b-3)" :db/id 17592186555134} {:answer/id #uuid "66800e86-33bf-5c7b-be8f-c2cc33cda489" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(a-3,\frac{b}{2})" :db/id 17592186555230} {:answer/id #uuid "9b1c6067-70b9-52ab-819a-3361ccb30529" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{a}{2},3b)" :db/id 17592186555374} {:answer/id #uuid "9c534194-d200-5f07-a6b7-e379535c43d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(a-3,2b)" :db/id 17592186555376}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555005} :answer-field/id #uuid "913d1116-3eaa-556f-b9b4-ea8a98a7fac9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555712}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8aef3688-a7db-5a18-95f7-9c000401998b" :question/math-academy-id "q-158537" :question/problem "The point $(a,b)$ lies on the curve $y={e}^{x}.$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y={e}^{2x}-3?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

To plot $y={e}^{2x}-3,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, we take the graph $y={e}^{x}.$

- Then, we stretch the graph by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ parallel to the $x$-axis and get the graph of  $y={e}^{2x}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(\frac{a}{2},b).
$$

- Finally, we shift the result vertically by $3$ units down and obtain the graph of $y={e}^{2x}-3.$ After this transformation, the point $(\frac{a}{2},b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(\frac{a}{2},b-3).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $y={e}^{x}$, we have that ${e}^{a}=b.$

Now consider the graph of $y={e}^{2x}-3.$ Substituting $x=\frac{a}{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2\cdot (a/2)}-3 \\  & ={e}^{a}-3 \\  & =b-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(\frac{a}{2},b-3)$ must lie on $y={e}^{2x}-3.$"} {:db/id 17592186555853 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2d9e3163-77a3-5b77-b6dd-5f9cc4183e81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,-4)" :db/id 17592186555102} {:answer/id #uuid "4aaceaf8-31cb-57d9-89f4-40f6fbb0f71e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{3}{4})" :db/id 17592186555164} {:answer/id #uuid "8720512d-ed7f-54db-9220-6ac8c52ec59f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{4},-\frac{3}{4})" :db/id 17592186555313} {:answer/id #uuid "d7eb0642-fe00-5e0f-a9ab-9dcbf769b12b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(4,3)" :db/id 17592186555520} {:answer/id #uuid "f60b95e6-696c-5f40-9e72-4690b1e4355c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4})" :db/id 17592186555611}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555611} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9f334df-9edf-56f6-b904-ca6fc39afbf1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555722}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c47ad7a3-3c57-54bc-8711-6eebfda1e26f" :question/math-academy-id "q-30452" :question/problem "Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $y=4{x}^{2}-2x+1.$" :question/worked-solution "The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=4$ and $b=-2$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{-2}{2(4)} \\  & =-\frac{-2}{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=\frac{1}{4}$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4{x}^{2}-2x+1 \\  & =4{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}-2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{2}{4}+\frac{4}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}).$"} {:db/id 17592186555854 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0824024b-c099-527a-8256-d5a6127f2786" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186555013} {:answer/id #uuid "2f22d275-c75b-5b64-9666-30863a46ed54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=\frac{15}{6}" :db/id 17592186555104} {:answer/id #uuid "4087805a-ed7e-522b-a9a2-c73758870563" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=3" :db/id 17592186555140} {:answer/id #uuid "76e3d3fa-3854-5450-9938-38191ec8e7d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=\frac{35}{12}" :db/id 17592186555274} {:answer/id #uuid "f412a256-5361-5b16-a302-db1d43b422fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=2" :db/id 17592186555602}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186555140} :answer-field/id #uuid "15067fae-69bc-5d5f-83e8-e1ebdc618e5e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186555649}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c4e9e89a-1628-511a-8a61-3e91affcd33c" :question/math-academy-id "q-106134" :question/problem "![](images/8c/8cd1c9ab91a23fae12dd45078ec44ca55e69da8aa787775d7a9583857a84cb71.png)

If $Y=3X+3\pi ,$ use the change-of-variables method to find the probability density function of $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function ${f}_{X}$ and $Y=u(X),$ where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)|, & y\text{ is between }u(a)\text{ and }u(b) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here, we have $Y=3X+3\pi .$ The transformation $u(x)=3x+3\pi $ is strictly monotonically *increasing*, so the change-of-variables method can be used.

First, we find ${u}^{-1}(y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u(y) & =3y+3\pi  \\ y & =3{u}^{-1}(y)+3\pi  \\ {u}^{-1}(y) & =\frac{y}{3}-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $({u}^{-1})^{′}(y):$

$$
({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)=\frac{1}{3}
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero ${f}_{Y},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)| \\  & ={f}_{X}(\frac{y}{3}-\pi )\cdot |\frac{1}{3}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{3}-\pi )\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{3}-\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${f}_{X}$ is nonzero on $0<x<\pi ,$ the bounds are $a=0$ and $b=\pi ,$ we have

$$
u(0)=3\pi ,\,u(\pi )=6\pi .
$$

Therefore, the probability distribution of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{3}-\pi ), & 3\pi <y<6\pi  \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "12587c01-8aed-5ac1-86ba-15ed1938d516" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}x)(\frac{5}{\sqrt{6}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we move all of the terms to the left-hand side and then factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{g}^{2} & =\frac{2g}{5} \\ 4{g}^{2}-\frac{2g}{5} & =0 \\ 2g(2g-\frac{1}{5}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the zero product rule to get

$$
2g=0\,\text{or}\,2g-\frac{1}{5}=0,
$$

which in turn gives

$$

Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x:$

\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-3x+5xy \\ {y}^{′}=5y-3xy\end{aligned}\right.

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

$(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x+5xy=0 \\ 5y-3xy=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+5xy & =0 \\ x(-3+5y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{3}{5}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-3(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{3}{5},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-3xy & =0 \\ y(5-3x) & =0 \\ \frac{3}{5}(5-3x) & =0 \\ 5-3x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{5}{3},\frac{3}{5}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{5}{3},\frac{3}{5}).$"} {:db/id 17592186557222 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50ba80ef-f04e-50df-b6d3-a54349425c28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola with semiaxes $5$ and $4$" :db/id 17592186556614} {:answer/id #uuid "99191248-3fa5-597a-8b54-a603b1f3f7cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An ellipse with semiaxes $\frac{1}{5}$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$" :db/id 17592186556797} {:answer/id #uuid "a1e84b15-e7c8-5fd4-aa6e-1f803de91be4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A single point" :db/id 17592186556826} {:answer/id #uuid "da3da08e-ab18-5b95-a7d3-b32ef06eaf72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A parabola" :db/id 17592186556972} {:answer/id #uuid "dc4ed344-c362-572c-a34e-eb57da043aa3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola with semiaxes $2$ and $\frac{1}{2}$" :db/id 17592186556977}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186556826} :answer-field/id #uuid "2872dfa0-d71b-51c3-93f9-e6e87fc08e6e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186557091}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "27762923-ddbc-55ca-b261-ca5c61feb064" :question/math-academy-id "q-95396" :question/problem "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$

$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}-\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{16}.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,\underbrace{24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}}_{Q(x)}-\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{16}
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}24{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+21{x}_{2}^{2}-\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2} & =-\frac{5}{16} \\ 25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2}-\sqrt{5}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})+2\sqrt{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2}) & =-\frac{5}{16} \\ 25{y}_{1}^{2}+20{y}_{2}^{2}+5{y}_{2} & =-\frac{5}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}^{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{2}) & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{2}+\frac{1}{64}-\frac{1}{64}) & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}_{2}+\frac{1}{64})-\frac{4}{64} & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}+\frac{1}{8})^{2}-\frac{1}{16} & =-\frac{1}{16} \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}+4({y}_{2}+\frac{1}{8})^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2}={y}_{2}+\frac{1}{8},\end{aligned}\right.

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{z}_{1}^{2}+4{z}_{2}^{2} & =0 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{\frac{1}{5}}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{\frac{1}{4}} & =0 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^{2}}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that the function $F(x)$ is a cumulative distribution function, where $F(a)=0,F(b)=1,$ and $F$ is strictly monotonic on $a<x<b.$ Then, the random variable $X,$ given by

$$
X={F}^{-1}(Y)
$$

is a continuous random variable with the cumulative distribution function $F(x).$

So, we need to find the inverse of $y=F(x).$ To do this, we solve the following equation for $x,$ taking into account that $0\le y\le 1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡({e}^{x}) \\ \frac{y\pi }{2} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡({e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{y\pi }{2}\right) \\ x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{y\pi }{2}\right))\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the numbers drawn from $U[0,1]$ into the above equation:

- For $y=0.321,$ we get $$
\displaystyle x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{0.321\pi }{2}\right))≈-0.595
$$

- For $y=0.567,$ we get $$
\displaystyle x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{0.567\pi }{2}\right))≈0.212
$$

- For $y=0.804,$ we get $$
\displaystyle x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{0.804\pi }{2}\right))≈1.146
$$"} {:db/id 17592186557253 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03c543b2-c742-5216-a976-704265096bf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A pair of intersecting lines" :db/id 17592186556437} {:answer/id #uuid "4d58c25d-4003-58d6-ba24-34ce3e87a8a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola with semiaxes $2$ and $\sqrt{3}$" :db/id 17592186556600} {:answer/id #uuid "e2716f9d-9b38-5af5-a1db-0a58828ce254" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A parabola" :db/id 17592186556989} {:answer/id #uuid "f08c1f85-9679-5c12-98ff-95ec5e74f12d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A hyperbola with semiaxes $3$ and $\sqrt{6}$" :db/id 17592186557023} {:answer/id #uuid "f4b9bfec-c82b-508d-8c85-f0390ed2dd71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "An ellipse with semiaxes $9$ and $\sqrt{6}$" :db/id 17592186557032}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186557023} :answer-field/id #uuid "c0e2b3fe-1fd8-5dda-acb7-cbb560deb0ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186557174}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "584e6ba7-6a66-5994-b1b0-75bfa6a71313" :question/math-academy-id "q-95392" :question/problem "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

and the curve $C,$ defined as
