Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg/min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $9\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $320\,\text{L}$ of water; clean water enters at $9\,\text{L/min},$ and mixed water leaves at $5\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is

$$
V(t)=320+9t-5t=(320+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the *concentration* of the water at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $5\,\text{L/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =\frac{5Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{4(80+t)}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{4(80+t)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{4(80+t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{4(80+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\,dQ & =-\frac{5}{4}\int \frac{1}{80+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
Q(t)=\frac{A}{(80+t)^{5/4}}.
$$

Using the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{A}{{80}^{5/4}} & =20 \\ A & =20(80)^{5/4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
Q(t)=20{\left(\frac{80}{80+t}\right)}^{5/4}.
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. Since the tank has a capacity of $500\,\text{L},$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =500 \\ 320+4{t}_{o} & =500 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =180 \\ {t}_{o} & =45\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(45)7 & =20{\left(\frac{80}{80+45}\right)}^{5/4} \\  & =20{\left(\frac{80}{125}\right)}^{5/4} \\  & ≈11.45\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Let $Q$ be the amount of sugar in the vat at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

Note that pure water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of sugar) enters the vat at a rate of $14\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the vat is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we first determine the volume of solution in the vat at time $t.$

The vat initially contains $500\,\text{L}$ of solution; water enters at $14\,\text{L/min}$ and drains out at $10\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the vat after $t$ minutes is 

$$
500+14t-10t=(500+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{2(125+t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{2(125+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{5}{2(125+t)}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{125+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(125+t)^{5/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains $15\,\text{kg}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=15,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =15 \\ \frac{A}{(125+0)^{5/2}} & =15 \\ A & =15\cdot {125}^{5/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=15{\left(\frac{125}{125+t}\right)}^{5/2}
$$

Finally, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=15{\left(\frac{125}{139}\right)}^{5/2}≈11.50\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{9}{12}(xy+1)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xy)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x={y}^{2}}^{x=1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}y-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{27}{y}^{9}-\frac{1}{12}{y}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{12}[\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12}-(-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12})] \\  & =\frac{9}{12}(\frac{2}{9}-\frac{2}{27}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}-\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{7}\right) \\  & =\frac{8}{315}.\end{aligned}
$$

We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=18{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 18{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(6{x}^{3})-\int (6{x}^{3})\left(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $$
\displaystyle \int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x\left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)-\int \left(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}-12D \\  & ={x}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4}{3})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-12D.$

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=6I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)=6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+2I=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+2{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+3(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ +2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-2\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-6\alpha -2\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2\alpha +6\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -6\alpha -2\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{3}{5}$ and $\beta =\frac{1}{5}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=3$ and $Q=1,$ and

$$
P+Q=3+1=4.
$$

Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=60$ and $p=0.44.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =60\cdot 0.44 \\  & =26.4 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60\cdot (1-0.44) \\  & =33.6 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(60)(0.44)=26.4
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(60)(0.44)(1-0.44)=14.784.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(26.4,14.784).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X>30).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X>30)=P(X\ge 31)≈P(Y\ge 30.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 30.5) & =P(Z\ge \frac{30.5-26.4}{\sqrt{14.784}}) \\  & ≈P(Z\ge 1.07) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.07) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.07) \\  & =1-Φ(1.07) \\  & =1-0.8577 \\  & =0.1423\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X>30)≈0.142.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.1431.$

Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100\cdot 0.5 \\  & =50 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =50 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(100)(0.5)=50
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(100)(0.5)(1-0.5)=25.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(50,25).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(43<X<53).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(43<X<53)=P(44\le X\le 52)≈P(43.5\le Y\le 52.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(43.5\le Y\le 52.5) & =P(\frac{43.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}\le Z\le \frac{52.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.30\le Z\le 0.50) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.50)-P(Z<-1.30) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.50)-P(Z\le -1.30) \\  & =Φ(0.50)-Φ(-1.30) \\  & =0.6915-0.0968 \\  & =0.5947\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(43<X<53)≈0.595.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.5947.$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of sugar) enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $450\,\text{gal}$ of solution.

- Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $15t\,\text{gal}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $10t\,\text{gal}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
450+15t-10t=(450+5t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Then, since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{90+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =0-\frac{2Q}{90+t} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t}\,Q.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{2}{90+t}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{90+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(90+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ \frac{A}{(90+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ A & =18\cdot {90}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=18{\left(\frac{90}{90+t}\right)}^{2}
$$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=14\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=14I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{24}}=24q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
15=14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(15) & =\frac{d}{dt}(14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =14\,\frac{dI}{dt}+24\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+12I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-4t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-4t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{15}{2}-7I-12q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{15}{2}-7I(0)-12q(0) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}-7\cdot 2-12\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{19}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-0}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-4B{e}^{-4t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{19}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{19}{2} & =-3A{e}^{-0}-4B{e}^{-0} \\ -\frac{19}{2} & =-3A-4B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2=A+B \\ -\frac{19}{2}=-3A-4B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $B=\frac{7}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-4t}.
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $0.3$ seconds, in amperes, is

$$
I(0.3)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-0.9}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-1.2}≈0.444,
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=14\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=14I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{24}}=24q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
15=14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(15) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}\right) \\ 0 & =14\,\frac{dI}{dt}+24\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+12I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-4t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-4t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{15}{2}-7I-12q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{15}{2}-7I(0)-12q(0) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}-7\cdot 2-12\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{19}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-0}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-4B{e}^{-4t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{19}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{19}{2} & =-3A{e}^{-0}-4B{e}^{-0} \\ -\frac{19}{2} & =-3A-4B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2=A+B \\ -\frac{19}{2}=-3A-4B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $B=\frac{7}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-4t}.
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $0.3$ seconds, in amperes, is

$$
I(0.3)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-0.9}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-1.2}≈0.444,
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ \\ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ \\ &= \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}48{y}^{3}(x-y)\,\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x/2}(x{y}^{3}-{y}^{4})\text{d}y\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{y=0}^{y=x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =48{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{64}{x}^{5}-\frac{1}{160}{x}^{5})\text{d}x \\  & =48\cdot \frac{3}{320}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{20}{[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}.
$$

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{Y}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{3})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-{\left(\frac{8}{5}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$ The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S=[0,1]\times [0,2].
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y)=g(x)\cdot h(y),
$$

where $g(x)=2x$ and $h(y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{4}.$

Hence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=0.$

$$

$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I) \\ I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-I \\ 2I & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\left(\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\right){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\left(\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )\right)-\left(\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi ))\right) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }}{2}-\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi }-{e}^{\pi }}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ &= \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi ) \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)}^{-}$ using L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))^{′}}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{′}}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi ) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the first hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{4}{-2\cdot {0}^{-}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, and the second hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{-2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{4}{-2\cdot {0}^{+}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

![](images/f9/f9a4fc8fa61dac84d3dbc4bc48f86e2b702f7854b1fd1d3b3e5f4303fe7769a7.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

$$

where ${\sigma }_{i}^{2}=\text{Var}[{X}_{i}],$ ${\sigma }_{12}=\text{Cov}[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}],$ and $\rho $ is the correlation, then the joint probability density function of $X$ is

$$

and $|Σ|$ denotes the determinant of $Σ.$

$$

$$

$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y=a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have ${\mu }_{1}=5$ and ${\mu }_{2}=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+3\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & ={\mu }_{1}+3\cdot {\mu }_{2} \\  & =5+3\cdot 1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}=1,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=5,$ and ${\sigma }_{12}={\sigma }_{21}=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var} [Y] & =\operatorname{Var} [{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}] \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 1+{3}^{2}\cdot 5+2\cdot 1\cdot 3\cdot (-2) \\  & =1+45-12 \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(8,34).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(1\le Y\le 5).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le Y\le 5) & =P(\frac{1-8}{\sqrt{34}}\le Z\le \frac{5-8}{\sqrt{34}}) \\  & =P(-1.20\le Z\le -0.51)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.20\le Z\le -0.51) & =P(Z\le -0.51)-P(Z<-1.20) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.51)-P(Z\le -1.20) \\  & =Φ(-0.51)-Φ(-1.20)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.20) & =0.1151 \\ Φ(-0.51) & =0.3050\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.20\le Z\le -0.51) & =Φ(-0.51)-Φ(-1.20) \\  & =0.3050-0.1151 \\  & =0.1899.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(1\le Y\le 5)=0.1899.
$$

When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & ={\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)({\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-3{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta ({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\cos }^{3}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{\cancel{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta }({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{\cancel{3}}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\right) \\  & =\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-3{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}

For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =-1-(-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ))}^{′}}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the limit in the numerator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ) \\  & =-(-1)+2\cdot (-1) \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the first hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{-}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{-}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Using the calculations from part II, and the second hint, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to (3\pi /2)^{+}}\left(\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta )+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta )}\right) \\  & =\frac{-1}{{0}^{+}} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Since the limits of our derivative are both infinite, there is a vertical tangent to the curve at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

$$

$$

$$

Using the given values of ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}$, and ${\sigma }_{12},$ our covariance matrix is

$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y=a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have ${\mu }_{1}=-2$ and ${\mu }_{2}=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[2{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}] \\  & =2\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+4\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & =2{\mu }_{1}+4{\mu }_{2} \\  & =2(-2)+4(3) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}=2,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=4,$ and ${\sigma }_{12}={\sigma }_{21}=-1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var} [Y] & =\operatorname{Var} [2{X}_{1}+4{X}_{2}] \\  & ={2}^{2}(2)+{4}^{2}(4)+2(2)(4)(-1) \\  & =8+64-16 \\  & =56.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(8,56).
$$

$$

$$

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.27)=0.6064.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(Y\le 10)=0.6064.

$$

$$

$$

$$
P(F)=0.48.
$$

P(C∣F)=0.026.

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x,\,y,\,xz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-2{v}^{2})+{v}^{2}\cdot (-u)+{u}^{2}v\cdot 2v \\  & =-2u{v}^{2}-u{v}^{2}+2{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}{v}^{2}-3u{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\cdot {u}^{2}{v}^{2}+(-3)\cdot u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2-3=-1.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{2}{x y},\,v=4 x^{3} y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{2}{x y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=2 & ⟹\, & u=2 \\  & y=\frac{2}{5 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{2}{x y}=5 & ⟹\, & u=5\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=4 x^{3} y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=\frac{7}{4 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 4 x^{3} y=7 & ⟹\, & v=7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v)\,:\,2\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 7\}
$$

![](images/d3/d3dd7067bbcb0a6e3c901d12a2795500e192594a14e7f1373dd325e4fd270363.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{2}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{2}{x y^{2}} \\ 12 x^{2} y & 4 x^{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{16 x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{y}{16 x}=\frac{x^{2} y^{2}}{16 x^{3} y}=\frac{1}{u^{2} v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{u^{2} v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{u^{2} v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\  & =\int_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{u^{2}}\,\mathrm d u\int_{1}^{7}\frac{1}{v}\,\mathrm d v \\  & =(- \frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2})\cdot (\ln 7-\ln 1) \\  & =\frac{3 \ln{\left(7 \right)}}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{3}{x y},\,v=2 x^{3} y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{3}{x y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{3}{4 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{3}{x y}=4 & ⟹\, & u=4 \\  & y=\frac{1}{3 x} & ⟹\, & \frac{3}{x y}=9 & ⟹\, & u=9\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=2 x^{3} y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{1}{x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 2 x^{3} y=2 & ⟹\, & v=2 \\  & y=\frac{7}{2 x^{3}} & ⟹\, & 2 x^{3} y=7 & ⟹\, & v=7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta=\{(u,v)\,:\,4\le u\le 9,\,2\le v\le 7\}
$$

![](images/07/075e4196e1ad4b6dafc70878555598bac64e8880b2c152d61c2a6437acbaaceb.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}- \frac{3}{x^{2} y} & - \frac{3}{x y^{2}} \\ 6 x^{2} y & 2 x^{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{12 x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{y}{12 x}=\frac{x^{2} y^{2}}{12 x^{3} y}=\frac{3}{2 u^{2} v}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{3}{2 u^{2} v}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\int_{4}^{9}\int_{2}^{7}\frac{3}{2 u^{2} v}\,\mathrm d v\,\mathrm d u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int_{4}^{9}\frac{1}{u^{2}}\,\mathrm d u\int_{2}^{7}\frac{1}{v}\,\mathrm d v \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \left(- \frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}\right)\cdot (\ln 7-\ln 2) \\  & =- \frac{5 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{24} + \frac{5 \ln{\left(7 \right)}}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{1}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{1}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=4{x}_{k}^{3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[4{(2+\frac{k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=4{x}^{3}$ and $b=3.$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$

$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)) \\  & \,-3(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)) \\  & \,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & -3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n})\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n})\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right) \\  & \,\,\,\,=-3+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{n\pi x}{3}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the coefficients next to sines and cosines, we obtain the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-3 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{a}_{n}=\frac{6}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}-3{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

We can calculate $\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}$ using synthetic division.

For synthetic division to work, we need the coefficient of $x$ in the denominator to be equal to $1.$ So first, we factor the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5} & =\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3(x-\frac{5}{3})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})}\end{aligned}
$$

Carrying out the synthetic division process on $$
\displaystyle \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})},
$$ we arrive at the following:

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrrrr} & {x}^{4} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{5}{3} & 9 & 12 & 0 & 0 & -25 \\  & ↓ & 15 & 45 & 75 & 125 \\ \hline  & 9 & 27 & 45 & 75 & 100\end{array}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{(x-\frac{5}{3})} & =\frac{1}{3}(9{x}^{3}+27{x}^{2}+45x+75+\frac{100}{(x-\frac{5}{3})}) \\  & =3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+15x+25+\frac{100}{3x-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, our final result is

$$
\frac{9{x}^{4}+12{x}^{3}-25}{3x-5}=3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}+15x+25+\frac{100}{3x-5}.
$$

The variable $y$ is being *divided* by $3.$ To isolate $y$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-3.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{3}\,\, & \le \,\,3 \\ (-3)\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{3}\right)\,\, & \ge \,\,(-3)\cdot 3 \\ (-3)\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{3}\right)\,\, & \ge \,\,-9\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)\cdot \left(-\frac{y}{3}\right) & \ge -9 \\ (\cancel{-}3)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{y}{3}) & \ge -9 \\ 3\cdot \frac{y}{3} & \ge -9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $3$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=224,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{56\,000}{100\,000}=0.56.$

Now, since

$$
np=224(0.56)=125.44>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=224(1-0.56)=98.56>5,
$$

and the $n=224$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,\frac{0.56(1-0.56)}{224}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,0.0011).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If between $112$ and $140$ of subscribers in the sample have a digital subscription, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{112}{224}\le \widehat{\,p} & \le \frac{140}{224} \\ 0.5\le \widehat{\,p} & \le 0.625.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.5\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.625).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.625) & =P(\frac{0.5-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}\le Z\le \frac{0.625-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.81\le Z\le 1.96) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.96)-P(Z\le -1.81) \\  & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.96)=0.9750,\,Φ(-1.81)=0.0351.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.625) & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81) \\  & =0.9750-0.0351 \\  & =0.9399.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we set up the two corresponding equations and solve them independently:

- If $|3-\frac{2}{3}y|=3-\frac{2}{3}y,$ we obtain:

$$

$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation by $-\frac{3}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}y & =2 \\ \left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)\cdot (-\frac{2}{3}y) & =\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)\cdot (2) \\ (\cancel{-\frac{3}{2}})\cdot (\cancel{-\frac{2}{3}}y) & =-\frac{6}{2} \\ y & =-3.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}|3-\frac{2}{3}y| & =5 \\ -(3-\frac{2}{3}y) & =5 \\ -3+\frac{2}{3}y & =5 \\ \frac{2}{3}y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Notice the following:

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $-3<x\le -1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $1\le y<9.$

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $-1<x<1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<1.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0<y<1.$ 

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-\sqrt{y}\le X\le \sqrt{y}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(\sqrt{y})-{F}_{X}(-\sqrt{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=80,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.4.$

Now, since

$$
np=80(0.4)=32>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=80(1-0.4)=48>5,
$$

and $n=80$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,0.0030).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $32$ but fewer than $36$ calls are complaints, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{32}{80}<\widehat{\,p} & <\frac{36}{80} \\ 0.4\le \widehat{\,p} & \le 0.45.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.4<\widehat{\,p}<0.45).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.45) & =P(\frac{0.4-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}<Z<\frac{0.45-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<0.91) \\  & =P(Z<0.91)-P(Z<0.00) \\  & =Φ(0.91)-Φ(0.00)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4<\widehat{\,p}<0.45) & =Φ(0.91)-Φ(0).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}=8{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2+x=2+4\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-xy=-2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

First, notice that the transformation $Y={(1-X)}^{2}$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-1<x<3.$ 

![](images/03/03718360bf910c74c22b36f34ad2f63bfad6d9387c0cdc62d3fb366a52f356c9.png)

Moreover, for $-1<x<3,$ we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $0\le y<4.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0\le y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({(1-X)}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}\le 1-X\le {y}^{1/2}) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}-1\le -X\le {y}^{1/2}-1) \\  & =P(1-{y}^{1/2}\le X\le 1+{y}^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0\le y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{1+{y}^{1/2}}{4}+\frac{1-{y}^{1/2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}, & 0\le y<4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where 

- $n\le 5\%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

We're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied in each case.

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =50(0.6) \\  & =30 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =50(1-0.6) \\  & =20 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =60(0.8) \\  & =48 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60(1-0.8) \\  & =12 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =40(0.9) \\  & =36 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =40(1-0.9) \\  & =4 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since $n(1-p)≯5,$ we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that the possible values of $X$ are $x\in (1,\infty ),$ and $Y=\frac{1}{X}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X$ when $X>1.$
 Moreover, for $x>1,$ we have $0<y<1.$

![](images/16/16f3dc78752c8cfcb6b6968e3d57bb3639a4205e2a32dfd569c8c2ca3c29a589.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(\frac{1}{X}\le y) \\  & =P(X\ge \frac{1}{y}) \\  & =1-{F}_{X}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<1,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =0-\left(-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\right)\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot {f}_{X}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot {f}_{X}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{{\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}1,\, & 0<y<1 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy)=2x-2x=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,1)$ to $B(5,4)$ and  ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](images/18/18b1a5bdc11ca3c2b4b728cf8df3a3e1c4b6c2fbbe86549e9ad773367495c533.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+j+t\cdot [(5\,i+4j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=(4t+1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}+8t+1, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2xy=-2(4t+1)(3t+1)=-24{t}^{2}-14t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((16{t}^{2}+8t+1)\cdot (3)-(-24{t}^{2}-14t-2)\cdot (4))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,144{t}^{2}+80t+11\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[48{t}^{3}+40{t}^{2}+11t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(48+40+11) \\  & =99.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=99.
$$

To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$

We focus on the term with the exponential ${e}^{-2s}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s-3)$ and a repeated linear factor ${s}^{2},$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{1}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{C}{s-3}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
1=As(s-3)+B(s-3)+C{s}^{2}.
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=0,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(-3)+C(0)\,⟹\,B=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

- Setting $s=3,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(0)+C(9)\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+C\,⟹\,A=-C=-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=-\frac{1}{9s}-\frac{1}{3{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{9(s-3)}.
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{1}{9s}-\frac{1}{3{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{9(s-3)}\} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{t}{3}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-2s}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=2.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-2)f(t-2) & =u(t-2)(-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{t-2}{3}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}) \\  & =u(t-2)(-\frac{3t-5}{9}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=5{e}^{3t}+u(t-2)\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}-\frac{3t-5}{9}.
$$

To solve the initial value problem, we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s).$

To find the inverse transform, we first ignore the exponential term ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ (which corresponds to a time shift) and focus on the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{2}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+1)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{2}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}=\frac{A}{s+1}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
2=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+1).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-1,$ we have

$$
2=A((-1)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,5A=2\,⟹\,A=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,B=-A=-\frac{2}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have

$$
2=4A+C\,⟹\,C=2-\frac{8}{5}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{2}{5}(\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{-s+1}{{s}^{2}+4})=\frac{2}{5}(\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{2}{5}({L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+1}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}\}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}({e}^{-t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ term in $Y(s).$ By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})f\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{2}{5}[{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}-\cos \,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{2}\sin \,(2\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-\pi /2))=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-\pi /2))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot \frac{2}{5}[{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\,u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})(2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the form given in the problem statement $$
\displaystyle y(t)=\frac{1}{5}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot g(t),
$$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{{y}^{3}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,3)$ to $B(5,3)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](images/3d/3d64ffb0e4cc313a2857d1c20922c1202619d0bdeb3d97f2808b4995c99f7f9f.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+3\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+3\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=-\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=-\sqrt{27}, \\ Q(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}=((4t+1)-1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\sqrt{27})\cdot (0)-(16{t}^{2})\cdot (4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-64{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{64{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-\frac{64}{3}.
$$
