- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{{y}^{3}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,3)$ to $B(5,3)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](images/3d/3d64ffb0e4cc313a2857d1c20922c1202619d0bdeb3d97f2808b4995c99f7f9f.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+3\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+3\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=-\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=-\sqrt{27}, \\ Q(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}=((4t+1)-1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\sqrt{27})\cdot (0)-(16{t}^{2})\cdot (4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-64{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\left[-\frac{64{t}^{3}}{3}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-\frac{64}{3}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}.$ So,

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{6},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 3,\,-2\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{6}-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}+4y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}+4L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0:$

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $f(t)=\cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3}).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. 

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} & ={e}^{-(\pi /3)s}\cdot L\{\cos \,(2\,(t+\frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s/3}\cdot L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s/3}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}\}+4L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cos \,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\ sY(s)+4Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+4)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/91/9168d2ed7eeaa5f1dd331a0a986ac7ecfd6b964217a2cb614deb0cdd54437d65.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 4 y$ and $Q(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 4 x y.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=4 x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=4 x.
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq 1,\quad 0\leq y\leq x^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds&=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx \\&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\&=\iint_D\left(8 x\right)\,dA \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{x^{2}}\left(8 x\right)\,dy\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left[8 x y\right]_{y=0}^{y=x^{2}}\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(8 x^{3}\right)\,dx \\&=\left[2 x^{4}\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\&=\left(2\right)-\left(0\right) \\&=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=61.7+6.8x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=61.7+6.8x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}=61.7.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $98\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.98=0.02\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.01.
$$

We are given that $P(T>6.965)=0.01.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.01}=6.965.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(2-3.5)^{2}+(3-3.5)^{2}+(4-3.5)^{2}+(5-3.5)^{2} \\  & =2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=6.965\cdot \sqrt{0.9\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{3.5}^{2}}{5})}≈10.9
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=61.7\pm 10.9
$$

To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1\. First, we perform the transformations *inside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out horizontal stretches and reflections, followed by horizontal translations.

2\. Then, we perform the transformations *outside* the argument of $f.$ We first carry out vertical stretches and reflections, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the $x$ inside the function:

$$
y=-f(\frac{1}{2}(x-2))
$$

To plot $y=-f(\frac{1}{2}(x-2)),$ we apply the following steps: 

- Take the curve $y=f(x).$

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=2$ parallel to the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}x).$

![](images/28/2891d009bd6f5d026ca47afe90f3ec4d6fafc654b7212392b325f76fe43f806e.png)

 

- Then, translate the result by $2$ units to the right to get the graph of $y=f(\frac{1}{2}(x-2)).$

![](images/ab/ab1f210741e01139618dc2fa1347cf1591cb90ca4f67906b89ebc7df29d77f32.png)

- Finally, reflect the result across the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=-f(\frac{1}{2}(x-2)).$

In the figure, $y$ is the kite's height, and $z$ is the distance between the boy and the kite. The quantity $z=20$ meters does not change with time because the string's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{20} \\ y & =20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(20\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Converting the given information from degrees to radians, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $$
\displaystyle \theta ={45}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\pi }{{180}^{∘}}=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(20\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{1}{20} & =\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{20}$ radians per second.

We use the following notations:

- $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x$ is the regression line that best fits the population, and

- $\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x$ is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that  

$$
\widehat{\,y}={\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}+{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{1}x=0.6+0.2x.
$$

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]\%$ confidence interval for the slope ${\beta }_{1}$ of our model can be written as

$$
{\beta }_{0}\,\pm \,\overbrace{{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]}^{\text{margin of error}}.
$$

Note the following:

- $\,{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}$ is our point estimate for the intercept, computed using the data points from our sample.

- $P(T>{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2},$ where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom.

- $\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]$ is the standard error of ${\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0},$ given by

$$
\text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=\sqrt{\text{MSE}\cdot (\frac{1}{n}+\frac{{\overset{―}{x}}^{2}}{{S}_{xx}})}
$$

where we have:

- $\text{MSE}$ is the mean squared error of the model:

$$
\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n-2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-{\widehat{\,y}}_{i})^{2}
$$

where ${\widehat{\,y}}_{i}$ is the estimate of ${y}_{i}$ given by our regression model.

- ${S}_{xx}$ is the usual sum of squares formula:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}
$$

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate. From the regression equation $\widehat{\,y}=0.6+0.2x,$ our point estimate is

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}=0.6.
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. 

- Since we are interested in finding a $80\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.8=0.2\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.1.
$$

We are given that $P(T>1.886)=0.1.$ As a result, 

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}={t}_{2,0.1}=1.886.
$$

- Computing ${S}_{xx},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} & =(34-38)^{2}+(36-38)^{2}+(40-38)^{2}+(42-38)^{2} \\  & =16+4+4+16 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

- Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=1.886\cdot \sqrt{0.0125\cdot (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{{38}^{2}}{40})}≈1.3
$$

- **Step 3.** Determine the limits of the confidence interval:

$$
{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,\pm \,{t}_{n-2,\alpha /2}\cdot \text{SE}[{\widehat{\,\beta }}_{0}\,]=0.6\pm 1.3
$$

Since $f$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,2\pi ).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $2\pi $-periodicity:

$$
f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $2\pi $-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $2\pi $-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi )=f\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=F\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=F\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

$$

$$

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y{e}^{x}-{e}^{z})\text{ }k \\  & =2y{e}^{x}\text{ }i+2{e}^{x}\text{ }j-{e}^{z}k \\ ∇\,f(1,1,-1) & =2(1)e\text{ }i+2e\text{ }j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =2e\,i+2e\,j-{e}^{-1}k \\  & =⟨2e,2e,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\end{aligned}

Let $y$ denote the vertical distance from the drone's projection to the starting point, and $z$ be the distance between the drone and the starting point, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={60}^{∘},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({60}^{∘}) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ z & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}y) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=4\text{km}/\text{h}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot 4≈4.62
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the speed of the drone is approximately $4.62\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/09/09acd3df62b333bdaeb7553599507d4dbad7412ef2770b00e8fc8855b38a774e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{2y}+4x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}-{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)[x]_{-1}^{0}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\cdot 1\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =[4y-{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(4(-1)-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4 - 4 t^{2},\quad y=4 t^{2},\quad z=\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\left(x + y\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- z\right)\,k \\ & =\left(4\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 - 4 t^{2}\right)\,i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(4 t^{2}\right)\,j+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k \\ & =\left(- 8 t\right)\,i+\left(8 t\right)\,j+\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t) & =\left(\left(4\right)\,i+\left(0\right)\,j+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\right)\cdot\left(\left(- 8 t\right)\,i+\left(8 t\right)\,j+\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\,k\right) \\ & =\left(4\right)\cdot\left(- 8 t\right)+\left(0\right)\cdot\left(8 t\right)+\left(- \sin{\left(\pi t \right)}\right)\cdot\left(\pi \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right) \\ & =\left(- 32 t\right)+\left(0\right)+\left(- \pi \sin{\left(\pi t \right)} \cos{\left(\pi t \right)}\right) \\ & =- 32 t - \frac{\pi \sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ=\oint_C F\cdot\mathrm dr & =\int_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\int_{-1}^{1}\left(- 32 t - \frac{\pi \sin{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm dt \\ & =\left[- 16 t^{2} + \frac{\cos{\left(2 \pi t \right)}}{4}\right]_{-1}^{1} \\ & =[\left(-16\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)]-[\left(-16\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)] \\ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}

$$
c=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.

$$

and for the variance of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 6 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ -4 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =14+4+7 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}

changed.before:
The change-of-variables method can be applied when a transformation $Y=u(X)$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing (i.e., strictly monotonic) over the entire support of $X.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each transformation in turn.

- Transformation I is strictly monotonic. The function $u(x)={x}^{5}+1$ is strictly increasing for $x\in (-1,1).$

- Transformation II is *not* strictly monotonic. The function $u(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ is strictly increasing for $x\in (0,\frac{\pi }{4})$ and strictly decreasing for $x\in (\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{2}).$

- Transformation III is *not* strictly monotonic. The function $u(x)=1-{x}^{4}$ is strictly increasing for $x\in (-\infty ,0)$ and strictly decreasing for $x\in (0,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

- First, we take the graph $y={e}^{x}.$

- Then, we stretch the graph by a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ parallel to the $x$-axis and get the graph of  $y={e}^{2x}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$

$$

- Finally, we shift the result vertically by $3$ units down and obtain the graph of $y={e}^{2x}-3.$ After this transformation, the point $(\frac{a}{2},b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$

$$

Since the point $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $y={e}^{x}$, we have that ${e}^{a}=b.$

Now consider the graph of $y={e}^{2x}-3.$ Substituting $x=\frac{a}{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2\cdot (a/2)}-3 \\  & ={e}^{a}-3 \\  & =b-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(\frac{a}{2},b-3)$ must lie on $y={e}^{2x}-3.$

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=4$ and $b=-2$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{-2}{2(4)} \\  & =-\frac{-2}{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=\frac{1}{4}$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4{x}^{2}-2x+1 \\  & =4{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}-2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{2}{4}+\frac{4}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}).$

If $X\in (a,b)$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function ${f}_{X}$ and $Y=u(X),$ where the function $u(x)$ is strictly monotonic, then according to the change-of-variables method, the probability density function of $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)|, & y\text{ is between }u(a)\text{ and }u(b) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Here, we have $Y=3X+3\pi .$ The transformation $u(x)=3x+3\pi $ is strictly monotonically *increasing*, so the change-of-variables method can be used.

First, we find ${u}^{-1}(y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u(y) & =3y+3\pi  \\ y & =3{u}^{-1}(y)+3\pi  \\ {u}^{-1}(y) & =\frac{y}{3}-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find $({u}^{-1})^{′}(y):$

$$
({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)=\frac{1}{3}
$$

According to the change-of-variables method, for nonzero ${f}_{Y},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={f}_{X}({u}^{-1}(y))\cdot |({u}^{-1})^{′}(y)| \\  & ={f}_{X}(\frac{y}{3}-\pi )\cdot |\frac{1}{3}| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{3}-\pi )\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{3}-\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${f}_{X}$ is nonzero on $0<x<\pi ,$ the bounds are $a=0$ and $b=\pi ,$ we have

$$
u(0)=3\pi ,\,u(\pi )=6\pi .
$$

Therefore, the probability distribution of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{3}-\pi ), & 3\pi <y<6\pi  \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x+5xy=0 \\ 5y-3xy=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+5xy & =0 \\ x(-3+5y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{3}{5}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-3(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{3}{5},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-3xy & =0 \\ y(5-3x) & =0 \\ \frac{3}{5}(5-3x) & =0 \\ 5-3x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{5}{3},\frac{3}{5}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{5}{3},\frac{3}{5}).$

Let the random variable $Y∼U[0,1]$ be uniformly distributed. Suppose that the function $F(x)$ is a cumulative distribution function, where $F(a)=0,F(b)=1,$ and $F$ is strictly monotonic on $a<x<b.$ Then, the random variable $X,$ given by

$$
X={F}^{-1}(Y)
$$

is a continuous random variable with the cumulative distribution function $F(x).$

So, we need to find the inverse of $y=F(x).$ To do this, we solve the following equation for $x,$ taking into account that $0\le y\le 1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡({e}^{x}) \\ \frac{y\pi }{2} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡({e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{y\pi }{2}\right) \\ x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{y\pi }{2}\right))\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the numbers drawn from $U[0,1]$ into the above equation:

- For $y=0.321,$ we get $$
\displaystyle x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{0.321\pi }{2}\right))≈-0.595
$$

- For $y=0.567,$ we get $$
\displaystyle x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{0.567\pi }{2}\right))≈0.212
$$

- For $y=0.804,$ we get $$
\displaystyle x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{0.804\pi }{2}\right))≈1.146
$$

Let the random variable $Y∼U[0,1]$ be uniformly distributed. Suppose that the function $F(x)$ is a cumulative distribution function, where $F(a)=0,F(b)=1,$ and $F$ is strictly monotonic on $a<x<b.$ Then, the random variable $X,$ given by

$$
X={F}^{-1}(Y)
$$

is a continuous random variable with the cumulative distribution function $F(x).$

First, we must find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ corresponding to our random variable. Since our PDF $f(x)$ is non-negative only for $1\le x\le 4,$ we have

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & \,x<1, \\ {\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & \,1\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & \,x>4.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Evaluating the integral, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}\,{|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =2(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & \,x<1, \\ 2(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}), & \,1\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & \,x>4.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we need to find the inverse of $y=F(x).$ So, we solve the following equation for $x,$ taking into account that $1\le x\le 4$ and $0<y<1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}) \\ \frac{y}{2} & =1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} & =1-\frac{y}{2} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} & =\frac{2-y}{2} \\ \sqrt{x} & =\frac{2}{2-y} \\ x & =\frac{4}{(2-y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+6=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{6}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}

Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.06\,\text{kg/L}$ of the salt enters the tank at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =2.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $560\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{560}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{40Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{14}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =2.4-\frac{Q}{14}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}Q=2.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/14},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{14}\alpha =2.4\,⟹\,\alpha =33.6.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=33.6.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$

T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=8 x - 2 y,\,v=x + y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $8 x - 2 y=u$ and $x + y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(8 x - 2 y)^{2}-(x + y)=0\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v=u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $x + y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=16.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} \\ v &=16\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 4,16).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-4\le u\le 4,\,u^{2}\le v\le 16\}.
$$

![](images/38/387e22e062c4ff7f24d26561fe369041f11f59a2b0305f8dc7b3ce49d411031a.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}8&-2\\1&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=10\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(10)^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |\frac{1}{10}|\,dudv \\ &=\frac{1}{10}\int_{-4}^{4}[\int_{u^{2}}^{16}dv]du \\ &=\frac{1}{10}\int_{-4}^{4}[v]_{u^{2}}^{16}du \\ &=\frac{1}{10}\int_{-4}^{4}(16)-(u^{2})du \\ &=\frac{1}{10}\int_{-4}^{4}(16 - u^{2})du \\ &=\frac{1}{10}[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 16 u]_{-4}^{4} \\ &=\frac{1}{10}(((64)+\left(- \frac{64}{3}\right))-((-64)+\left(\frac{64}{3}\right))) \\ &=\frac{1}{10}\left(\frac{256}{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{128}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 4 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 4 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 4 y)^{2}-(y)=4\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=4\,⟹\,v=u^{2} - 4.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=8.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} - 4 \\ v &=8\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 2 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2 \sqrt{3},8).$

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,- 2 \sqrt{3}\le u\le 2 \sqrt{3},\,u^{2} - 4\le v\le 8\}.

$$

$$

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-5<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=1$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{1+2}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{3}{2}$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$

$$

We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+4y &=1 \\ 2x-2y &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $2,$ then we will get a $-4y$ term that can cancel with the $4y$ in the first equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+4y &=1 &&  \\ 2x-2y &=3 && |\,\times 2\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+4y &=1 \\ 4x-4y &=6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{array}{rl}3x+\cancel{4y} & =1 \\ 4x-\cancel{4y} & =6 \\ \hline (3x+4x) & =(1+6) \\ 7x & =7 \\ x & =1\end{array}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=1$ into the equation $2x-2y=3$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-2y & =3 \\ 2(1)-2y & =3 \\ 2-2y & =3 \\ -2y & =1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1,\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(1,-\frac{1}{2}).$

Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$

$$
\{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta \}
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

The set $A$ consists of all points that lie to the left of the parabola ${y}^{2}=4x.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

![](images/8f/8f182873a8384097b56152284e67189e36f0a79a0b2bbda8926a2f8279db7ddd.png)

Let's add the points $P(0,1)$ and $Q(2,\frac{4}{3})$ and some neighborhoods of these points to our diagram.

![](images/66/66c8cb59cceadd43e3c4316925f1dd624c2e77a6ec547c9f9a1a02846bb537fb.png)

Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The coordinates of $P(0,1)$ do not satisfy the equation $y=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}.$ Hence, $P$ does not lie on the boundary of the set.

- Statement II is true. The coordinates of $P(0,1)$ satisfy the inequality $y>\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $A.$

- Statement III is false. Every open neighborhood of $Q$ contains points that belong to $A$ and points that do not belong to $A.$ The point $Q$ is a boundary point for the given set.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II only.'

The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ \\ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ \\ &= \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{a}_{7}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡(7x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(14x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{28}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{28}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(28\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

changed.before:
Since $f$ is the $\frac{\pi }{3}$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  

- $f(x+\frac{\pi }{3})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0\frac{\pi }{3}).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi /3$-periodicity:

$$
f(x+\frac{\pi }{3})=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)=f(0+\frac{\pi }{3})=f(0)=F(0)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+\frac{\pi }{6})=f(0+\frac{\pi }{6})=f\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=F\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})=\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=f(0)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x+\frac{\pi }{6})\ne f(x)$ for $x=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

I. $$
\displaystyle F(x,y)=\left\langle 3 y^{3} - \frac{y}{8},\,9 x y^{2} + \frac{7 x}{8}\right\rangle 
$$

II. $F(x,y)=⟨3 y e^{3 x},\,x - 3 e^{3 x}⟩$

III. $$
\displaystyle F(x,y)=\left\langle \frac{y}{8} + 3 e^{3 x + 3 y},\,\frac{9 x}{8} + 3 e^{3 x + 3 y}\right\rangle 
$$

According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field I gives the required area. In this case,
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=9 y^{2} - \frac{1}{8}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=9 y^{2} + \frac{7}{8},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\left(9 y^{2} + \frac{7}{8}\right)-\left(9 y^{2} - \frac{1}{8}\right)=\left(\frac{7}{8}\right)+\left(9 y^{2}\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{8}\right)-\left(9 y^{2}\right)=1.
$$

- Vector field II does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3 e^{3 x}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1 - 9 e^{3 x},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\left(1 - 9 e^{3 x}\right)-\left(3 e^{3 x}\right)=\left(1\right)+\left(- 9 e^{3 x}\right)-\left(3 e^{3 x}\right)=1 - 12 e^{3 x}\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field III gives the required area. Notice that
$$
\displaystyle \frac{∂P}{∂y}=9 e^{3 x + 3 y} + \frac{1}{8}
$$
and
$$
\displaystyle \frac{∂Q}{∂x}=9 e^{3 x + 3 y} + \frac{9}{8},
$$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\left(9 e^{3 x + 3 y} + \frac{9}{8}\right)-\left(9 e^{3 x + 3 y} + \frac{1}{8}\right)=\left(\frac{9}{8}\right)+\left(9 e^{3 x + 3 y}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)-\left(9 e^{3 x + 3 y}\right)=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-4<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=1$ and ${x}_{2}=4,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{1+4}{2}=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{5}{2}$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4(x-1)(x-4) \\  & =-4(\frac{5}{2}-1)(\frac{5}{2}-4) \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(\frac{5}{2},9),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,9],$ i.e. $-\infty <f(x)\le 9.$

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{7{x}^{5}-4{x}^{3}}{2{x}^{3}+9} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7{x}^{5}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{9}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(7{x}^{2}-4)}{(2+\frac{9}{{x}^{3}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the term $\frac{9}{{x}^{3}}$ becomes very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(7{x}^{2}-4)}{(2+\frac{9}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ≈\frac{7{x}^{2}-4}{2+0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(7{x}^{2}-4).\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

$$

$$

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir.

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =12.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $25\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $20\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=60+25t-20t=5(12+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min},$ *disinfectant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{4Q}{12+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12.5-\frac{4Q}{12+t}\end{aligned}

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{12+t}\,Q=12.5.

$$

$$V(t)=1200+24t-36t=(1200-12t)\,\text{L}.$$

$$\begin{aligned}Q'_{\text{out}}&=(36\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot(\frac{Q}{1200-12t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\\

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}&=Q'_{\text{in}}-Q'_{\text{out}}\\&=0.96-\frac{3Q}{100-t}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus,

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,3,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$

$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

Note that pure water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of sugar) enters the vat at a rate of $14\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the vat is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we first determine the volume of solution in the vat at time $t.$

The vat initially contains $500\,\text{L}$ of solution; water enters at $14\,\text{L/min}$ and drains out at $10\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the vat after $t$ minutes is 

$$
500+14t-10t=(500+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$

$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{2(125+t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{2(125+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{5}{2(125+t)}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{125+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(125+t)^{5/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains $15\,\text{kg}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=15,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =15 \\ \frac{A}{(125+0)^{5/2}} & =15 \\ A & =15\cdot {125}^{5/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=15{\left(\frac{125}{125+t}\right)}^{5/2}
$$

Finally, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=15{\left(\frac{125}{139}\right)}^{5/2}≈11.50\,\text{kg},
$$

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$ So,

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=14\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=14I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{24}}=24q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
15=14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(15) & =\frac{d}{dt}(14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =14\,\frac{dI}{dt}+24\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+12I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-4t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-4t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{15}{2}-7I-12q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{15}{2}-7I(0)-12q(0) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}-7\cdot 2-12\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{19}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-0}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-4B{e}^{-4t}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{19}{2} & =-3A{e}^{-0}-4B{e}^{-0} \\ -\frac{19}{2} & =-3A-4B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2=A+B \\ -\frac{19}{2}=-3A-4B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-{e}^{-x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\int {e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+J.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

![](images/0f/0f3cf395fe5f442212e057f73ef48ab458370e914424e186611c70f1c9f29953.png)"] [:db/cas 17592186548063 :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ &= \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=224,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{56\,000}{100\,000}=0.56.$

Now, since

$$
np=224(0.56)=125.44>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=224(1-0.56)=98.56>5,
$$

and the $n=224$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,\frac{0.56(1-0.56)}{224}) \\  & ∼N(0.56,0.0011).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If between $112$ and $140$ of subscribers in the sample have a digital subscription, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{112}{224}\le \widehat{\,p} & \le \frac{140}{224} \\ 0.5\le \widehat{\,p} & \le 0.625.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.5\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.625).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.625) & =P(\frac{0.5-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}\le Z\le \frac{0.625-0.56}{\sqrt{0.0011}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.81\le Z\le 1.96) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.96)-P(Z\le -1.81) \\  & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.96)=0.9750,\,Φ(-1.81)=0.0351.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.5\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.625) & =Φ(1.96)-Φ(-1.81) \\  & =0.9750-0.0351 \\  & =0.9399.\end{aligned}

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=80,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.4.$

Now, since

$$
np=80(0.4)=32>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=80(1-0.4)=48>5,
$$

and $n=80$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0.4,0.0030).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $32$ but fewer than $36$ calls are complaints, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{32}{80}<\widehat{\,p} & <\frac{36}{80} \\ 0.4\le \widehat{\,p} & \le 0.45.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.4<\widehat{\,p}<0.45).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.45) & =P(\frac{0.4-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}<Z<\frac{0.45-0.4}{\sqrt{0.0030}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<0.91) \\  & =P(Z<0.91)-P(Z<0.00) \\  & =Φ(0.91)-Φ(0.00)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

We focus on the term with the exponential ${e}^{-2s}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:

$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s-3)$ and a repeated linear factor ${s}^{2},$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{1}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{C}{s-3}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
1=As(s-3)+B(s-3)+C{s}^{2}.
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=0,$ we have

$$

$$

- Setting $s=3,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(0)+C(9)\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+C\,⟹\,A=-C=-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

$$

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+1)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{2}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}=\frac{A}{s+1}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
2=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+1).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-1,$ we have

$$

- $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,2\pi ).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $2\pi $-periodicity:

$$
f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $2\pi $-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $2\pi $-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi )=f\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=F\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=F\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"." "Since $f$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

$$

\displaystyle 60\,\text{g/L}\cdot\frac{1\,\text{kg}}{1000\,\text{g}}=0.06\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.06\,\text{kg/L}$ of the salt enters the tank at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =2.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $560\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{560}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{40Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{14}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =2.4-\frac{Q}{14}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}Q=2.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/14},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{14}\alpha =2.4\,⟹\,\alpha =33.6.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=33.6.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/14}+33.6.
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $16\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=16,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =16 \\ A{e}^{-0/14}+33.6 & =16 \\ A & =-17.6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=33.6-17.6{e}^{-t/14}
$$

Finally,  the amount of salt in the tank $2$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
Q(2)=33.6-17.6{e}^{-2/14}≈18.34\,\text{kg},
$$

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 6 y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 6 y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 6 y)^{2}-(y)=0\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v=u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=16.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=u^{2} \\ v &=16\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 4,16).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-4\le u\le 4,\,u^{2}\le v\le 16\}.
$$

![](images/38/387e22e062c4ff7f24d26561fe369041f11f59a2b0305f8dc7b3ce49d411031a.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\ &=\begin{vmatrix}1&-6\\0&1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}[\int_{u^{2}}^{16}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}[v]_{u^{2}}^{16}du \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}(16)-(u^{2})du \\ &=1\int_{-4}^{4}(16 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 16 u]_{-4}^{4} \\ &=1(((64)+\left(- \frac{64}{3}\right))-((-64)+\left(\frac{64}{3}\right))) \\ &=1\left(\frac{256}{3}\right) \\ &=\frac{256}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" "The area of the required region is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y & =2 \\ y & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =3{x}^{2}+20xy \\ C & =3{x}^{2}+20x\cdot \frac{2}{{x}^{2}} \\ C & =3{x}^{2}+\frac{40}{x}.\end{aligned}

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ \\ &= ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ \\ &= \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{a}_{7}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡(7x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(14x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{28}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{28}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(28\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\frac{\pi }{2})}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =2(x-1) \\ z & =2x-2\end{aligned}

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
