$$"]] "assertions" [[17592186539387 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,5\le v\le 6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{3y}{{x}^{2}}\right)}=-\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(xy)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{{v}^{2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}\left[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\right]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1}^{4}]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}{\int }_{5}^{6}{v}^{2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}\,{|}_{5}^{6} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{9}\cdot (216-125) \\  & =\frac{182\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186539398 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir minus the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of disinfectant enters the reservoir at a rate of $25\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *disinfectant* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right)\cdot \left(25\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right)\cdot \left(25\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =12.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $25\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $20\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=60+25t-20t=5(12+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min},$ *disinfectant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(20\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{5(12+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{4Q}{12+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12.5-\frac{4Q}{12+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{12+t}\,Q=12.5.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 4/(12+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{4\operatorname{ln}⁡|12+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(12+t)^{4}} \\  & =(12+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(12+t)^{4}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(12+t)^{4}\cdot \left(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{4}{12+t}\,Q\right) & =(12+t)^{4}\cdot 12.5 \\ (12+t)^{4}\frac{dQ}{dt}+4(12+t)^{3}Q & =12.5(12+t)^{4} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{4}) & =12.5(12+t)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{4})\,dt & =\int 12.5(12+t)^{4}\,dt \\ Q(12+t)^{4} & =12.5\cdot \frac{1}{5}(12+t)^{5}+C \\ Q(t) & =2.5(12+t)+\frac{C}{(12+t)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $10\,\text{lb}$ of disinfectant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 2.5(12+0)+\frac{C}{(12+0)^{4}} & =10 \\ 30+\frac{C}{(12)^{4}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{12}^{4}} & =-20 \\ C & =-20(12)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2.5(12+t)-\frac{20(12)^{4}}{(12+t)^{4}} \\  & =2.5(12+t)-20{\left(\frac{12}{12+t}\right)}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 60+25{t}_{o}-20{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 60+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =120 \\ {t}_{o} & =24\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(24) & =2.5(12+24)-20{\left(\frac{12}{12+24}\right)}^{4} \\  & =90-20{\left(\frac{12}{36}\right)}^{4} \\  & ≈89.8\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186539401 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir minus the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir.

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.8\,\text{lb/gal}$ of disinfectant enters the reservoir at a rate of $20\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *disinfectant* enters the reservoir is 

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which disinfectant exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which disinfectant leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $300\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $20\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=300+20t-12t=8(37.5+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *disinfectant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{8(37.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{1.5Q}{37.5+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =16-\frac{1.5Q}{37.5+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1.5}{37.5+t}\,Q=16.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 1.5/(37.5+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{1.5\operatorname{ln}⁡|37.5+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(37.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =(37.5+t)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(37.5+t)^{1.5}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(37.5+t)^{1.5}\cdot \left(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1.5}{37.5+t}\,Q\right) & =(37.5+t)^{1.5}\cdot 16 \\ (37.5+t)^{1.5}\frac{dQ}{dt}+1.5(37.5+t)^{0.5}Q & =16(37.5+t)^{1.5} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(37.5+t)^{1.5}) & =16(37.5+t)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(37.5+t)^{1.5})\,dt & =\int 16(37.5+t)^{1.5}\,dt \\ Q(37.5+t)^{1.5} & =16\cdot \frac{1}{2.5}(37.5+t)^{2.5}+C \\ Q(t) & =6.4(37.5+t)+\frac{C}{(37.5+t)^{1.5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $160\,\text{lb}$ of disinfectant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=160,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =160 \\ 6.4(37.5+0)+\frac{C}{(37.5+0)^{1.5}} & =160 \\ 240+\frac{C}{(37.5)^{1.5}} & =160 \\ \frac{C}{{37.5}^{1.5}} & =-80 \\ C & =-80(37.5)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =6.4(37.5+t)-\frac{80(37.5)^{1.5}}{(37.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =6.4(37.5+t)-80{\left(\frac{37.5}{37.5+t}\right)}^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $368\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=368$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =368 \\ 300+20{t}_{o}-12{t}_{o} & =368 \\ 300+8{t}_{o} & =368 \\ 8{t}_{o} & =68 \\ {t}_{o} & =8.5\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of disinfectant in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(8.5) & =6.4(37.5+8.5)-80{\left(\frac{37.5}{37.5+8.5}\right)}^{1.5} \\  & =294.4-80{\left(\frac{37.5}{46}\right)}^{1.5} \\  & ≈235.5\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186539408 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =10\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $213\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $9\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=213+15t-9t=6(35.5+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{6(35.5+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(9\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{6(35.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(9\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{6(35.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{9Q}{6(35.5+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{1.5Q}{35.5+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =10-\frac{1.5Q}{35.5+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1.5}{35.5+t}\,Q=10.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 1.5/(35.5+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{1.5\operatorname{ln}⁡|35.5+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(35.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =(35.5+t)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(35.5+t)^{1.5}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(35.5+t)^{1.5}\cdot \left(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1.5}{35.5+t}\,Q\right) & =(35.5+t)^{1.5}\cdot 10 \\ (35.5+t)^{1.5}\frac{dQ}{dt}+1.5(35.5+t)^{0.5}Q & =10(35.5+t)^{1.5} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(35.5+t)^{1.5}) & =10(35.5+t)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(35.5+t)^{1.5})\,dt & =\int 10(35.5+t)^{1.5}\,dt \\ Q(35.5+t)^{1.5} & =10\cdot \frac{1}{2.5}(35.5+t)^{2.5}+C \\ Q(t) & =4(35.5+t)+\frac{C}{(35.5+t)^{1.5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $\frac{142}{3}\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=\frac{142}{3},$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =\frac{142}{3} \\ 4(35.5+0)+\frac{C}{(35.5+0)^{1.5}} & =\frac{142}{3} \\ 142+\frac{C}{(35.5)^{1.5}} & =\frac{142}{3} \\ \frac{C}{(35.5)^{1.5}} & =-\frac{284}{3} \\ C & =-\frac{284}{3}(35.5)^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4(35.5+t)-\frac{\frac{284}{3}(35.5)^{1.5}}{(35.5+t)^{1.5}} \\  & =4(35.5+t)-\frac{284}{3}{\left(\frac{35.5}{35.5+t}\right)}^{1.5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =8.4-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=8.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q\right) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 8.4 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =8.4(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =8.4(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 8.4(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =8.4\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $24\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=24,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =24 \\ 2.8(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =24 \\ 84+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =24 \\ \frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =-60 \\ C & =-60(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)-\frac{60(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =2.8(30+t)-60{\left(\frac{30}{30+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $220\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=220$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =220 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =100 \\ {t}_{o} & =25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =2.8(30+25)-60{\left(\frac{30}{30+25}\right)}^{2} \\  & =154-60{\left(\frac{30}{55}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈136.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186541077 :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(x)=4x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}$ and $g(x)=2x.$

$$"] [17592186541081 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$

which is equivalent to

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+y.$ So,

$$"] [17592186541084 :question/problem "For two independent random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{Var}[X]=16$ and $\text{Var}[Y]=6.$ Find $\text{Var}\left[\frac{3}{8}X+\frac{1}{2}Y\right].$"] [17592186541084 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are independent variables, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$"] [17592186541090 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:

So, we can write

$$

$$"] [17592186541094 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $1.25\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminant enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right)\cdot \left(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right)\cdot \left(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =15\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $8\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=120+12t-8t=4(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =15-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=15.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q\right) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 15 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =15(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =15(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 15(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =15\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =5(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $40\,\text{lb}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=40,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =40 \\ 5(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =40 \\ 150+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =40 \\ \frac{C}{{30}^{2}} & =-110 \\ C & =-110(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =5(30+t)-\frac{110(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =5(30+t)-110{\left(\frac{30}{30+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =60 \\ {t}_{o} & =15\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(15) & =5(30+15)-110{\left(\frac{30}{30+15}\right)}^{2} \\  & =225-110{\left(\frac{30}{45}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈176.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186541096 :question/worked-solution "The horizontal velocity of the eagle is given by ${x}^{′}(t),$ where

The formula for the derivative of arctangent is

Therefore, the horizontal velocity of the eagle is given by the function ${x}^{′}(t)=\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}}\,\text{m/s}.$"] [17592186541100 :question/worked-solution "The tangent line approximation to $y(t)$ at the point $a=5$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =2\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}\right)}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right)}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{2}-2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\left(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =\left(1-2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-1 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\left(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =\left(1-2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,\sqrt{3}).$

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}x+3\sqrt{3} \\ y & =3\sqrt{3}x+4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$"] [17592186544863 :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j}\le 8-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to 

$$
8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j}\le 8-({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\left[8-({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\right]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le 8{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({2}^{2}-{0}^{2})(3-2)=4 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({3}^{2}-{2}^{2})(2-0)=5 \\ 8{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =8(2-0)(3-2)=16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 16-4-5\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 7\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=7.
$$"] [17592186544868 :question/worked-solution "First, we want to find the interval for $\theta $ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or

Since there are $5$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{total}} & =5\cdot {A}_{\text{petal}} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}{(4\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5\cdot \frac{16}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}{\sin }^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =40\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(10\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =20{\left(\theta -\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10\theta )\right)|}_{0}^{\pi /5} \\  & =20\left[\left(\frac{\pi }{5}-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )\right)-\left(0-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\right)\right] \\  & =20\cdot \frac{\pi }{5} \\  & =4\pi \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186544869 :question/worked-solution "Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}+1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot 1+({t}^{3}+1-1)\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={\left[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186544883 :question/worked-solution "First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-2={X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-4=-2{X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$

Rewriting the system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(s-1){X}_{1}(s)-3{X}_{2}(s)=2 \\ 2{X}_{1}(s)+(s-1){X}_{2}(s)=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, from the second equation, we have 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{4-(s-1){X}_{2}(s)}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(s-1)\left[\frac{4-(s-1){X}_{2}(s)}{2}\right]-3{X}_{2}(s) & =2 \\ 4(s-1)-(s-1)^{2}{X}_{2}(s)-6{X}_{2}(s) & =4 \\ 4(s-1)-[(s-1)^{2}+6]{X}_{2}(s) & =4 \\ 4(s-1)-({s}^{2}-2s+7){X}_{2}(s) & =4 \\ -({s}^{2}-2s+7){X}_{2}(s) & =4-4(s-1) \\ -({s}^{2}-2s+7){X}_{2}(s) & =-4s+8 \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{4(s-2)}{{s}^{2}-2s+7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${X}_{1}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{4-(s-1){X}_{2}(s)}{2} \\  & =\frac{4-(s-1)\cdot \frac{4(s-2)}{{s}^{2}-2s+7}}{2} \\  & =\frac{4({s}^{2}-2s+7)-(s-1)\cdot 4(s-2)}{2({s}^{2}-2s+7)} \\  & =\frac{4{s}^{2}-8s+28-4(s-1)(s-2)}{2({s}^{2}-2s+7)} \\  & =\frac{4s+20}{2({s}^{2}-2s+7)} \\  & =\frac{2(s+5)}{{s}^{2}-2s+7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{2(s+5)}{{s}^{2}-2s+7},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{4(s-2)}{{s}^{2}-2s+7}.
$$"] [17592186544996 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u-v,\,3u+2,\,u+2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+2v)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨2,\,3,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u+2),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+2v)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨6,\,-5,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨6,\,-5,\,3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{70}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$"] [17592186545007 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

rounded to $2$ decimal places."] [17592186546978 :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.5947.$"] [17592186547077 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of sugar) enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $450\,\text{gal}$ of solution.

- Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $15t\,\text{gal}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $10t\,\text{gal}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
450+15t-10t=(450+5t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Then, since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{90+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =0-\frac{2Q}{90+t} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t}\,Q.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{2}{90+t}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{90+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(90+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ \frac{A}{(90+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ A & =18\cdot {90}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=18{\left(\frac{90}{90+t}\right)}^{2}
$$"] [17592186547079 :question/worked-solution "The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](images/e4/e44f91621134e91a9f742811897940b87ffc24bea4b15100e43d2aa15a8c4330.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=14\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=14I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{24}}=24q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
15=14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(15) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}\right) \\ 0 & =14\,\frac{dI}{dt}+24\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+12I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-4t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-4t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{15}{2}-7I-12q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{15}{2}-7I(0)-12q(0) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}-7\cdot 2-12\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{19}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-0}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-4B{e}^{-4t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{19}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{19}{2} & =-3A{e}^{-0}-4B{e}^{-0} \\ -\frac{19}{2} & =-3A-4B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2=A+B \\ -\frac{19}{2}=-3A-4B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $B=\frac{7}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-4t}.
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $0.3$ seconds, in amperes, is

$$
I(0.3)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-0.9}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-1.2}≈0.444,
$$

rounded to three decimal places."] [17592186547084 :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

![](images/f5/f5de147e69639b8cfbbe591241603d437650b88d523058df09dd30b60a6482da.png)"] [17592186547996 :question/worked-solution "The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ &= \left\langle \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\right\rangle  \\ &= \left\langle \frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\right\rangle +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ \\ &= \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{3}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\left[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\right]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(12\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"] [17592186548000 :question/worked-solution "The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 1$ is 

$$

$$"] [17592186548004 :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the indefinite integral by $$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =\left\langle \frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 2v & u\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & v \\ 2v & u\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨-2{v}^{2},\,-u,\,2v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186552433 :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $$
\displaystyle L(x)={\left(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b\right)}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{2}Ax-b\right)

$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}?
$$"] [17592186552433 :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=\frac{1}{2}Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

we have that

$$"] [17592186552449 :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N\left(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\right),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the population proportion is $p=0.3.$

Now, since

$$
np=60(0.3)=18>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=60(1-0.3)=42>5,
$$

and $n=60$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N\left(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\right) \\  & ∼N\left(0.3,\frac{0.3(1-0.3)}{60}\right) \\  & ∼N(0.3,0.0035).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\widehat{\,p}>0.4).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}>0.4) & =P\left(Z>\frac{0.4-0.3}{\sqrt{0.0035}}\right) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.69) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.69) \\  & =1-Φ(1.69)\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186552452 :question/worked-solution "The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-as}\,L\{g(t+a)\},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L\{u(t-4)({t}^{2}+6t+2)\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=4,$ and we have 

$$
L\{u(t-4)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-4s}\,L\{g(t+4)\},
$$

where $g(t)={t}^{2}+6t+2.$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+4) & =(t+4)^{2}+6(t+4)+2 \\  & ={t}^{2}+8t+16\,+\,6t+24\,+\,2 \\  & ={t}^{2}+14t+42.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t+4)\} & =L\{{t}^{2}+14t+42\} \\  & =L\{{t}^{2}\}+14L\{t\}+42L\{1\} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+14\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+42\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{42}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-4)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-4s}\,L\{g(t+4)\} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\left(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{42}{s}\right).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186552455 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the transformation $Y={X}^{2}+1$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-2<x<2.$ 

![](images/8a/8a03bd46aa6d415d8e1a49ff74557886702c1dc4bc9164ce2a5a1252874e1b4e.png)

Moreover, for $-2<x<2,$  we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $1\le y<5.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $1\le y<5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}+1\le y) \\  & =P(-(y-1)^{1/2}\le X\le (y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $1\le y<5,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[{f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2})].\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[{f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\left[\frac{3}{16}{((y-1)^{1/2})}^{2}+\frac{3}{16}{(-(y-1)^{1/2})}^{2}\right] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\left(\frac{3}{16}(y-1)+\frac{3}{16}(y-1)\right) \\  & =\frac{3}{16}(y-1)^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{y-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{y-1}, & 1\le y<5 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$"] [17592186552463 :question/worked-solution "To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- First, we find an expression for ${F}_{Y}$ in terms of ${F}_{X},$ where ${F}_{Y}$ and ${F}_{X}$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $Y$ and $X,$ respectively.

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that $Y=\frac{X}{3}$ is a strictly decreasing function of $X.$ Moreover, for $0<x<1,$ we have $0<y<\frac{1}{3}.$

![](images/42/42a3c2510927b66842ec0360eabfb169a306ccaf52292132f31769036e608e69.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<\frac{1}{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P\left(\frac{X}{3}\le y\right) \\  & =P(X\le 3y) \\  & ={F}_{X}(3y).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<\frac{1}{3},$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =3\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(3y) \\  & =3\cdot {f}_{X}(3y).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =3\cdot {f}_{X}(3y) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{3}{2}(1-(3y)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(1-9{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}(1-9{y}^{2}), & \,0<y<\frac{1}{3} \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$"] [17592186552467 :question/worked-solution "To compute the probability density function of a random variable $Y,$ where $Y=u(X)$ is a continuous, strictly monotonic function of a continuous random variable $X,$ we follow two steps:

- Then, we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ to get the probability density function ${f}_{Y}.$

Before we start, note that $Y=2X$ is a strictly increasing function of $X.$  Moreover, for $1<x<2,$ we have $2<y<4.$

![](images/60/60342277a025cb26cebab2ac534fad4aa1b49fc2285571c303c4e829eb464606.png)

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $2<y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(2X\le y) \\  & =P\left(X\le \frac{y}{2}\right) \\  & ={F}_{X}\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $2<y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}\left(\frac{y}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {f}_{X}\left(\frac{y}{2}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {f}_{X}\left(\frac{y}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)}{3} \\  & =\frac{y}{6}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{6}, & \,2<y<4 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$"] [17592186552469 :question/worked-solution "First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=\frac{1}{2}|X-1|$ over the interval $0<x<4.$

$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<\frac{1}{2},$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

Consequently, $g(y)=\frac{1}{2}.$"] [17592186552477 :question/worked-solution "First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=(X-3)^{2}$ over the interval $0<x<5.$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

Consequently, $h(y)=\frac{1}{4}(2y+1).$"] [17592186552492 :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x,

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.

Therefore,

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186552499 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the transformation $Y={(1-X)}^{2}$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-1<x<3.$ 

![](images/03/03718360bf910c74c22b36f34ad2f63bfad6d9387c0cdc62d3fb366a52f356c9.png)

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186553508 :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- The flux $$

$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

$$

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+j+t\cdot [(5\,i+4j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$

$$

$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((16{t}^{2}+8t+1)\cdot (3)-(-24{t}^{2}-14t-2)\cdot (4))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,144{t}^{2}+80t+11\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[48{t}^{3}+40{t}^{2}+11t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(48+40+11) \\  & =99.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=99.
$$"] [17592186553509 :question/worked-solution "To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$

We focus on the term with the exponential ${e}^{-2s}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s-3)$ and a repeated linear factor ${s}^{2},$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{1}{{s}^{2}(s-3)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{C}{s-3}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
1=As(s-3)+B(s-3)+C{s}^{2}.
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=0,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(-3)+C(0)\,⟹\,B=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

- Setting $s=3,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(0)+C(9)\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+C\,⟹\,A=-C=-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=-\frac{1}{9s}-\frac{1}{3{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{9(s-3)}.
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{1}{9s}-\frac{1}{3{s}^{2}}+\frac{1}{9(s-3)}\} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{t}{3}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-2s}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=2.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-2)f(t-2) & =u(t-2)\left(-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{t-2}{3}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}\right) \\  & =u(t-2)\left(-\frac{3t-5}{9}+\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=5{e}^{3t}+u(t-2)\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3(t-2)}-\frac{3t-5}{9}.
$$"] [17592186553511 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$

which is equivalent to

$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/84/848dfedddea9803dcf39b4624f2966b63f080920ed19b875dc691e8fe9d3b038.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y.$ So,

$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}\left(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}\right)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}.$"] [17592186553515 :question/worked-solution "The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})Δx,

where $n$ is the number of subintervals,   ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx$, and  $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

The endpoints indicate that $a=-2$ and $b=1,$ so the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{1-(-2)}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.

Therefore, using sigma notation, the left Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})Δx & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f(a+jΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f\left(-2+j\cdot \frac{3}{n}\right)\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f\left(-2+\frac{3j}{n}\right)\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}{\left(-2+\frac{3j}{n}+2\right)}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{3}{n}{\left(\frac{3j}{n}\right)}^{3} \\  & ={\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{3}{n}\cdot \frac{27{j}^{3}}{{n}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{81}{{n}^{4}}{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}\,{j}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186553521 :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic secant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(2x+1)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsech}⁡(2x+1)) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}-\left(-\frac{1}{(2x+1)\sqrt{1-(2x+1)^{2}}}\right)\cdot (2x+1)^{′} \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}+\frac{1}{(2x+1)\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}-4x-1}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}+\frac{2}{(2x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-4x}} \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{-4x(x+1)}}\right) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+1}\left(1+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{-x(x+1)}}\right).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186553530 :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables with the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.

Let's draw the region $D$ in the $uv$-plane where the function $f(u,v)$ is nonzero. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

For the purposes of computation, we're only interested in the region inside $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. This is given by

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v & ={\int }_{0}^{y}{\int }_{1}^{x}\frac{1}{4}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡v{\int }_{1}^{x}u\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡v{\left[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}\right]}_{u=1}^{u=x}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡v({x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1){\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)[\operatorname{sin}⁡v]_{v=0}^{v=y} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186553533 :question/worked-solution "The left Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$"] [17592186553543 :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}+y={u}_{\pi /2}(t)\cdot \sin \,(2t-\pi )\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /2}(t)=u\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ is the unit step function.

You're given that the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ is

$$

$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as

$$

Find the function $g(t).$ 

Hint: You may make use of the following results:

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$"] [17592186553543 :question/worked-solution "To solve the initial value problem, we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s).$

To find the inverse transform, we first ignore the exponential term ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ (which corresponds to a time shift) and focus on the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{2}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+1)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+4),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{2}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+1)}=\frac{A}{s+1}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+4}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
2=A({s}^{2}+4)+(Bs+C)(s+1).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-1,$ we have

$$
2=A((-1)^{2}+4)+0\,⟹\,5A=2\,⟹\,A=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,B=-A=-\frac{2}{5}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have

$$
2=4A+C\,⟹\,C=2-\frac{8}{5}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{-s+1}{{s}^{2}+4}\right)=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}\right).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{2}{5}\left({L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+1}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+4}\}\right) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\left({e}^{-t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-\pi s/2}$ term in $Y(s).$ By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)f\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =u\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\cdot \frac{2}{5}\left[{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}-\cos \,\left(2\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\sin \,\left(2\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\right)\right].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-\pi /2))=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-\pi /2))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\cdot \frac{2}{5}\left[{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\,u\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)(2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the form given in the problem statement $$
\displaystyle y(t)=\frac{1}{5}u\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\cdot g(t),
$$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$"] [17592186553547 :question/worked-solution "To solve the initial value problem, we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s).$

To find the inverse transform, we first ignore the exponential term ${e}^{-3s}$ (which corresponds to a time shift) and focus on the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{(s-4)(s+5)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains distinct linear factors, the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{1}{(s-4)(s+5)}=\frac{A}{s-4}+\frac{B}{s+5}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
1=A(s+5)+B(s-4).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A$ and $B.$

- Setting $s=4,$ we have

$$
1=A(9)+B(0)\,⟹\,A=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

- Setting $s=-5,$ we have

$$
1=A(0)+B(-9)\,⟹\,B=-\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{9}\left(\frac{1}{s-4}-\frac{1}{s+5}\right).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{1}{9}\left({L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+5}\}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{-5t}).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-3s}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=3.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-3)f(t-3) & =u(t-3)\cdot \frac{1}{9}({e}^{4(t-3)}-{e}^{-5(t-3)}).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=u(t-3)\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=\frac{1}{9}({e}^{4(t-3)}-{e}^{-5(t-3)}).
$$"] [17592186553574 :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s
$$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{{y}^{3}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,3)$ to $B(5,3)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](images/3d/3d64ffb0e4cc313a2857d1c20922c1202619d0bdeb3d97f2808b4995c99f7f9f.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+3\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+3\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=-\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=-\sqrt{27}, \\ Q(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}=((4t+1)-1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\sqrt{27})\cdot (0)-(16{t}^{2})\cdot (4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-64{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\left[-\frac{64{t}^{3}}{3}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-\frac{64}{3}.
$$"] [17592186553576 :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}\left(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}\right)\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e1/e1e4386f3cc75afb63823d74daa27b517e8e47d51fa08c5c9e5bf3ca6f3ca88c.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{6},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 3,\,-2\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}\left(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}\right)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{6}-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186553578 :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}+4y={u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,\left(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3}\right)\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /3}(t)=u\,\left(t-\frac{\pi }{3}\right)$ is the unit step function.

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0

This represents a circle of radius $1.$"] [17592186557577 :question/worked-solution "The feed concentration must use kilograms: $$
\displaystyle 60\,\text{g/L}\cdot\frac{1\,\text{kg}}{1000\,\text{g}}=0.06\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.06\,\text{kg/L}$ of the salt enters the tank at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right)\cdot \left(40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0.06\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right)\cdot \left(40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =2.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $560\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{560}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $40\,\text{L/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(40\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right) \\  & =\left(40\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{40Q}{560}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{14}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =2.4-\frac{Q}{14}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}Q=2.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{14}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/14},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{14}\alpha =2.4\,⟹\,\alpha =33.6.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=33.6.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/14}+33.6.
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $16\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=16,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =16 \\ A{e}^{-0/14}+33.6 & =16 \\ A & =-17.6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=33.6-17.6{e}^{-t/14}
$$

Finally,  the amount of salt in the tank $2$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
Q(2)=33.6-17.6{e}^{-2/14}≈18.34\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places."] [17592186557578 :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of dye in the vat at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative

rounded to two decimal places."] [17592186557580 :question/worked-solution "The feed concentration must use kilograms: $$

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186558981 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint_S\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D\left\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\right\|\,\mathrm{d}A.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u &=\left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial u},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\right\rangle \\  &=\left\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(u + v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(3 - v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(3 u + 5 v + 1\right)\right\rangle \\  &=\langle 1,\,0,\,3\rangle \\ \mathbf r_v &=\left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial y}{\partial v},\,\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\right\rangle \\  &=\left\langle \frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(u + v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(3 - v\right),\,\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\left(3 u + 5 v + 1\right)\right\rangle \\  &=\langle 1,\,-1,\,5\rangle\end{aligned}

$$

and
